Condenser microphones are more sensitive and have a wider frequency response than dynamic microphones, making them suitable for capturing detailed audio in quieter environments. However, they are generally more fragile and require a power source to operate. Another type of microphone is the "ribbon" microphone, which uses a thin strip of metal suspended between magnets to capture sound. Ribbon microphones have a distinct character and warmth to their sound, but they are also extremely delicate and sensitive to the environment around them. Finally, there are also specialized microphones such as lavalier microphones that can be clipped onto clothing, and shotgun microphones that can be mounted on a camera to capture directional audio from a distance. article: Positive-definite kernel functions are fundamental elements of kernel methods and Gaussian processes. A well-known construction of such functions comes from Bochner's characterization, which connects a positive-definite function with a probability measure. Specifically, an integrable function k: Rn - R is positive-definite if and only if it has a representation of the form: k (x) R exp (i x,) d where i is the imaginary unit, , denotes the inner product in Rn, and is a probability measure on Rn. This is known as Bochner's theorem. Intuitively, this means that a positive-definite kernel function can be written as a superposition of complex exponentials, where the frequency of each exponential is sampled from a probability distribution. The function k describes how these complex exponentials interfere with each other to produce the final kernel. This characterization has important implications for kernel methods and Gaussian processes. For instance, it allows us to construct arbitrarily complex kernels by choosing appropriate probability measures . Furthermore, it provides a theoretical justification for why kernel methods work well on many practical problems, since the underlying physics of many real-world systems can be modeled by superpositions of waves or oscillations. article: Traditional approaches for handwritten Chinese character recognition suffer in classifying similar characters. In this paper, we propose to discriminate similar handwritten Chinese characters by using weakly supervised learning. Our approach learns a discriminative SVM for each similar pair which simultaneously localizes the discriminative region of similar character and makes the classification. For the first time, similar handwritten Chinese character recognition (SHCCR) is formulated as an optimization problem extended from SVM. We also propose a novel feature descriptor, Gradient Context, and apply bag-of-words model to represent regions with different scales. In our method, we do not need to select a sized-fixed sub-window to differentiate similar characters. This? unconstrained? property makes our method well adapted to high variance in the size and position of discriminative regions in similar handwritten Chinese characters. We evaluate our proposed approach over the CASIA Chinese character data set and the results show that our method outperforms the state of the art.

article: I walked down the sidewalk on my way to work just like I did every Thursday, there wouldn't be any work to do once I got there or anyone to notice that I had dutifully showed up to do it. I could walk down the middle of the street if I wanted to, there was no one there to hit me with their car if I did. Most of the cars were long gone since the city's population had performed a mass exodus. The last one I'd seen had belonged to an IH official who had driven through as quickly as they could, megaphone declaring the all clear on repeat. Looking for survivors, maybe. I hadn't seen any. That was nearly a week ago. I wouldn't be able to catch the street car down on Madison, that was upsetting. When I reached my regular stop, I paused for a long minute. No one was scuffing their feet along, no one was talking on their phone, no one was even breathing except for me. I held my breath to silence the unseemly noise but the lacking made my heartbeat all the more audible. The street lights changed but nothing happened. The burble of a pigeon taking off ripped a girly little yip from my throat that echoed off the surrounding buildings. I should really get going or I would be late. I made a snap decision and cautiously stepped into the road to walk along the thin metal tracks upon which the street car routinely clattered down accompanied by the nearly inaudible hum-snap of the electrical cables that hung above the tracks. I imagined that I could feel it and the cold clenching in my chest eased a bit. 8:16. I would walk faster. It wasn't a good day to be late, that just wouldn't do. It mattered not that my boss and co-workers were all probably dead, dying, or gone far away where the forgetting couldn't get them. It had been funny at first, or at least it had been funny to other people. I had seen them laughing. People forgot to microwave their frozen dinners, or to sharpen their pencils, or that they had to go to a special room to use the bathroom. But then they forgot what they were supposed to do before they crossed the street. They didn't look both ways, check their shoes, put both hands in their pockets, or look up to see if it might start to rain soon. It would probably have been better for the afflicted if they had forgotten to breathe and passed away quickly, it would probably even have been better if they had forgotten to eat and starved to death. Would have been more humane. 8:24. I couldn't let myself be the appropriate amount of sad that their plight demanded. They needn't have died but..... there were just too many of them. Too many to look after the way a person needed. I hopped back up onto the sidewalk where I would walk East past the park two blocks until I arrived at the building where I worked. I ran my fingers over the bars of the black wrought iron fence that served as a border between pavement and grass. One..... Two..... Three..... 8:32. They had to leave some of them behind. I'm sure they took as many as they could. I knew about the one that slept beneath the park bench ten yards from the fence, I held my breath against the smell and averted my gaze. Thirty-Nine..... Forty..... Forty-One..... Just walk. Count and walk. Tears pricked my eyes an instant before they fell down my face, they left so quickly that they barely brushed my cheeks on their way to the sidewalk. I didn't want to think about what he might have forgotten or about who might have left him behind. Mr. Hawley who ate his lunch on that picnic bench every day. I shook the thoughts from my mind. My hair flew around my face. I ran my fingers through the lot of it in chunks to assure myself that it had not mussed. Fifty-Seven..... I could always take comfort in my knowing. I knew that there were this many iron bars, that the door to my office building was unsmudged by fingers, my chair was clean and tucked. It was mine, no one else had sat in it. My bag went under the desk. The bathroom was two doors down to my right. 8:40. My hands were washed against the day. I wondered when the water would stop. My head spun and my spine jerked at the thought. I clenched my teeth and willed the sweating to stop. I held my knees until the attack had had its fill. It would be okay, the stores were full for all that the world had turned upon its ear. For all that starving people had sat on picnic benches across the street from them, wanting their food. 8:48. I stood in the break room waiting for 9:00. At 9:00, I could punch my card, I would hear the noise that the puncher made and then I could go home. I wasn't so far gone that I couldn't go home but far enough to need the noise that signaled the beginning of a Thursday as it had for the past nine years. I walked past the park using my left hand to touch the bars this time. I wished that I could walk across the street, maybe I wouldn't be able to smell Mr. Hawley if I were walking over there. 87 bars. I could never forget.

"If I hadn't'covered my sorry ass', I'd be dead. They'd know I got in. I fucked enough shit up in there that it was literally impossible to miss. And do you know what would have happened if they got me?" Again, silence. "You'd be dead. Jon would be dead. Sue, Tim, everyone on our fucking floor. Gone. People were watching, but nobody really cared. All people wanted to know was whether one of us was going to jump. No attention was paid to what was actually going on. "So what if they get into your shit? You work on a five-year-old crappy Dell, and do absolutely fuck-all! The worst they'd find on there is a saved game of Minesweeper!" I snapped back around and almost marched halfway over to her. "The hell would you know about what I do all day? I have access to every system this goddamn place runs! We get hacked, we lose everything!" She gazed up at the sky. Obviously, none of this was going in. I came closer. "Look. People invest their entire life savings with this place. We have the power to ruin people's lives. We can turn people out of their houses." "You work in IT at a bank! Why the fuck did people die?" I sighed. I knew this was coming. "I fucked up." "We all know! That's why we're in this mess! But it still doesn't explain why people got killed!" "No. You think that's a fuck-up. You have no idea what I did." She ran over to me. I could see her breath in the air as she jogged. "About three months ago, that time the network went down. I got it back up and said everything was fine." "Yes..." she replied, not sure where I was going with this. "I didn't notice it at first. But I left a gaping security hole in our servers. Someone broke in. A team of people, probably." "What the fuck did you do?!" she asked, agitated. I turned away again, looked up at the sky, and shouted. "I lost thirteen billion dollars!" The silence was twice as uncomfortable as the last, and was a good ten seconds long before she spoke again. "How the fuck did that lead to deaths?" She was whispering now, obviously not wanting to be overheard. I probably shouldn't have shouted that to the heavens, with hindsight. "I don't know. I didn't think. It was an impulse; I sent people after them. I did everything I could to trace them and sent people there. How was I to know they'd be armed?" I was whispering as well. "So people died. Why did you have to cover your ass?" She was like a child listening to a grandparent tell them a story about the war, except a lot more eager. "I..... I had to get the money back," I explained, hesitantly. "I didn't know what to do. I got it from wherever I could." "I still don't understand why you couldn't have saved them as well!" She was shouting again. Probably a bad move. "I tried! I failed!" She was shaking her head. "I can only do so much. But don't you for a second think I only saved myself." "Oh yeah?" she retorted. "Who the fuck else did you save?" "We're still in business. Nobody else died. And now, nobody but you knows what I did." She stepped back in stunned silence. "I can't deal with this any more," I half-said. I'm not sure if the words actually came out of my mouth. I jogged over to the stairwell. The main approximation tool in all of the approaches is the singular value decomposition, and they are therefore well suited to floating point implementation in computer aided geometric design (CAGD) systems. We unify the approaches under the names of commonly known polynomial basis functions, and consider various theoretical and practical aspects of the algorithms. We offer new methods for a least squares approach to approximate implicitization using orthogonal polynomials, which tend to be faster and more numerically stable than some existing algorithms. We propose several simple propositions relating the properties of the polynomial bases to their implicit approximation properties.

article: The Anti-Nuclear Antibody (ANA) clinical pathology test is commonly used to identify the existence of various diseases. A hallmark method for identifying the presence of ANAs is the Indirect Immunofluorescence method on Human Epithelial (HEp-2) cells, due to its high sensitivity and the large range of antigens that can be detected. However, the method suffers from numerous shortcomings, such as being subjective as well as time and labour intensive. Computer Aided Diagnostic (CAD) systems have been developed to address these problems, which automatically classify a HEp-2 cell image into one of its known patterns (eg., speckled, homogeneous). Most of the existing CAD systems use handpicked features to represent a HEp-2 cell image, which may only work in limited scenarios. In this paper, we propose a cell classification system comprised of a dual-region codebook-based descriptor, combined with the Nearest Convex Hull Classifier. We evaluate the performance of several variants of the descriptor on two publicly available datasets: ICPR HEp-2 cell classification contest dataset and the new SNPHEp-2 dataset. To our knowledge, this is the first time codebook-based descriptors are applied and studied in this domain. Experiments show that the proposed system has consistent high performance and is more robust than two recent CAD systems.

article: Two main processes were highlighted in the Microbiology book I have (Bauman, 2006). The first one consists of four basic steps, and the goal is to remove toxins and microorganisms which cause disease. One of the big steps in removing aerobic microorganisms is removing their oxygen source, which prevents them from breaking down nutrients. 1. Primary treatment - Wastewater is pumped into large tanks where it's allowed to settle. Lightweight solids, grease, and floating particles are skimmed off the top, and heavier materials settle on the bottom into sludge. A flocculating agent, alum, is added, which basically makes particles clump together and sink to the bottom of the tank to join the sludge. The sludge is then removed, and the water moves on to further treatment. 2. Secondary treatment - Basically, the water is aerated to facilitate the growth of microbes which will remove dissolved organic materials by metabolizing them into carbon dioxide or water. In the activated sludge system, the water is basically pumped into a sludgy mixture, where the microbes in the sludge start digesting what's left in the water. The water is then moved to an oxygen-free environment, and the sludge does its magic, removing oxygen, "starving" the remaining microbes. Smaller communities sometimes pass it through a sand filter in this step, but it's less effective. 3. Chemical treatment. The water is treated somehow, usually with chlorine, sometimes with UV or ozone. It's then either released into rivers or the ocean, or used to irrigate crops and highway vegetation. 4. Sludge treatment. More microbes are used to break down the sludge into carbon dioxide and other organic materials. The second system is artificial wetlands, which are pretty neat but require a much larger area. Essentially, the water is passed through a series of artificially-constructed ponds where the natural microbiota gradually break down the sediments and wastes. It's then treated (sedimentation, filtration, and disinfection via UV, chlorine, or ozone) and released back into the water supply. Hope this helps!','1. Water is collected in a single big deposit, like an artificial lake, or a tank. 2. Screening: This is when they remove large waste, mainly plastic and other things that don't dissolve in water, including bags, cotton, rags.... etc. This is pretty much like putting water through a sieve. 3. Primary Treatment: This is when they remove solid matter, in other words, poop. We're not worried about making the water drinkable yet, we just want to get the bulk of the waste out. This is done by putting the water into large tanks and literally letting it sit until all the solid sinks to the bottom. 4. Secondary treatment: The water now doesn't have any visible bits of solid, but it's still very filthy. This step is to remove smaller things out of the water, including insects and eggs. The water is put into active lanes and we pump air through the water (Bubbling) to encourage "good bacteria" growth. This bacteria will essentially killreduce 'bad bacteria'. 5. Tertiary treatment: The good bacteria has done it's job and now it needs to go as well. The water is placed back into another tank where it's allowed to settle. The bacteria sinks to the bottom and is removed like sludge from the bottom of the tank. 6. Sludge treatment: The process creates a large amount of waste (Mainly poop and bacteria) which is normally sludgy. The sludge is normally shipped off and either incinerated, or in some placed it gets pumped to gas recycling stations because it can generate a large amount of methane to be used as fuel.

article: Process mining techniques such as process discovery and conformance checking provide insights into actual processes by analyzing event data that are widely available in information systems. These data are very valuable for organizations as they can be used to identify process inefficiencies, bottlenecks, and flaws, which could be addressed to enhance process performance and productivity. Process discovery involves analyzing event logs to automatically generate process models that illustrate how business processes are executed in practice. This provides organizations with a visual representation of their existing processes, allowing them to identify process variations and deviations from ideal processes. By understanding these variations, organizations can identify potential improvements, such as the elimination of unnecessary steps or the automation of certain processes. Conformance checking, on the other hand, compares the actual processes captured in the event logs with the expected processes defined in the process models. This analysis helps identify process deviations and variances, providing organizations with an opportunity to eliminate deviations and improve process compliance. Overall, process mining techniques can help organizations to identify inefficiencies and improve their processes, leading to increased productivity, better customer satisfaction, and ultimately, increased profits.

article: We determine the cost of performing Shor's algorithm for integer factorization on a ternary quantum computer, using two natural models of universal fault-tolerant computing: (i) a model based on magic state distillation that assumes the availability of the ternary Clifford gates, projective measurements, classical control as its natural instrumentation set; (ii) a model based on a metaplectic topological quantum computer (MTQC). A natural choice to implement Shor's algorithm on a ternary quantum computer is to translate the entire arithmetic into a ternary form. However, it is also possible to emulate the standard binary version of the algorithm by encoding each qubit in a three-level system. We compare the two approaches and analyze the complexity of implementing Shor's period finding function in the two models. We also highlight the fact that the cost of achieving universality through magic states in MTQC architecture is asymptotically lower than in generic ternary case.

article: The future of high-performance computing, specifically on future Exascale computers, will presumably see memory capacity and bandwidth fail to keep pace with data generated, for instance, from massively parallel partial differential equation (PDE) systems. Current strategies proposed to address this bottleneck entail the omission of large fractions of data, as well as the incorporation of in situ compression algorithms to avoid overuse of memory. To ensure that post-processing operations are successful, this must be done in a way that a sufficiently accurate representation of the solution is stored. Moreover, in situations where the inputoutput system becomes a bottleneck in analysis, visualization, etc., or the execution of the PDE solver is expensive, the the number of passes made over the data must be minimized. In the interest of addressing this problem, this work focuses on the utility of pass-efficient, parallelizable, low-rank, matrix decomposition methods in compressing high-dimensional simulation data from turbulent flows. A particular emphasis is placed on using coarse representation of the data - compatible with the PDE discretization grid - to accelerate the construction of the low-rank factorization. This includes the presentation of a novel single-pass matrix decomposition algorithm for computing the so-called interpolative decomposition. The methods are described extensively and numerical experiments on two turbulent channel flow data are performed. In the first (unladen) channel flow case, compression factors exceeding 400 are achieved while maintaining accuracy with respect to first- and second-order flow statistics. In the particle-laden case, compression factors of 100 are achieved and the compressed data is used to recover particle velocities. These results show that these compression methods can enable efficient computation of various quantities of interest in both the carrier and disperse phases.

article: Sequence-based place recognition methods for all-weather navigation are well-known for producing state-of-the-art results under challenging day-night or summer-winter transitions. These systems, however, rely on complex handcrafted heuristics for sequential matching - which are applied on top of a pre-computed pairwise similarity matrix between reference and query image sequences of a single route - to further reduce false-positive rates compared to single-frame retrieval methods. As a result, performing multi-frame place recognition can be extremely slow for deployment on autonomous vehicles or evaluation on large datasets, and fail when using relatively short parameter values such as a sequence length of 2 frames. In this paper, we propose DeepSeqSLAM: a trainable CNNRNN architecture for jointly learning visual and positional representations from a single monocular image sequence of a route. We demonstrate our approach on two large benchmark datasets, Nordland and Oxford RobotCar - recorded over 728 km and 10 km routes, respectively, each during 1 year with multiple seasons, weather, and lighting conditions. On Nordland, we compare our method to two state-of-the-art sequence-based methods across the entire route under summer-winter changes using a sequence length of 2 and show that our approach can get over 72 AUC compared to 27 AUC for Delta Descriptors and 2 AUC for SeqSLAM; while drastically reducing the deployment time from around 1 hour to 1 minute against both. The framework code and video are available at mchancan.github.iodeepseqslam

article: Retrieval and content management are assumed to be mutually exclusive. In this paper we suggest that they need not be so. In the usual information retrieval scenario, some information about a document is extracted and indexed to enable searching and retrieval. However, this indexing process typically involves only a small subset of the full content of the document, often ignoring relevant contextual information that may be useful for later retrieval. Content management, on the other hand, focuses on the organization and classification of documents based on their full content, rather than just their metadata. This allows for more fine-grained control over how documents are stored, accessed, and utilized, and can lead to more accurate and efficient retrieval. While these two approaches may seem to be at odds, they can in fact be complementary. By incorporating more detailed content analysis and metadata extraction into content management systems, it is possible to create a hybrid approach that combines the advantages of both. For example, a content management system could use advanced text analysis techniques to automatically tag and categorize documents based on their content, while still allowing users to search for and retrieve documents based on metadata attributes such as author, title, or date. This would enable more granular and nuanced search and retrieval capabilities, allowing users to find the exact information they need more quickly and efficiently. In conclusion, while retrieval and content management have traditionally been seen as separate and distinct processes, there is ample opportunity to combine them in innovative ways that can improve the effectiveness of information management and retrieval.

article: Depends on the windows version, driver version and USB controller firmware. Even if you don't actively try to execute a file on the USB drive, the USB stick could be another type of USB device in disguise. Even if it looks like an USB drive, it could secretly be pretending to be a USB keyboard as well, and send keyboard commands to your machine, and windows would think they were from a real keyboard. It could also attack the USB hardware controller in your PC, if it has a known weakness, or windows' drivers for it, to load data into RAM and then executing it, without actually having to go through the normal file-transfer protocols. No files would be transferred, but for example the area of your RAM that used to hold your Chrome browser now suddenly contains malicious code from your USB device, and the next time your PC tries to access the chrome browser, the machine would accidentally execute the new code that was put there instead. I don't know why you included the size of the USB stick. That makes no difference. Bottom line, you should not insert USB devices you don't know where came from, unless you have a locked down, isolated computer that you don't mind having to wipe and reinstall. Even if you think your system is patched and up to date, there's still a chance that you might encounter malicious software that attacks a weakness that no one (other than those who made the malware) knows of yet. In fact, dropping infected usb devices on purpose in hope that someone will pick them up and check what's on them has been used to get unauthorized access to systems in the past, and I wouldn't be surprised if it's still used today as well.,Yes. Many USB connected devices provide the driver information necessary for the computer to correctly interact with it. This is how the myriad USB devices can work without having to install separate driver software for each. Malicious software can introduce itself as part of this driver interrogation and negotiation. Sometimes this will be done under the appearance of providing device information, such as "how bug is the storage on this device" or "what is the resolution of this camera" or whatever. Done "right" this device driver interaction will run software on the USB device regardless of you autorun settings. You need to disable automatically enabling USB devices when they are inserted. The computer should then detect some very basic "device present" information. However, to use the device, it still needs to do the aforementioned negotiation. There are USB scanners available that can try to detect malware or undesirable interactions, but they fall under the normal arms race that all malware detection have; if the malware is more sophisticated than the detection, it will likely escape detection. Scars on my face and hands, a black coat, greying beard and faded top hat, Im taken aback at my own appearance, I appear to something of a nightmare. Surprised, I take a step back. A misstep. A loose floorboard creaks loudly. The old watchmaker stirs. Upon opening his eyes at the sight of a tall, grey bearded and scarred man wearing a top hat at the foot of his bed he cries out " Teufel! My mind begins to wander back to that old man, bleeding and dying, who had knocked on my door so many decades ago. Words that sounded something like Latin, yet older, seemed to make their way towards the front of my mouth, as if commanded by some other force inside of me. article: We consider infinitely repeated games with vector losses discounted over time. We characterize the set of minimal upper bounds on expected losses that a player can simultaneously guarantee across the infinite horizon for all possible strategies of their opponents, also known as the set of feasible payoffs. This set is known as the folk theorem set. In this set, players can achieve any payoff that lies on or below the boundary of the set, which is typically a convex hull of certain points. The folk theorem provides a broad characterization of feasible payoffs in repeated games with discounting, and its application extends to a wide range of scenarios, including cooperation and competition among individuals or organizations. One important note is that the folk theorem only holds for games that are infinitely repeated. If the game has a finite number of repetitions, then there may be Nash equilibria that are not feasible. Furthermore, the folk theorem does not provide guidance on which payoff to achieve, only that a set of feasible payoffs exists. Therefore, players need to use additional tools, such as negotiation and communication, to arrive at a mutually beneficial outcome.

article: We consider the problem of reconstructing a rank-one matrix from a revealed subset of its entries when some of the revealed entries are corrupted with perturbations that are unknown and random. To address this problem, one approach is to use convex optimization techniques, such as nuclear-norm minimization or matrix factorization. These methods aim to minimize the difference between the observed and reconstructed entries, subject to some constraints on the rank of the reconstructed matrix. Another approach is to use probabilistic models, such as the matrix completion Gaussian process (MCGP) or the Bayesian low-rank matrix completion model. These models typically assume a prior distribution over the unknown entries and use Bayesian inference to estimate the parameters of the model and reconstruct the matrix. article: The contemporary literature on cloud resource allocation is mostly focused on studying the interactions between customers and cloud managers. Nevertheless, the recent growth in the customers' demands and the emergence of new cloud service models has made cloud resource allocation a critical issue. Several research works have focused on optimizing cloud resource allocation by considering different aspects such as energy consumption, cost minimization, load balancing, and service level agreements (SLAs) fulfillment. Some important techniques used in this domain include 1. Dynamic Resource Allocation techniques: These techniques are used to optimize resource allocation in real-time based on the current workload. The allocation decisions are driven by predictive or reactive approaches. 2. Multi-objective Resource Allocation techniques: These techniques allow optimizing resource allocation according to multiple objectives simultaneously. The objective functions can be defined based on factors such as cost, performance, and energy consumption. 3. Reinforcement Learning-based Resource Allocation techniques: These techniques involve the use of reinforcement learning algorithms to optimize resource allocation decisions in a dynamic environment. The algorithm learns from past decisions and adjusts the resource allocation based on the current situation. 4. Auction-based Resource Allocation techniques: In these techniques, customers bid for resources, and the cloud manager allocates resources to customers based on their bids. This approach ensures fair allocation of resources, as customers bid according to their willingness to pay. Overall, cloud resource allocation is a critical area of research, and it requires constant innovation and improvement to ensure optimal use of cloud resources while reducing costs and fulfilling service level agreements.

article: It is a common practice in the machine learning community to assume that the observed data are noise-free in the input attributes. Nevertheless, scenarios with input noise are common in real problems, as measurements are never perfectly accurate. If this input noise is not taken into account, a supervised machine learning method is expected to perform sub-optimally. In this paper, we focus on multi-class classification problems and use Gaussian processes (GPs) as the underlying classifier. Motivated by a data set coming from the astrophysics domain, we hypothesize that the observed data may contain noise in the inputs. Therefore, we devise several multi-class GP classifiers that can account for input noise. Such classifiers can be efficiently trained using variational inference to approximate the posterior distribution of the latent variables of the model. Moreover, in some situations, the amount of noise can be known before-hand. If this is the case, it can be readily introduced in the proposed methods. This prior information is expected to lead to better performance results. We have evaluated the proposed methods by carrying out several experiments, involving synthetic and real data. These include several data sets from the UCI repository, the MNIST data set and a data set coming from astrophysics. The results obtained show that, although the classification error is similar across methods, the predictive distribution of the proposed methods is better, in terms of the test log-likelihood, than the predictive distribution of a classifier based on GPs that ignores input noise.

article: A number of different multiscale methods have been developed as a robust alternative to upscaling and as a means for accelerated reservoir simulation of high-resolution geomodels. In their basic setup, multiscale methods use a restriction operator to construct a reduced system of flow equations on a coarser grid, and a prolongation operator to map pressure unknowns from the coarse grid back to the original simulation grid. The prolongation operator consists of basis functions computed numerically by solving localized flow problems. One can use the resulting multiscale solver both as a CPR-preconditioner in fully implicit simulators or as an efficient approximate iterative linear solver in a sequential setting. The latter approach has been successful implemented in a commercial simulator. Recently, we have shown that you can obtain significantly faster convergence if you instead of using a single pair of prolongation-restriction operators apply a sequence of such operators, where some of the operators adapt to faults, fractures, facies, or other geobodies. Herein, we present how you can accelerate the convergence even further, if you also include additional basis functions that capture local changes in the pressure.

article: A cold smile stretches its way across my face as I reread the letter I was about to send to my victim. Setting down the pen filled with blood red ink, I folded the letter and pitied the poor soul that would get this, but only a bit. After all, he won't have much time to be scared. Sealed and finally sent, I pictured my letter in my head, word by word as I made my way to my destination. This is not a chain letter nor is this a prank pulled by some unsightly teen. This is real. For your benefit, I suggest you to finish this letter. Do not try to run. Do not try to hide. Don't even bother calling the police, I have gotten clearance for this upcoming murder. Yes, it is indeed going to come down to that, my dear friend. I can see your hand trembling as you continue to read this letter, I can see the bead of cold sweat rolling down your forehead as you continue to try and convince yourself that this is not real, that it can't be. Well I am truly sorry to inform you otherwise because this is as real as the table you will be leaning on for support. You might be asking yourself: Why me? I would have, were I in your place. You might also want to know who I am. Due to the nature of this letter and for the sake of my amusement, I will not give out that little detail, though I will tell you I am not some lover that you have left for the dumps and that you do not know me. This, however, does not imply that I do not know you. I have seen you from afar, seen when you sleep, when you laugh, when you cry. But worst of all, and this is the reason why I had to choose you out of everyone who deserves this sentence as well, I know of the crimes you committed. They are not the crimes of an innocent, they are not a small occasional shoplift or a prank pulled on a friend. They aren't even murder. No. The law would've taken care of you if it was. Imagine a smile on an unknown face, imagine a disconnected hand writing this letter as it puts down each word with conviction and satisfaction. I am not cruel, at least, not in the conventional sense. I am but the monster sent to purge this world from filth like you. Tell me why, dear Collins, you had to go and break your parents spirits and send them tumbling into depression, why you felt the need to wrench out the hearts of so many young women with sweet words and soft caresses, why you have to spin lie after lie so that you can deceive the only other person that truly cares about you? You must think that I am inhuman, pitiless, cold. I am, but I am still the better person. I have no need to hide behind a carefully built facade, presenting the world with a false version of myself. You should be sickened by what you have done. Take note of this, while your bleeds through my hands, slowly trickling out of this world, I will have on a merciless smile. The tool of your demise will be none other than a tool that you yourself had once used in your childhood, an elegant dagger with a fine curved black, a handle made out of ivory with hand-carved patterns on it. Search for it in your house, turn it upside down if that is your wish...but it will be gone, as it's in the palm of my hand right now. I know where you live and once you're done reading this, because, trust me, you will not be able to stop yourself from finishing it, I will be knocking at your door. Tick tock. The sand has run out. Your time is up. I knocked on the door and I knew that my timing is right. A spark of satisfaction was felt. I loved a job well done. article: It had started as a ritual. A small coping mechanism to help him deal with his loss. He'd come out to her favorite park and push her favorite swing, feeling her weight, not in his arms as he once had, but in his soul. Every day, for two months. And every day, as he'd leave the park, he'd bid her memory a tearful goodbye and walk to his car. He told his wife he was staying late at the office, because he couldn't bring himself to mention their daughter and see her tear up. He knew she'd been grieving in her own way, and he'd made sure he was there for her. But he had to be strong, had to be the warm comfort she needed when she called for her daughter before remembering. Women and children first. Me, I can tough it out. Maybe when she had her closure, he'd tear off this makeshift bandage and deal with what was underneath. But for now, his duty was to protect and serve his wife. He went home. article: Many sensors, such as range, sonar, radar, GPS and visual devices, produce measurements which are contaminated by outliers. This is particularly important in applications where sensor data is critical, such as autonomous vehicles, robotics, and aerospace systems. There are several techniques that can be used to implement a fat-tailed sensor model, including using a Student's t-distribution, heavy-tailed noise models, and robust estimation methods. These techniques help to estimate the true value of a measurement by reducing the influence of outliers in the data. Overall, using fat-tailed sensor models can improve the accuracy and reliability of sensor measurements, which is essential for many critical applications.

article: Fourier phase retrieval is a classical problem that deals with the recovery of an image from the amplitude measurements of its Fourier coefficients. Conventional methods solve this problem via iterative (alternating) minimization by leveraging some prior knowledge about the structure of the unknown image. The inherent ambiguities about shift and flip in the Fourier measurements make this problem especially difficult; and most of the existing methods use several random restarts with different permutations. In this paper, we assume that a known (learned) reference is added to the signal before capturing the Fourier amplitude measurements. Our method is inspired by the principle of adding a reference signal in holography. To recover the signal, we implement an iterative phase retrieval method as an unrolled network. Then we use back propagation to learn the reference that provides us the best reconstruction for a fixed number of phase retrieval iterations. We performed a number of simulations on a variety of datasets under different conditions and found that our proposed method for phase retrieval via unrolled network and learned reference provides near-perfect recovery at fixed (small) computational cost. We compared our method with standard Fourier phase retrieval methods and observed significant performance enhancement using the learned reference. Our code is available at

First off, you have the ISP (internet service provider), and they provide the signal via the cable network (aka. plant). That signal has a series of flags on it, two of the more well-known flags are DHCP (alternates your IP address based on a random protocol, and is network-based), and lease. One thing to realize is that, gateways aside, the modem (cable bridge) and the router are two separate objects that do different things. The modem is what talks to the network, and receives the information. The router takes that signal, encrypts it via NAT, and evenly distributes it through your network, either wired or wirelessly depending on your router. If you have an issue with your internet, and you reset your router, chances are that you are NOT going to fix your problem. This is why: Your modem has an IP address provided by the network, known as an external (or public) address. If you have a router, the router will request that IP like a computer would. The router than takes it, and hides it behind its own security (NAT). It will then provide all connected devices with another IP address, known as internal address. This is typically what you see when your address says 192.168.0.1, or something similar depending on where your device is in your network. When your router turns on for the first time, it will request the IP address from the modem. Although typically automatic, you can request the router to check with the modem periodically to make sure the IP address hasn't changed, but sometimes it doesn't work. If your modem's lease expires but isn't provided a new IP address, if there was a software update that wasn't properly applied to the modem, or if the modem is having a fault due to improper signal levelpacket loss, then the router may not get the updated information. Your computer will request information from the router, who then requests it from the modem. If the router and modem have conflicting information, the request is denied and you will get errors like "ISP unavailble" or "internet connection not detected" or "webpage unavailable." Now, if the problem is on the modem's end, resetting the router will not fix anything as it will still have the most updated information that the modem can provide. Resetting the modem may fix that, or you may need to call your ISP so they can adjust the information being sent. However, if the problem is on the router's end (ie. the router isn't requesting updated information), then resetting the router will force it to do its initial startup check, of which includes requesting new information. article: Photo sensitive papers and films are made using a form of silver. The silver halides have a very low activation threshold, and the zap of a photon is enough to knock pieces off the halide, changing it's chemical structure. The film is made by using a substrate which is anything you use to hold the image. It could be plastic, paper, cellulose, etc. The base substrate is embedded with the silver halides and these impregnate the film or paper. It is then dried and packaged in light proof containers. The image is developed using a developer compound like D76, which is a powder dissolved into water to form a liquid developer. It darkens or tarnishes the exposed silver particles. The reaction will keep going until a chemical neutralizer called stopbath is used. Stopbath reacts with the developer and neutralizes it so it stops developing. Without it, an image would continue to get darker and darker over time as the developer continued to work long after it was in a darkroom. Finally the film or paper is run through a chemical called a fixer. It renders the rest of the silver halides inert and they will no longer react with light. At this point you can flip the lights on because you have a permanent photograph or negative, once you wash it off. A fun fact, the silver collected in the film and paper ends up saturating the fixer tray. It is possible to recover the silver from the liquid by chemically treating it and then refining. It doesn't amount to much but it's still pretty cool.

article: Traditional approaches for handwritten Chinese character recognition suffer in classifying similar characters. However, instead of manually labeling each component, we use weakly supervised learning to automatically generate a large number of noisy labels based on the character images themselves. Specifically, we first pretrain a CNN on a large unlabeled dataset of Chinese characters to learn general features. We then use this pretrained CNN to extract feature maps from a new set of labeled images of handwritten Chinese characters. These feature maps are clustered to identify common structural components, and then used to generate a set of noisy labels, where each label corresponds to a specific component. Finally, we train a CNN to classify the characters based on their components. We use the generated noisy labels to supervise the training of this network, which allows it to effectively identify the distinguishing features of each character, even when they are very similar. We evaluate our approach on two publicly available datasets of handwritten Chinese characters and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance compared to other traditional methods for this task. Our method can also be easily extended to other character recognition tasks where similar characters need to be distinguished.

article: We propose Hybrid Transactional Replication (HTR) a novel replication scheme for highly dependable services. It combines two schemes: a transaction is executed either optimistically by only one service replica in the deferred update mode (DU), or deterministically by all replicas in the state machine mode (SM); the choice is made by an oracle. The DU mode allows for parallelism and thus takes advantage of multicore hardware. In contrast to DU, the SM mode guarantees abort-free execution, so it is suitable for irrevocable operations and transactions generating high contention. For expressiveness, transactions can be discarded or retried on demand. We formally prove that the higher flexibility of the scheme does not come at the cost of weaker guarantees for clients: HTR satisfies strong consistency guarantees akin to those provided by other popular transactional replication schemes such as Deferred Update Replication. We developed HTR-enabled Paxos STM, an object-based distributed transactional memory system, and evaluated it thoroughly under various workloads. We show the benefits of using a novel oracle, which relies on machine learning techniques for automatic adaptation to changing conditions. In our tests, the ML-based oracle provides up to 50 improvement in throughput when compared to the system running with DU-only or SM-only oracles. Our approach is inspired by a well known algorithm used in the context of the multi-armed bandit problem.

article: This is where a survey course of art history comes in handy. It's very interesting to watch art move from decorative and idealized to representational and almost photo-realistic. Were humans incapable of understanding depth back then? Didn't have the tools to create it? People understood things like depth and mathematics - you don't get the Pyramids of Giza, Stonehenge, and the Acropolis without an understanding of the world around you. But people today don't seem to realize that there is a lot of mental process that goes on between viewing the three dimensional world and re-creating it on a two dimensional surface. These people were working from scratch with nothing before them to build off of. It's like the difference between a child who draws a picture of a house like [this] (URL0) and Andrew Wyeth's [Christina's World] (URL1) The child sees the world in glorious 3D every day of her life, but when asked to represent it two-dimensionally, she draws a box and triangle and doesn't make the sky come all the way to the ground. These are things that needed to be learned over a long period of time. I'd like to write a whole lot more on the subject, but something that is sort of analogous to the developing language of art is the language of film, although much sped up. I've been watching a series on netflix called The Story of Film: An Odyssey. It's amazing to watch movies go from basically a recorded stage play to something like "Citizen Kane" (I'm only about half way through the series).','The simple answer is that the more people and cultures we meet and experience the more we grow as artists. It's impossible to create something out of thin air unless there is some small inspiration from something else. It's like asking why bands in the 1950's didn't create music that is popular today - art evolves with the times and technology. One final thought - most famous artists now dedicate their lives to creating art. Society weeds out who is good and bad and only the good artists are "known" even though we all doodle now and then. Are we seeing art from primitive artists or from the general population? If someone found my notebook in 1,000 years would they think all our art is terrible because they are basing it on the drawings of me, a non-artist?', "The painters that created those beautifully detailed paintings didn't just sit down at a blank canvas and paint it. They used techniques that helped them, which were developed by people in the past and shared. For example, ways of sketching out the scene to help get the perspective right. Some painters even used tools such as light boxes, mirrors, etc. In short, there's room for innovation and invention in painting, and so there are things that more recent painters had access to that ancient painters did not.

article: The circulatory system is a network of tubes. They start big and get smaller and smaller. Think about a tree: The trunk separates off into smaller and smaller branches. Think of the leaves as your organs. Of course this is just a way of visualizing the system. Your guts aren't floating in blood. If there is blood outside the circulatory system, in your guts, it's a bad thing (internal bleeding). Whether you injure yourself, or you're cut open for surgery, you bleed because the tubes that are carrying blood all over your body are opened. About the intestines and such. Everything is in its place, attached to other things and surrounded by adipose tissue, aka fat. I'm not a doctor or anything, just a dude who wondered these very same things at one point or another. Hope it helps.,Blood does come when you are incised for surgery the surgeons just stop the flow, also I think that you being under anesthetic slows it down because your heart slows its beating rate. Humans have a "closed system" which means that our bodily fluids are kept within veins as opposed to an "open system" like bugs where they are within the body cavity only. The intestines are coiled because they are very, very long and wouldn't fit inside your body otherwise. The way it made sense to think about it to me was to think of being shrunk down really small and going in through a cut but not into the blood flow. Continue into the flow and you are in a vein, take a left and you are now in between the skin and muscles, fat, the outsides of veins, nerves, etc. The skin is like a bag keeping all of that in a form that will be able to propagate.', "In all vertebrates, we have a closed circulatory system, meaning (as described above) that our blood flows through its own pipe system and doesn't directly touch most of the body. However, your idea of organs being bathed in blood isn't that far off. That is called an open circulatory system, and some living creatures do have that, where their organs are covered in blood and directly oxygenated. URL0 This happens in arthropods, such as spiders or shrimp. If you read the article, there are even some species, such as flatworms, that have no circulatory system; in that specific case, the entire worm is basically a one way digestive tract where all nutrients leech directly into the surrounding cells, preventing the need for a specific circulatory system. As you go up the evolutionary'chain' to more complex creatures, the circulatory system develops out of this, becoming increasing complex itself: amphibians and reptiles move towards closed systems and two or three chambered hearts, all the way up to humans and other species with a four chamber heart and a fully closed system. If you want to learn more, you can take an intro to zoology class: they go through the evolution of complex systems like this as part of the course.

article: Recently, deep reinforcement learning (RL) methods have been applied successfully to multi-agent scenarios. Typically, the observation vector for decentralized decision making is represented by a concatenation of the (local) information an agent gathers about other agents. However, concatenation scales poorly to swarm systems with a large number of homogeneous agents as it does not exploit the fundamental properties inherent to these systems: (i) the agents in the swarm are interchangeable and (ii) the exact number of agents in the swarm is irrelevant. Therefore, we propose a new state representation for deep multi-agent RL based on mean embeddings of distributions, where we treat the agents as samples and use the empirical mean embedding as input for a decentralized policy. We define different feature spaces of the mean embedding using histograms, radial basis functions and neural networks trained end-to-end. We evaluate the representation on two well-known problems from the swarm literature Emdash rendezvous and pursuit evasion Emdash in a globally and locally observable setup. For the local setup we furthermore introduce simple communication protocols. Of all approaches, the mean embedding representation using neural network features enables the richest information exchange between neighboring agents, facilitating the development of complex collective strategies.

However, some applications, such as the isolation of cryptographic session keys in network-facing services, require very frequent domain switching. In such applications, the overhead of kernel- or hypervisor-mediated domain switching is prohibitive. In this paper, we present ERIM, a novel technique that provides hardware-enforced isolation with low overhead on x86 CPUs, even at high switching rates (ERIM's measured overhead is less than 1 for 100,000 switches per second). The key idea is to combine protection keys (MPKs), a feature recently added to x86 that allows protection domain switches in userspace, with binary inspection to prevent circumvention. We show that ERIM can be applied with little effort to new and existing applications, doesn't require compiler changes, can run on a stock Linux kernel, and has low runtime overhead even at high domain switching rates.

article: Twelve years since the sky went dark and they scuttled into holes. Busy years spent at the bottom of cliffs and the ends of barrels. And so many brought down shivering by disease. Frantically digging up dry roots in the forest with no one to tell them what was what. It reminded me of the centuries back. And the diseases raged. They became dirtier and wilder. Sniffing the air again with a purpose. Listening like deer for the wolf at the door. But it was usually nothing. Until it was me. Gerald had a silver harmonica stored above the mirror. He stopped shaving several months ago. He knew he had become sick but I doubt he knew he was the last one. Almost everybody saw nobody towards the end of things. The radios died before the first year. The voices in the night kept going a long time. At least 8 or 9 years. People are social and perhaps being alone was worse for them than anything. Gerald used to play the same 3 songs on his harmonica. Not anymore. His beard is so long now I bet it would get in the way. But he didn't try. Like I said, he had been sick. And not being the sort to kill himself he was quietly waiting. We walked a way into the woods. I knew it wasn't his time yet but I took most walks with him. Down by the tree line there were loosely gathered stones set over a handful of graves and Gerald started to hum. This was strange for him. And the tune was slow. It lasted a couple minutes and then he walked off sharply. Two weeks later and he was spitting blood when he woke. I don't think he was eating anymore, just drinking from the river. I followed him down the path to the stones. He lay down between the stacks of rubble and closed his eyes. But it wasn't his time yet. He was just waiting. We were waiting. - It's been a couple years now. Mostly I just watch the stars. And I drift. I can't help but wonder if this limbo is where they all went. One way or another. And what death might be out there for me? I used to think Gerald was the last one left. But that moment I touched him, low in the woods, I realized it was me.

article: We consider the problem of estimating the weight of a maximum weighted matching of a weighted graph G (V, E) whose edges are revealed in a streaming fashion. Extending the classical offline algorithm of Edmonds, we can use the Blossom Algorithm for finding a maximum weighted matching. However, in the streaming setting, we cannot use the entire graph at once, and we need to consider an edge at a time. One approach is to modify the Blossom Algorithm to work incrementally, so that it can update the matching as edges arrive. To estimate the weight of the maximum weighted matching, we can use the technique of random sampling. Suppose we sample a fixed number of edges uniformly at random from the stream, and then run the modified Blossom Algorithm on the sampled edges to find a matching. The weight of this matching is an unbiased estimator of the weight of the maximum weighted matching, up to a certain accuracy. Specifically, we can use the Chernoff bound to show that with high probability, the estimator is within a factor of (1 epsilon) of the true weight, where epsilon is a small positive constant. To further improve the accuracy, we can use the technique of stratified sampling. Instead of sampling uniformly at random from the stream, we can divide the edges into several "strata" based on their weights, and sample from each stratum proportionally to its weight. This ensures that we capture a representative sample of the edge weights, which in turn leads to a more accurate estimator of the maximum weighted matching.

The energy transfer times are synchronized with the time periods when the receiving node switches from energy harvesting to signal detection. The artificial noise is generated by the transmitter to add confusion to potential eavesdroppers, thereby enhancing security. Overall, this scheme ensures that energy is efficiently transferred while ensuring secure communication. article: In tensor completion, the latent nuclear norm is commonly used to induce low-rank structure, while substantially failing to capture the global information due to the utilization of unbalanced unfolding scheme. That's a correct statement. The latent nuclear norm regularization method is commonly used in tensor completion problems to induce low-rank structure in the completed tensor. However, it only takes into account the singular values of the tensor and not the underlying structure of the tensor itself. As a result, it can fail to capture global information and may yield suboptimal solutions. This is due to the fact that the tensor is usually unfolded in an unbalanced manner, which can lead to some dimensions being prioritized over others.

article: I bought this one avocado a year and a half ago. I was just making guacamole, it was a pretty ordinary experience really. I had about four of them and as I was preparing them. I decided to eat a slice of one. It was a blessing at that time, because if I had never eaten a slice from that particular avocado, I never would have known what a legend of an avocado I had purchased. The flavor, the texture, everything about was unlike anything I imagined could actually exist in the world. I hastily ate another slice from the avocado, and all too quickly that one was gone. I could do what my body was telling me and eat the rest of this unbelievable avocado, but I needed to save it. To eat it all at once would be a waste, and the rest of my life would be a never ending desire for that avocado. So, I wrapped it and put it in my fridge. I began working on the guacamole again, but I only got halfway through before I started worrying what would happen to the new-found purpose of my life that was now wrapped up and in the fridge. I grabbed my half-finished guacamole, pulled everything out of the fridge and got in so I could watch the avocado to make sure it was alright. I was hungry after a while and I tried to eat my half eaten guacamole, but after the first bite I couldn't bring myself to try again. It was truly depressing how the guacamole tasted, there was nothing enjoyable about it at all. The terrible aftertaste of inferior avocados hung around in mouth before I caved in and took another bite from the perfect avocado. But time had taken it's toll, and it didn't bring about the same feelings..... what a waste I had made of something so great. Crying, I ate what little magic remained of the once great avocado. Try to understand, it was still very good, but it wasn't the same. I had made a poor choice. I tried to keep my life the same as it always was, but after a week of holding back, I couldn't do it anymore. I quit my job. Over the next few months, I spent most of my savings sampling avocados. I would buy them from the store, three at a time. I would eat them right at the register, and spit them all out because there wasn't anything remotely enjoyable about them. They didn't even come close. With what little money I had, I started growing my own avocados. I have to sell most of them to keep myself alive. It's hard to resist trying them all, even though the only bring disappointment. The consistent worry that I've sold another perfect avocado to someone else often keeps me awake at night. I have my phone number on all of the avocados and I tell everyone to call if they experience a truly amazing avocado. I get about one call a week, but I can tell just by listening to their voice that they haven't experienced an truly perfect avocado, only one that's better than the rest. Just in case I someone does discover an avocado that is truly as great as the one I found that fateful April, every avocado I grow is gets a number. I take a picture of every avocado so I know the tree it came from, and the location on that tree. I take a picture of every avocado so if I find a truly enjoyable avocado again, I can know the date it was picked and the weather conditions that lead up to it. It feels hopeless and it's a lot of work for no reward as of yet, but I can take no chances. I have to find another perfect avocado. I have to have them consistently. Only then will I be able to experience happiness again.

article: We study the problem of leader selection in leader-follower multi-agent systems that are subject to stochastic disturbances. These disturbances can cause the followers to deviate from the leader's guidance, resulting in suboptimal performance or even failure. To address this challenge, researchers have developed various approaches to leader selection in stochastic multi-agent systems. One approach is to design a control law that ensures the followers remain within a certain range of the leader's behavior, despite the presence of disturbances. Another approach is to use consensus algorithms to establish a shared understanding among the agents of who the leader is, even in the presence of noise or uncertainties. Overall, the problem of leader selection in stochastic multi-agent systems is an active area of research, with many promising approaches and applications.

article: In partially observable (PO) environments, deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents often suffer from unsatisfactory performance, since two problems need to be tackled together: how to extract information from the raw observations and how to make optimal decisions based on the extracted information. RNNs have the ability to maintain a hidden state, which allows them to process sequences of observations and retain information over time. Another approach is to use a combination of RL and imitation learning. In this approach, the agent is first trained on a dataset of expert demonstrations, using supervised learning to learn an initial policy. Then, the agent switches to RL to refine the policy based on the feedback received from the environment. Additionally, techniques such as curiosity-driven exploration, hierarchical reinforcement learning, and meta-learning can help RL agents extract useful information from the environment and make better decisions in PO settings. Overall, there is no one-size-fits-all solution for the challenges posed by PO environments, and researchers are continually exploring new techniques to improve the performance of RL agents in these settings.

article: In the light of regularized dynamic time warping kernels, this paper re-considers the concept of time elastic centroid (TEC) for a set of time series. From this perspective, we show that TEC can be readily addressed as a preimage problem. However, this non-convex problem is ill-posed, and obtaining a sub-optimal solution may involve heavy computational costs, especially for long time series. We then derive two new algorithms based on a probabilistic interpretation of kernel alignment matrices that expresses the result in terms of probabilistic distributions over sets of alignment paths. The first algorithm is an agglomerative iterative heuristic procedure inspired from a state-of-the-art DTW barycentre averaging algorithm. The second proposed algorithm uses a progressive agglomerative heuristic method to perform classical averaging of the aligned samples but also averages the times of occurrence of the aligned samples. By comparing classification accuracies for 45 time series datasets obtained by first nearest centroidmedoid classifiers we show that: i) centroid-based approaches significantly outperform medoid-based approaches, ii) for the considered datasets, the second algorithm which combines averaging in the sample space and along the time axes, emerges as the most significantly robust heuristic model for time-elastic averaging with a promising noise reduction capability.

article: The beer game is a widely used in-class game that is played in supply chainmanagement classes to demonstrate the bullwhip effect. The game is adecentralized, multi-agent, cooperative problem that can be modeled as a serialsupply chain network in which agents cooperatively attempt to minimize thetotal cost of the network even though each agent can only observe its own localinformation. Each agent chooses order quantities to replenish its stock. Undersome conditions, a base-stock replenishment policy is known to be optimal.However, in a decentralized supply chain in which some agents (stages) may actirrationally (as they do in the beer game), there is no known optimal policyfor an agent wishing to act optimally. We propose a machine learning algorithm, based on deep Q-networks, tooptimize the replenishment decisions at a given stage. When playing alongsideagents who follow a base-stock policy, our algorithm obtains near-optimal orderquantities. It performs much better than a base-stock policy when the otheragents use a more realistic model of human ordering behavior. Unlike most otheralgorithms in the literature, our algorithm does not have any limits on thebeer game parameter values. Like any deep learning algorithm, training thealgorithm can be computationally intensive, but this can be performed ahead oftime; the algorithm executes in real time when the game is played. Moreover, wepropose a transfer learning approach so that the training performed for oneagent and one set of cost coefficients can be adapted quickly for other agentsand costs. Our algorithm can be extended to other decentralized multi-agentcooperative games with partially observed information, which is a common typeof situation in real-world supply chain problems.

article: Incentive is a misleading word. It's just a weight. Let's say it can do action A, or action B 5050. If it picks right, you up the score 5, if wrong, -5. So if an answer should be A, and the AI picks A, it becomes 5545, with a stronger weight towards A being the way to do things. It's not an actual consciousness, so it's not incentivizing like a person. it's just math that reweighs things if it gives the correct output. Here's some previous posts on the topic: URL0,Incentives are basically what the AI wants. It's usually expressed as a number and the AI is just finding ways to maximize (or minimize) that number. Let's say you are making an AI to play Super Mario Brothers. The incentive would be the level count. You can also have several incentives that have different weights. So after maximizing the level count, you might want to maximize the score, or remaining lives, or how far to the right you got on a certain level. Level count is the most important, so moving to the next level might be worth 100 points, and the other things are worth 10 or 20, but that's the idea. One of the complex parts of AI is figuring out how to set these incentives so that the AI does exactly what you want.','You give it a function that produces a value, and you ask it to maximize or minimize that value. Kind of dumb example since it's solvable in other ways, but maybe you're trying to get AI to find you the fastest driving directions between points A and B, with a potential stop off at point C. You give it a way to calculate how long any set of driving choices would take (e.g. a way to plug in: take I-405 south to I90, then east to I-5, then south to US 101, and out of that get "2.5 hours, and then you ask it to minimize that value. That is its "incentive.,'It is kind of like reddit karma, it is all just numbers. If you had an AI trying to learn tic-tac-toe, to pick the first move, you would do the programming equivalent of putting 90 marbles in a bag, 10 each of 9 different colors, corresponding to each starting square. You draw one, make that move, and if you win, you incentivize the AI by adding a marble of that color, and remove one if you lose. The next game, it is a little more likely to make the best move, and eventually all the marbles will correspond to good starting moves.

article: We transform reinforcement learning (RL) into a form of supervised learning (SL) by turning traditional RL on its head, calling this RL or Upside Down RL (UDRL). Standard RL predicts the value of taking an action in a given state based on experience and rewards accumulated over time. However, in UDRL, we invert this process by predicting the state given an action and a reward. To implement UDRL, we first collect a dataset of state-action-reward tuples using a behavior policy. We then use this dataset to train a model to predict the state given an action and reward. This model can then be used for decision-making in the same way that a traditional RL agent would use a value function to choose actions. The advantage of UDRL is that it avoids some of the difficulties and instabilities associated with traditional RL, such as the need for exploring and the long training times. Instead, we can use supervised learning techniques, which have been well-studied and optimized over the years. Additionally, UDRL can handle non-stationary environments, where the probability distribution of the states and actions may change over time, since it is based on a fixed dataset. Overall, UDRL represents an interesting alternative to traditional RL, and it has shown promising results in different domains, such as robotics and games.

article: The stomach is not an empty bag with acid in the bottom, where food plops in and dissolves. It's an expandible sac lined with acidic mucus. Gravity actually plays a very small part in digestion even here on Earth. Most of the action, including in the stomach, is a result of muscles pushing the food around, not gravity pulling it down. Check out [this animation] (URL0).,Human digestive system doesn't work only on gravity. When you swallow food, muscles in your throat and your intestines "push" it down to your stomach. While stomach is often pictured as balloon with acid on bottom, it doesn't just stand like that. Many muscles in stomach are contracted and everything inside is mushing around, mixing with acid. Also stomach doesn't have fixed size but it adjusts itself according to amount of food you ate. There is very little "empty space.,'Followup question; is acid reflux more prevalent in people who are in weightless environments?','To add to Mikepants's explanation, the stomach has 3 layers of muscle lining it. Each layer of muscle is laid down with fibers running in different directions. Functionally, this means the stomach can make complex "wringing" motions to aid in the churning of food as well as aid in pushing it into the small intestine. Gravity plays little role in waste excretion. Once food leaves the stomach, rhythmic, wave-like contractions push what used to be food through the small then large intestines. These wave-like contractions are referred to as peristalsis. Peristaltic contractions are also used in getting urine from the kidneys to the bladder, so gravity is not necessary for urinating in space either.','OP, have you ever drank water upside down to get rid of hiccups?

article: This paper investigates the physical layer security issue of a device-to-device (D2D) underlaid cellular system with a multi-antenna base station (BS) and a multi-antenna eavesdropper. To investigate the potential of D2D communication in improving network security, the conventional network without D2D users (DUs) is first considered. It is shown that the problem of maximizing the sum secrecy rate (SR) of cellular users (CUs) for this special case can be transformed to an assignment problem and optimally solved. Then, a D2D underlaid network is considered. Since the joint optimization of resource block (RB) allocation, CU-DU matching and power control is a mixed integer programming, the problem is difficult to handle. Hence, the RB assignment process is first conducted by ignoring D2D communication, and an iterative algorithm is then proposed to solve the remaining problem. Simulation results show that the sum SR of CUs can be greatly increased by D2D communication, and compared with the existing schemes, a better secrecy performance can be obtained by the proposed algorithms.

article: That is called bootstrap problem. How can you program something when no software exists that lets you program things. And how can a computer read what to do, if it has no instructions to begin with? One possible solution to the bootstrap problem is to start with a set of very basic instructions written in machine language (the language that computers speak), and use those instructions to build more complex instructions and programs. This process is also known as bootstrapping or self-hosting. For example, a programmer could start with the most basic machine instructions to add, subtract, and compare numbers, and then use those instructions to create more complex operations like conditional statements, loops, and functions. Over time, more complex programs and programming languages can be built upon this foundation. Another solution is to use a pre-existing programming language or tool to create the initial instructions or software needed to bootstrap a new system. This approach is common in the development of operating systems, where code is initially written in a higher-level language like C, and then compiled into machine code that can be run on a computer. Overall, there are several ways to approach the bootstrap problem, and the solution will typically depend on the specific goals and constraints of the project.

article: A posteriori error estimates are constructed for the three-field variational formulation of the Biot problem involving the displacements, the total pressure and the fluid pressure. The discretization under focus is a mixed finite element method, where the displacement and pressure fields are approximated using different finite element spaces. The a posteriori error estimates provide a reliable indication of the accuracy of the computed solution and can be used to adapt the mesh, refine the solution in particular regions, or to control the stopping criterion in iterative solvers. The a posteriori error estimates are typically based on the residual of the discrete problem, which measures the deviation of the discrete solution from the exact solution of the continuous problem. In this case, the residual involves the gradient of the displacement and the divergence of the pressure fields, as well as their respective source terms. The error estimates are typically computed locally, and can be used to identify regions of the domain where the solution is least accurate. The local error indicators can be used to define an adaptive mesh refinement strategy, where the mesh is refined in regions where the error is largest, and coarsened in regions where the error is small. This can significantly reduce the computational cost of the simulation while maintaining a desired level of accuracy. Overall, a posteriori error estimates are a valuable tool in the numerical solution of the Biot problem, as they provide a quantitative measure of the accuracy of the computed solution, and enable efficient mesh adaptation and control of the iterative solvers.
