article: It was 11:59 on July 12. In a few long seconds, I would be 18 years old. The big one eight. A milestone for any adolescent. Oh sure, I wasn't born precisely at midnight, but nobody ever was. All that mattered was that I was born on July 13 and soon, oh so soon, it would be July 13. But there's a catch. A good one believe it or not. Everyone receives a superpower on their 18th birthday and I'm one of the last of my class to get theirs being a summer baby and all, but it won't matter soon. I'm sitting in my room alone. Most people celebrate with friends so they can show off, but not me. No sir, if this power is a good one, I want to keep it a secret as long as I can. Hopefully it will be something cool, like ice breath or spontaneous explosions with a snap of my fingers...... But what if it's lame? One kid got a heightened sense of smell, like beyond animal levels, and now people rip the rankest farts since the funk of 40,000 years all to watch him vomit up last night's dinner. I can't even imagine getting a full whiff of weeks old B.O. Damn, it really sucked to be that kid. It was a flip of the coin really. Some people would get something exciting, others weren't so lucky. I hope I'm a lucky one. God, how much longer is this minute going to take? I feel like its 12:10 by now or something. Nope, still 11:59. COME ON! Ugh, its like being a kid waiting for Christmas all over again. "Is it Christmas yet?" "No, it's still only November." They say a watched pot never boils; well I guess a watched clock never ticks either. The first thing I'm going to do with my newfound power is run to the nearest open field and test it out. It'll be dark so I won't easily be seen and the emptiness will make for no casualties. Oh man, what if I get a power that will let me rule this world...? I could be a regular super-villain! Watch as entire cities crumble before my might. Forge a throne of melted tanks and jets and sit from on high as my subjects cater to my every whim. Mwahahahaha I can taste it already. I should really work on my evil laugh, though. I have a bike, not James Bond as an advisory. Is it seriously not 12:00 yet? What the hell man. I know what I need to do. I'm going to turn away from this clock and when I turn back around, it will midnight. Past that. Hell, I won't even look at the clock. I'll know it's time and I'll just run right outside and see what I got. But that poor fool had no idea his birthday had already come and gone. The minute the clock struck 12, his power manifested: an eternity of living in the present moment with all the time in the world to accomplish his heart's desires. But all it ever did was drive him to madness.

article: Tone is a prosodic feature used to distinguish words in many languages, some of which are endangered and scarcely documented. In this work, we use unsupervised representation learning to identify probable clusters of syllables that share the same phonemic tone. Our method extracts the pitch for each syllable, then trains a convolutional autoencoder to learn a low-dimensional representation for each contour. We then apply the mean shift algorithm to cluster tones in high-density regions of the latent space. Furthermore, by feeding the centers of each cluster into the decoder, we produce a prototypical contour that represents each cluster. We apply this method to spoken multi-syllable words in Mandarin Chinese and Cantonese and evaluate how closely our clusters match the ground truth tone categories. Finally, we discuss some difficulties with our approach, including contextual tone variation and allophony effects.

article: We prepared for every eventuality. We walled the entire town with an impenetrable barrier only broken by a sturdy gate, manned 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Weapons stations were positioned every thirty feet, and every citizen carried at least one gun and one knife at all times. Food and water, blankets, generators, ammunition, medicines, barrels of gasoline, all were stored in secure underground bunkers. In fact, the only structures above-ground were watch-stations and training yards. All the rest was meticulously managed plots of land, already producing enough food to sustain the entire town, and rows upon rows of solar panels. A fully functioning sewage system was installed.Living quarters were located in a network of bunkers and corridors underground, fitted with air vents, air filters, and automatic locks timed to match our strict schedules. We drilled daily, and every person, child or adult, was rigorously trained and expected to adhere to the structure that the town ran by. Curfews were enforced. We were safe, completely sealed off from the outside world, save for a carefully monitored communications system, updating us regularly on the efforts of epidemiologists all over the world. We all took shifts in there, flagging the WHO's alerts of possible outbreaks of disease. We knew we were mocked, but we knew that in the end, we would be the ones with the last laugh. For all our preparation, though, it still took us by surprise. And I, I am the only survivor. This is my story. I shouldn't have survived, really. It was only chance that I was kept awake by nightmares, unable to find peace. I tossed in my ship-shape quarters long after the rest of the rest of the'town' was asleep. I could hear soft breathing from my neighbors; doors were impractical down here; we found what privacy we could behind curtains. Afraid of further nightmares, I slipped from my bunk, taking caution not to disturb the two others on the bunks below me. Company would distract me from the terrors in my subconscious, I remember thinking. So I padded through the corridors, my bare feet whispering on the grating beneath, to seek human comfort in the Communications shack. I punched my number into the code-box beside the only door in the entirety of the living quarters. The door opened with a hiss, and the rhythm of sleepful breath was replaced with the sound of gentle static and hushed conversation. The door closed quietly behind me. I was greeted with a nod by the man and woman on duty, but otherwise they paid me little heed. It was not uncommon for sleepless occupants to drift to the communications room at the darkest hours of the night. I regarded the screen idly. Nothing stirred, as usual. It was comforting to watch, assurance that we were safe. The woman broke me from my distraction. "You mind holding fort for us for a few minutes? We're going to make ourselves fresh coffees. Can bring you one too, if you like." I waved my hand in acknowledgement. She and the man exited the room, leaving me to keep an eye one the faintly flickering display. The time in the corner read 3:08. I must confess, I dozed a bit. The next time I looked, it was 4:21. I was alone. Even in the containment of the Communications room I could hear muffled noises from outside. The next shift should have been here twenty minutes ago. Could it be that I had missed the start of the zombie apocalypse? The rest of the town must have been industriously following procedure outside while I, alone and unnoticed, kipped in the safety of the locked room. Furious at myself, I snatched a gun from a rack on the wall, and, feeling ridiculous in my slightly-too-small pajamas, disengaged the lock to join the fray out-side. The muffled noises crescendoed into a thunder of sound. Gunfire deafened my left ear. This threw me, completely. I had expected orders shouted and people to be running to their stations. But not gunfire. Gun use was restricted to above-ground. In the confines of the bunker, the gunshots, so many as to be indistinguishable from each other, roared. I saw blood, heard screams; not the screams of adrenaline-pumped squadron leaders, but the unmistakable screams of dying men. I saw raging, relentless bodies thrown together, biting, clawing, scratching, tearing. The grid was sticky with blood, the air thick with the churning stench of bodily fluids, rent flesh, and sweat. I tore myself from my stupor, leaping back into the Communications room. The sudden silence was oppressive. My heart could not be tamed, nor my breathing stilled. My fingers, usually steady on the trigger, would not cease trembling. This shouldn't have happened. The apocalypse was supposed to happen outside, among the foolish skeptics that laughed at our preparations, not inside the fortress that was our town. My training told me to overcome my shock, to muster my courage, and to stand alongside my dying friends and send bullet after bullet into dead flesh. My limbs disobeyed. They scrabbled at the grating on the floor, and when it came up I threw myself into the space it offered. Had I followed my training, I would have died heroically and horrendously. I would have been shredded by cruel, mindless beings once my family. Instead I dragged myself down miles of pipe, sobbing the whole way, unable to erase bloody images from my retinas. When at last I crawled into clean moonlight I could only lie on the ground and stare back at the mighty walls of our town, our fortress. No my town. My fortress. Their tomb.
label: human

article: Neural image inpainting has achieved promising performance in generating semantically plausible content. Most of the recent works mainly focus on inpainting images depending on vision information, while neglecting the semantic information implied in human languages. To acquire more semantically accurate inpainting images, this paper proposes a novel inpainting model named N eural I mage Inpainting G uided with D escriptive T ext (NIGDT). First, a dual multi-modal attention mechanism is designed to extract the explicit semantic information about corrupted regions. The mechanism is trained to combine the descriptive text and two complementary images through reciprocal attention maps. Second, an image-text matching loss is designed to enforce the model output following the descriptive text. Its goal is to maximize the semantic similarity of the generated image and the text. Finally, experiments are conducted on two open datasets with captions. Experimental results show that the proposed NIGDT model outperforms all compared models on both quantitative and qualitative comparison. The results also demonstrate that the proposed model can generate images consistent with the guidance text, which provides a flexible way for user-guided inpainting. Our systems and code will be released soon.

This is especially important for professions that require precise scheduling and tracking of time, such as military, transportation, and healthcare industries. article: Time-harmonic far-field source array imaging in a two-dimensional waveguide is analyzed. A low-frequency situation is considered in which the diameter of the waveguide is slightly larger than the wavelength, so that only the lowest-order mode propagates. The waveguide is assumed to be lossless and homogeneous with a known wave speed. Assuming that the array sources have known complex amplitudes and positions, the goal is to reconstruct the source distribution based on the measured far-field data at a set of receiver locations outside the waveguide. To perform this imaging, numerical algorithms such as the linear sampling method, the factorization method, or the MUSIC method can be employed. These algorithms use the far-field data to determine the location and strength of the sources inside the waveguide. Overall, this type of imaging is useful for non-destructive testing, biomedical imaging, and other applications where accurate imaging of the interior of a waveguide is important.

article: "And since when has swearing in public been an imprisonable offence?" I asked. The officer didn't even break stride as he put my arms behind my back. The cafe owner, one of the few left trading honestly, looked terrified. He hadn't meant to provoke me to the point of swearing. Once I had said'for fuck's sake' the police had been called in, and as is usual in this day and age they come pretty quick - after all, there were very few people left to arrest. I resisted. "Resisting isn't going to get you anywhere," the police officer said. "You are under arrest I looked at the shopkeeper. Did he dare? The cop had his handcuffs out. I kicked out, my heel striking the cop's shinbone, and as he reeled backwards I turned around to face him. He looked surprised, but there was something more - terror. US cops were not used to resistance anymore. Seeing this, I threw everything into my punch. The crunch of the cop's nose breaking was followed with the thud as his back hit a table. I stuck out my foot, and the cop went over it, crashed into the table, and moved no more. In the sudden silence the sounds of the fight were magnified many times over. I looked at the shopkeeper. Oh, I was really in for it now. Attacking a cop was one of those old-fashioned criminal offences that could now earn you life in prison. And as surprising as it might sound, I didn't want to spend my life in prison. It was really ironic how I, the dangerous criminal, was on the loose while my friends were all on the inside for something simple like texting while driving. At their case, the prosecution had said it was the singular worst case of texting and driving he had ever seen. He had looked down for five whole seconds. Now, we can't have that, now can we? Anything but texting and driving. Six months minimum was handed down. It would definitely be way more in my case. The shopkeeper stared at me as if I had just murdered his mom. I hesitated. He'd seen me. "Sorry about the damage," I said to the shopkeeper. He shook his head instantly. "No, it's nothing! Don't worry about it, man." I saw that he looked absolutely terrified. Heh, being a criminal was fun. When you've done something to deserve life imprisonment anything goes. So I screwed up my mouth, put on my best gangster face, and snarled, "If you say anything, I'll be back, and there'll be no more second fucking chances. Now is that clear, amigo?" He nodded quickly. I strolled out of the shop. There wasn't much time to lose. Every citizen of the US had a contigency plan for moments like these. You never knew when you were going to be arrested, and hovercar getaways were exclusively reserved for the 0.001. Mine was to go to the end of this street. Could I get there? I saw another officer approaching, and quickly I ducked into a side street. There were two thirteen-year old boys - possibly brothers - hiding out there, and they both jumped back in surprise. "You Before they could say a word, I lunged for them, and put one hand on either mouth. "Now listen to me, you cocksuckers, " I said. The swear had the desired effect - their eyes bulged. Both of them now knew they were dealing with a proper criminal. "Don't say a word to the police. I'm going to need your help to get away. You boys heard of a getaway plan? Nod for yes or shake for no." They both nodded. Now came the part that was complete bullshit. "You're going to help me, or I'll kill you two." Hearing this, they struggled a bit, but I had them both under control. Quickly, their shakings subsided. "But I won't, if you help me. Will you help me?" Two nods. I released them both. "Very well. There's a policeman out there and I want one of you to be a decoy. The other person will come with me to the end of the road. If we meet someone else on the way, I'm your father and I'm taking you to see the execution, alright?" They both nodded a third time. "Alright, let's get going," I said. "Won't want to miss when a judge is shot dead, now won't we?" One of them was already moving. Seeing the police officer through the side street, I took a deep breath. This was either going to work or fail spectacularly. Would there be more? - The first inkling that the officer got of trouble came from the boy's screech. "Stop!" the officer said. "You are wanted for truancy!" I pushed the other boy ahead of me. "Walk," I said. "Your brother will join us." That was the second lie. I had no idea what would happen for his brother. Did it matter? The boy was walking ahead of me. The policeman was looking the other way, chasing the screams of a thirteen year old boy who was running for his brother's life. Such was life for the few free citizens in the land of the free. What could possibly go wrong? I reached the end of the road without incident. There was an abandoned shop on the corner. I could see my grab bag in there. A gun peeked out of the top. Hey, at least the prison lobbyists left the Second Amendment untouched. I got over and stuffed the weapon deeper into the bag, before I noticed that the boy was still standing there. "What?" I asked, playing the part. "What're you still doing here? Scram!" "Did you..... did you say there was going to be an execution?" I shouldered my pack. "Yeah, Chief Justice of some sort. Why?" He didn't say anything. I looked at him, saw how well his face matched his brother's. In my head I was already rehearsing my story to the Canadian border force. And then I looked at the boy again, and it hit me. "Oh, no, no..... he's not your father, now is he?" The boy was silent. I sighed, knowing now that there was no choice. The boy had saved my life. Canada could wait. "Right, let's go," I said. "We're going to save your dad."
label: human

article: Deep learning has dramatically improved the performance of speech recognition systems through learning hierarchies of features optimized for the task at hand. However, true end-to-end learning, where features are learned directly from the raw audio waveform, has also shown promising results in recent years. This approach, known as end-to-end speech recognition, bypasses the need for hand-crafted feature engineering and instead allows the model to learn relevant features on its own. End-to-end speech recognition systems typically consist of a neural network that takes raw audio as input and outputs the corresponding transcript. This neural network can be a combination of convolutional and recurrent layers, followed by a fully connected layer for the final classification. The input audio is usually segmented into smaller frames, and these frames are passed through the network to create a sequence of predictions. End-to-end speech recognition has shown to produce state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks, and it has the added benefit of being more flexible and easier to maintain compared to traditional systems. However, it requires large amounts of labeled data and longer training times due to the increased complexity of the model.

article: Erasure-correcting codes, that support local repair of codeword symbols, have attracted substantial attention recently for their application in distributed storage systems. In particular, this paper studies a class of codes with the following property: any small set of codeword symbols can be reconstructed (repaired) from a small number of other symbols. This is referred to as cooperative local repair . The main contribution of this paper is bounds on the trade-off of the minimum distance and the dimension of such codes, as well as explicit constructions of families of codes that enable cooperative local repair. Some other results regarding cooperative local repair are also presented, including an analysis for the well-known HadamardSimplex codes.

article: A common approach to implementing similarity search applications is the usage of distance functions, where small distances indicate high similarity. In the case of metric distance functions, metric index structures can be used to accelerate nearest neighbor queries. On the other hand, many applications ask for approximate subsequences or subsets, e.g. searching for a similar partial sequence of a gene, for a similar scene in a movie, or for a similar object in a picture which is represented by a set of multidimensional features. Metric index structures such as the M-Tree cannot be utilized for these tasks because of the symmetry of the metric distance functions. In this work, we propose the SuperM-Tree as an extension of the M-Tree where approximate subsequence and subset queries become nearest neighbor queries. In order to do this, we introduce metric subset spaces as a generalized concept of metric spaces. Various metric distance functions can be extended to metric subset distance functions, e.g. the Euclidean distance (on windows), the Hausdorff distance (on subsets), the Edit distance and the Dog-Keeper distance (on subsequences). We show that these examples subsume the applications mentioned above.

article: A sparsifier of a graph G (Benczur and Karger; Spielman and Teng) is a sparse weighted subgraph G that approximately retains the same cut structure of G . For general graphs, non-trivial sparsification is possible only by using weighted graphs in which different edges have different weights. Even for graphs that admit unweighted sparsifiers (that is, sparsifiers in which all the edge weights are equal to the same scaling factor), there are no known polynomial time algorithms that find such unweighted sparsifiers. We study a weaker notion of sparsification suggested by Oveis Gharan, in which the number of cut edges in each cut (S , S) is not approximated within a multiplicative factor ( 1 ), but is, instead, approximated up to an additive term bounded by times d S vol (S), where d is the average degree of the graph and vol (S) is the sum of the degrees of the vertices in S . We provide a probabilistic polynomial time construction of such sparsifiers for every graph, and our sparsifiers have a near-optimal number of edges O ( - 2 n polylog ( 1 . We also provide a deterministic polynomial time construction that constructs sparsifiers with a weaker property having the optimal number of edges O ( - 2 n). Our constructions also satisfy a spectral version of the "additive sparsification" property. Notions of sparsification have also been studied for hypergraphs. Our construction of "additive sparsifiers" with O (n) edges also works for hypergraphs, and provides the first non-trivial notion of sparsification for hypergraphs achievable with O (n) hyperedges when and the rank r of the hyperedges are constant. Finally, we provide a new construction of spectral hypergraph sparsifiers, according to the standard definition, with poly ( - 1 , r) n log n hyperedges, improving over the previous spectral construction (Soma and Yoshida) that used O (n 3) hyperedges even for constant r and .

Of course, they like to show off their ability to fly, or punch through stone, or blast lasers from their eyes. I always used to wish I could do such things, and I spent my childhood in perpetual jealousy of my friends and all of the fun things they could do. But while they enjoyed their garden of physical wonders, I turned inwards to my own secret world. I turned to reading, studying, and growing my own inner abilities, instead of simply making-do with what fate had granted me. article: At the core of any inference procedure in deep neural networks are dot product operations, which are the component that require the highest computational resources. For instance, deep neural networks such as VGG-16 require up to 15 giga-operations in order to perform the dot products present in a single forward pass, which results in significant energy consumption and therefore limit their use in resource-limited environments, e.g., on embedded devices or smartphones. A common approach to reduce the cost of inference is to reduce its memory complexity by lowering the entropy of the weight matrices of the neural network, e.g., by pruning and quantizing their elements. However, the quantized weight matrices are then usually represented either by a dense or sparse matrix storage format, whose associated dot product complexity is not bounded by the entropy of the matrix. This means that the associated inference complexity ultimately depends on the implicit statistical assumptions that these matrix representations make about the weight distribution, which can be in many cases suboptimal. In this paper we address this issue and present new efficient representations for matrices with low entropy statistics. These new matrix formats have the novel property that their memory and algorithmic complexity are implicitly bounded by the entropy of the matrix, consequently implying that they are guaranteed to become more efficient as the entropy of the matrix is being reduced. In our experiments we show that performing the dot product under these new matrix formats can indeed be more energy and time efficient under practically relevant assumptions. For instance, we are able to attain up to x42 compression ratios, x5 speed ups and x90 energy savings when we convert in a lossless manner the weight matrices of state-of-the-art networks such as AlexNet, VGG-16, ResNet152 and DenseNet into the new matrix formats and benchmark their respective dot product operation.

In synchronous SGD, all workers update their parameters simultaneously, ensuring consistency. One solution to this problem is to periodically synchronize the model state across workers or to use techniques such as elastic averaging SGD, which dynamically adjusts the learning rate based on the divergence of model parameters across workers. article: We study the problem of optimizing expensive blackbox functions over combinatorial spaces (e.g., sets, sequences, trees, and graphs). Unfortunately, BOCS scales poorly for large number of binary andor categorical variables. Based on recent advances in submodular relaxation for solving Binary Quadratic Programs, we study an approach referred as Parametrized Submodular Relaxation (PSR) towards the goal of improving the scalability and accuracy of solving AFO problems for BOCS model. PSR approach relies on two key ideas. First, reformulation of AFO problem as submodular relaxation with some unknown parameters, which can be solved efficiently using minimum graph cut algorithms. Second, construction of an optimization problem to estimate the unknown parameters with close approximation to the true objective. article: Senior reactor operator here. You withdraw the control rods. The control rods absorb neutrons needed for the reaction, so when you take them out, the neutrons are allowed to start interacting. You slowly withdraw the control rods and watch the neutron counts increase on your monitors. If the reactor is still offline after withdrawing a control rod, the neutron counts slowly increase then steady out. When enough control rods are withdrawn to bring the reactor supercritical, the counts will continue to exponentially increase. Operators monitor the reactor doubling time, or the reactor period. The doubling time is how long it takes for power to double. When the reactor is supercritical, the doubling time is constant, and power keeps exponentially increasing until it's high enough to heat the fuel up. When the power level is high enough to start heating the fuel, this is called the "Point of Adding Heat," and the temperature increase in the core causes the power level to stabilize. The reactor returns to exactly critical, and is now self sustaining. Power stops going up or down, it just sits steady. At this point operators will slowly withdraw rods to continue heating up the core, start producing steam, and start bringing the steam side of the plant online.', "Load the fuel rods with the control rods in place, and the reactor won't start to go critical until you start withdrawing the control rods.

Then, by training a machine learning model on this sample data, we can approximate the reach set for the system much more efficiently compared to traditional methods. This approach has several advantages over existing methods. Firstly, it can handle systems with a large number of continuous state variables without suffering from poor scalability. Secondly, it does not require the computation of the system's exact dynamics or the solution of complex optimization problems. Finally, it allows for quick exploration of the system's behavior and can be used to analyze the impact of various inputs on the system's reachability. article: Retrieving videos of a particular person with face image as query via hashing technique has many important applications. While face images are typically represented as vectors in Euclidean space, characterizing facial features using hashing techniques can help improve the efficiency and accuracy of face recognition systems. Hashing techniques allow for fast comparisons of facial features and can help identify individuals even in large datasets. One such hashing technique used in facial recognition is called locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). LSH is a process that compresses high-dimensional data, such as facial vectors, into lower-dimensional representations while still preserving significant information about the original data. This technique operates by randomly projecting the high-dimensional data onto a lower-dimensional subspace. Points in the same cluster in the high-dimensional space are likely to be close to each other after the projection, allowing for efficient similarity comparisons of facial features. Hashing techniques are also useful in protecting the privacy of individuals. Instead of storing facial vectors or images, a hash can be stored instead. This ensures that the facial data is not easily accessible in case of a security breach or data leak, while still allowing for efficient face recognition.

Motivated by this gap, we proposed a variant of the Barzilai-Borwein (BB) method, referred to as the Random Barzilai-Borwein (RBB) method, to calculate step size for SARAH in the mini-batch setting, thereby leading to a new SARAH method: MB-SARAH-RBB. We prove that MB-SARAH-RBB converges linearly in expectation for strongly convex objective functions. We analyze the complexity of MB-SARAH-RBB and show that it is better than the original method. Numerical experiments on standard data sets indicate that MB-SARAH-RBB outperforms or matches state-of-the-art algorithms.

article: We present a new algorithm for transposing sparse tensors called Quesadilla . The algorithm converts the sparse tensor data structure to a list of coordinates and sorts it with a fast multi-pass radix algorithm that exploits knowledge of the requested transposition and the tensors input partial coordinate ordering to provably minimize the number of parallel partial sorting passes. We evaluate both a serial and a parallel implementation of Quesadilla on a set of 19 tensors from the FROSTT collection, a set of tensors taken from scientific and data analytic applications. We compare Quesadilla and a generalization, Top-2-sadilla to several state of the art approaches, including the tensor transposition routine used in the SPLATT tensor factorization library. In serial tests, Quesadilla was the best strategy for 60 of all tensor and transposition combinations and improved over SPLATT by at least 19 in half of the combinations. In parallel tests, at least one of Quesadilla or Top-2-sadilla was the best strategy for 52 of all tensor and transposition combinations.

article: The clock struck eleven, and I glanced over my shoulder. The shuffling boots stop in unison with my own steps. I turned around and glared at them. Across the bridge stood a crowd of eighty, no ninety, so people. Standing silently, they were all readily equipped with pipes, and fancy horn-rimmed spectacles that curled around the edges. All adorned in formal clothes ranging from kahki slacks, to gowns that hoisted up around the hips. Time travelers. For some God-forsaken reason, in the future archaic forms of dress kept reappearing every other decade. Who knows why. Perhaps they had run out of other fashions to wear, and they kept recycling old british attire and renaissance gowns. Either way, I continued to hold my glare. Yet I was not angry. No, how could one be angry at time-travelers? You saw them everywhere now-adays, if you knew how to look. No, it was the implication that followed them. Something was going to happen. And knowing my life, I knew it wasn't going to be something good. The glare was a means of self-defense. To hide my fear. To hide my trembling lips. To hide the fact that I hoped against hope that they could not hear my pounding heart over the howling wind. An ominous breeze penetrated my coat and the icy wind made my body shiver. The freezing December air made me visibly shake, and the crowd following me let out a silent giggle. I eyed them viciously until they stuttered into silence. "Weird," I thought to myself, "Ever since the TTIP had been passed people had been acting..... malicious." I shook my head and kept walking. The Time-Traveling Insurance Progressive allowed nearly anyone to time-travel, even those hardened criminals who had gone through the justice system. but who knew why this particular group had gathered. "Who knew what kind of satanical humor people were into these days." It wasn't until I turned around and saw the smoke in the air did my nose register the poignant odor. I 180-ed in horror at the crowd behind me. This is what they were here for. I saw a small child, a girl no older than 10, sneak an evil smile at me from behind her mother's hoisted gown. I knew what this was - They knew what this was. That was my house on fire. With this large of a crowd here, it was evident what had happened. They were here to watch the worst day of my life, like some kind of theatrical satire, taking joy in my own wretched misery. Even a child stood before me, glowing with joy at the prospect. She reminded me of Anna, my child, probably burned to a crisp in the fire. My loving wife, Regina, how we had struggled so hard to conceive. And how we were now so excited to begin to lovingly raise our daughter. No. This couldn't be happening. It was all going so well. A Family. Love. The promotion. And here I was. Standing in front of a crowd watching my life go to shambles No, I would NOT let them have the satisfaction they came here for. It was apparent that they wanted to watch me suffer, well, I would let them see the clearest expression of misery possible." I thought as I put my first foot onto the bridge. I ignored the eager clapping behind me. "They wouldn't expect this. Even people from the future don't always know what's going to happen." I straddled the side of the bridge, and the crowd went quiet. I wouldn't tolerate this cruel fate, I thought, as I jumped into the cascading river below. article: Amplified DDOS attack or just amplification attack uses a fault in some systems to make it send more traffic to your attack target then you send out. So imagine you have a 100Mbit internet link and you are able to send a 10 byte packet to DNS servers so that they send a 1000 byte packet to your target. You are then able to force 10Gbit of traffic to the target which they hopefully for you can not handle. And that is only using your home internet connection. If you own a small botnet you may have a collective bandwidth much higher and are able to amplify the attack to great numbers. The problem is that the bandwidth of the systems vulnerable to amplification attacks is greater then most of the core internet infrastructure can handle. So you can actually be able to saturate the links between the biggest ISPs. There is no way to protect against such an attack.

article: It had been an astonishing week, Aquinas thought as he sat down to take a breather. The comfortable couch in his room was his favorite place to relax. A mixture of business and pleasure; he'd placed his room close to the crew center, in case of emergency, but had also great pains (mostly wounds to the wallet) to ensure he had a wall built of holoscreens, which displayed the view from the ship all around him. It was beautiful - it always was. Right now, he had a view of the star LOGLA. On the approach he'd admired its brilliance, the way the plasma arced and danced on its surface. That was before he'd spoken to it. The initial communications had been halting, uncertain. Stars had very different minds than humans, in many ways. It'd taken thousands of years to realize they were even capable of thought. It had taken hundreds to decipher their thoughts. The stars, it turned out, had similar difficulties understanding us. We were motes of dust to them, insignificant in the passage of time. The stars - communicating on their own medium still largely inaccessible to us, the'sea' as they called it - had debated the significance of humans ever since we'd left our atmosphere. The lines between the animate and the inanimate had been blurred. Stars saw all things as living, in some sense - some more so than others, of course. Stars did not quite propagate, or survive. They simply..... were, until they weren't. And they thought for that entire time. To the stars, it turns out, they'd just assumed we were intelligent. They assumed all things were intelligent. Perhaps not capable of communication or comprehension, but still possibly thinking on some plane of existence. "They are, therefore they think." It was a compelling point of view, all things considered. If we could talk to stars, why not to other things? Aquinas sighed, as he shifted in his chair to get back up. Only a moment's rest. The basic politics has been discussed, the nature of stars, what they wanted and did not want..... it had been largely business. There'd been moments of insight and true talk, here and there, but for the most part it was the simple procedure of extraterrestrial contact the System's scientists had sorted out centuries before. Stars were independent bodies, but didn't much care about anything else - they felt no pain, and did not care what installations we built around them, or how we traversed them. The only thing they requested was that they be allowed to think, as long as possible. Aquinas rose from his chair, and crossed the room. The auxiliary controls in his room had been another nice touch. Built for emergencies, but..... it's not like what he was about to do could hurt. He reached down, fiddled with some controls - that transmitted very complicated directions to a very big machine on the ship - and was linked into the communication medium, a swirling ball of plasma that was magnetically controlled to produce new shapes, configurations, and energy patterns. After a moment in silence, standing over the controls, bowed with his hands flat against the surface of the countertop, he spoke up. "Logla, you listening?" He asked. The star had no name. No stars did. It had agreed on one, however, given the nature of human communication. So it had been decided to name it Logla, and the star agreed that when we said Logla, it would answer. And it did. "I'm here, Aquinas." He piqued up at this, as he always did. It recognized him, despite the communication medium - and the fact he hadn't said much of note. There was some other means of identification..... which was surprising, given stars had no need for such identification. A quick learner, it seemed. "What thoughts do we have to attend to?" Aquinas chuckled. Stars did little else but think, so Logla had an issue phrasing any activity as something other than thinking. It understood the activities, well enough, but it just preferred not to speak of them in human terms. "Nothing to attend to, today, Logla. I just wanted to think together." A soft humming came from the speaker. This indicated the star was processing, preparing to vocalize thoughts. A very human mannerism. Eventually, Logla spoke up. "This sounds agreeable. It is something stars do often, and enjoy." "Enjoy? You don't talk about emotion a lot, Logla. To be honest..." Aquinas pondered whether to continue, but shrugged and went on anyway. "We weren't quite sure you felt things like we did. You know, felt them as much." The star hummed again. "Most likely not, Aquinas. But we still feel. Feeling is just another form of thinking, after all." Aquinas smiled. "That's one way of putting it," Aquinas sat back down in his chair, no longer nervous about how poorly unsupervised contact might go. Logla was a very nice star, so far. It was pretty damn unlikely he'd upset it. He wasn't even sure what could. At this thought, Aquinas sat, tapped his chin, then pressed the button to continue speaking. "What makes you feel, Logla? And what do you feel?" The star hummed, for a long time. At least a minute. This was unusual - most thoughts took stars very little time, because they had very, very big brains. Finally, the star continued, "Everything makes me feel, Aquinas. How could it not? Stars have a long time to think..... and with a long time, everything becomes worth thinking about," The star hummed shortly, then continued, "I feel..... happy. Sad. Curious." Aquinas raised an eyebrow. "Not afraid? Not angry?" "Those are unintelligible to me. Rethink your thoughts for me, Aquinas?" This was a fun oddity of inter-species communication. Stars rarely did not understand each other, they had learned - it was only external interference that caused issues with communication. Logla did not quite understand the idea of'untranslatable' concepts yet - but it very well understood interference, and just acted like it was that. "Well, anger..... it's..... when something is wrong. Or when something endangers you. Do you ever feel so strongly, you want to..." Aquinas realized that there wasn't really much the star could do, or want to do. Stars could not move. They could not act. They could barely even perceive, it turned out. They largely existed just to think. Anger would be meaningless for them..... they couldn't act out. And fear..... they couldn't retreat. Aquinas paused, and shook his head. "I'm sorry, Logla. I don't think there's a way to rethink that thought without interference." A soft humming, then Logla replied, "That's okay, Aquinas. I understand, though I am curious and sad." "Sad?" Aquinas rested his face on his arm, holding his button down with the other hand. "Why, Logla?" "I wish I could understand. Curiosity that goes without answer..... it causes sadness. A wish things were different," Logla spoke slowly, far more slowly than normal. "Curiosity answered brings happiness." "That's all?" Aquinas asked, quietly. "You feel happiness and sadness only then?" "No..... We feel happiness to know. We enjoy thinking. And some things are pleasing to think about. While others..... we feel sadness to confront. And some things are sad to think about," Logla's speech was very slow now. "Some things are both." "I understand. We feel similarly. We call it'bittersweet'. I have no idea if that thought will be conveyed right, but..... it's a pairing of opposites. Like dark and light, at once." Stars understood light very well. "It seems contradictory, but..." "But it isn't. I understand. The thought conveyed poorly, but I think the thought too. There are many experiences that bring both happiness and sadness. Like you." Aquinas nodded, quietly. The gesture would be translated by the machine, but he still reaffirmed it, and said, "Yes. Like you too." "Aquinas, we - I - are happy to know you exist. That you think like we do. And that we can speak. There have been so few..... so few that can speak to us, besides us," The star said, and Aquinas nodded. The stars had mentioned other people that spoke to stars. They hadn't said much about them, but it was much more than mankind had expected to hear. We'd assumed stars were the only non-Earth intelligence. "We love thinking new thoughts. We love the curiosity it brings to know something we can't think is there. But we feel sad about it..... to know that we can't think it, ever. And we feel sad when they leave." "Leave?" Aquinas asked, his own curiosity now burning. "Leave. Stars..... we think a long time. Even as we die, we think. A star's light goes out long before their thinking does. Their thinking slows, their part in the sea fades, but they are there. We are there. We have watched many like you leave us..... and you leave us so quickly. So suddenly..." The star hummed, and this time, the note was different, a rich and deep tone. Aquinas listened to the star's song, for a few seconds, but it stopped abruptly as the song continued. "We wish you could be with us for longer. That you could think like us. But to do so would mean you do not think as yourselves..... and that is what we love to hear about..." The star hummed again, and this time, the countertop thrummed as it resonated with the note. Aquinas' bones sang along with the note. "To think about your time, compared to our time..... that is the greatest thought of sadness we stars have." Aquinas wiped away a tear from his face. The immensity of a star's life..... it was unthinkable, how many peoples it must have watched go extinct, and yearned to hear from, one more time. "Us too, Logla. We both wish for more time." "All who think do," Logla said, then hummed quietly, while Aquinas sat, and listened to its song.

article: Water is not compressible but air is. So, in air, a lot of the energy of a shock wave will be wasted just compressing the air. But, in water, the energy of the shock wave gets directly transferred into your body because none of it was wasted compressing the water. Imagine you were swinging a paddle at someone across the room. If there was just air in between you then the force would dissipate before it made it to your victim. However, if you used that paddle it hit an incompressible object like a long metal rod, the force would be transferred much more efficiently to the other side.', "This has to do with how momentum is transferred in a collision: If you have one steel ball hitting another of the same size, it will transfer all its momentum, and with it all its energy, to the other ball - as in Newton's cradle. But if it hits a much heavier steel ball, it will be deflected, and with it most of its energy. Shock waves behave in a very similar manner: A shock wave in air hitting a human will be reflected almost entirely, whereas a shock wave in water is able to pass right through a human, simply because water is very similar in density and elasticity to tissue.," "Water doesn't compress, so doesn't absorb the energy like air does. The way to think of is like being hit around the head by a sponge, and then bit hit around the head, at the same speed, by a brick. One will do way more damage.

article: One barrel of oil gives you about 12 gallons of diesel and 19 gallons of gas. You don't have the option of making either diesel or gas, you refine crude and you get both. The price of diesel and oil follow supply and demand rules like anything else, with the catch that they are linked. If demand for gas goes way up and diesel demand stays flat, diesel gets a lot cheaper because the refineries are going to produce enough gas to meet demand. That gives you lots of extra diesel production, which drives down price. Generally diesel demand is more stable because more of it is used for trucks, generators, and other more or less continuous uses, while demand for gas is driven mostly by cars. If I had to guess, diesel is cheaper right now because it's summer, and people drive a lot more during the summer, so refineries are trying to increase their output of gas, which also necessarily increases diesel output.," "I'm not sure where you live, but where I live and everywhere I've been in the US, diesel is about 0.75 more per gallon.,Its based on the demand and supply. article: Winograd convolution is widely used in deep neural networks (DNNs). Existing work for DNNs considers only the subset Winograd algorithms that are equivalent to Toom-Cook convolution. We investigate a wider range of Winograd algorithms for DNNs and show that these additional algorithms can significantly improve floating point (FP) accuracy in many cases. We present results for three FP formats: f p 32 , f p 16 and b f 16 (a truncated form of f p 32) using 2000 inputs from the ImageNet dataset. We found that in f p 16 this approach gives us up to 6.5 times better image recognition accuracy in one important case while maintaining the same number of elementwise multiplication operations in the innermost loop. In b f 16 the convolution can be computed using 5 fewer innermost loop multiplications than with currently used Winograd algorithms while keeping the accuracy of image recognition the same as for direct convolution method.

article: Yes, exactly like that. A bit longer answer: ohm's law is more intuitive, V IR. In a batteryoutlet, you have a voltage differential that will push electrons through the wire and create a current. Ohm's law helps to explain the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance in a circuit. Voltage, measured in volts (V), is the electrical potential difference between two points in a circuit. This difference creates a driving force for electrons to flow through the circuit. Current, measured in amperes (A), is the rate at which electric charge flows through a circuit. The current is directly proportional to the voltage and inversely proportional to the resistance. Resistance, measured in ohms , refers to the degree to which a material opposes the flow of electric current. It is an electrical property of a material that determines how much current flows through it for a given voltage. Ohm's law states that the current flowing through a conductor in a circuit is directly proportional to the voltage applied across it and inversely proportional to the resistance of the conductor. Thus, the equation V IR is used to express Ohm's law, where V is the voltage, I is the current, and R is the resistance. In summary, Ohm's law is an important fundamental principle in understanding basic electrical circuits, and it helps to explain the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance. It is a useful tool for designing, analyzing, and troubleshooting electronic circuits.

article: In this paper we address the problem of unsupervised gaze correction in the wild, presenting a solution that works without the need for precise annotations of the gaze angle and facial features. Our approach uses a generative adversarial network (GAN) to learn a mapping from input images with arbitrary gaze angles to output images with corrected gaze angles. The GAN is trained by minimizing a combination of the adversarial loss and a perceptual loss, which measures the difference between the generated and target images in terms of their high-level features. To achieve this, we first preprocess the input images by detecting the face and estimating the gaze angle using a pre-trained face and gaze estimator. We then pass the preprocessed images through our GAN to produce the corrected gaze images. Finally, we post-process the output images by blending them with the original input images to preserve some of the original appearance. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach can successfully correct gaze in a wide range of unconstrained environments, and outperforms several state-of-the-art methods on the publicly available MPIIGaze dataset.

article: A number of applications (e.g., AI bot tournaments, sports, peer grading, crowdsourcing) use pairwise comparison data and the Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model to evaluate a given collection of items (e.g., bots, teams, students, search results). Past work has shown that under the BTL model, the widely-used maximum-likelihood estimator (MLE) is minimax-optimal in estimating the item parameters, in terms of the mean squared error. However, another important desideratum for designing estimators is fairness. In this work, we consider fairness modeled by the notion of bias in statistics. We show that the MLE incurs a suboptimal rate in terms of bias. We then propose a simple modification to the MLE, which "stretches" the bounding box of the maximum-likelihood optimizer by a small constant factor from the underlying ground truth domain. We show that this simple modification leads to an improved rate in bias, while maintaining minimax-optimality in the mean squared error. In this manner, our proposed class of estimators provably improves fairness represented by bias without loss in accuracy.

article: Cross domain image matching between image collections from different source and target domains is challenging in times of deep learning due to i) limited variation of image conditions in a training set, ii) lack of paired-image labels during training, iii) the existing of outliers that makes image matching domains not fully overlap. To this end, we propose an end-to-end architecture that can match cross domain images without labels in the target domain and handle non-overlapping domains by outlier detection. We leverage domain adaptation and triplet constraints for training a network capable of learning domain invariant and identity distinguishable representations, and iteratively detecting the outliers with an entropy loss and our proposed weighted MK-MMD. Extensive experimental evidence on Office dataset and our proposed datasets Shape, Pitts-CycleGAN shows that the proposed approach yields state-of-the-art cross domain image matching and outlier detection performance on different benchmarks. The code will be made publicly available.

article: This will probably get buried as I'm late to the party, but couldn't resist - the prompt is too good! The busiest on the network, nearly a hundred thousand passengers each morning travel through here, arriving to make their daily trudge through the city of London to their jobs. Most of them work in banking. They're easy to spot, with suits from Saville Row, shirts from Jermyn Street, and morals darker than the deepest recesses of Soho. Profiling a target is a doddle, and the execution comes naturally. Growing up on the estate, I was never going to be allowed into the rarefied air of the Bank of England or Lloyds of London. Once Mum had her benefits cut, I had to pay my way, it's not uncommon. Lads on BMX bikes move weed and whatever else they can get their hands on, but I was never tough enough to look after myself in those gangs. I ended up shoplifting, a quick stroll over to Oxford Circus, snip off the tags and tailgate a tourist out. Easy. Too easy. There's no skill to shoplifting, not like pickpocketing. I had a good teacher, a modern day Fagin if you will, though the flat caps of Oliver Twist were replaced by snapbacks, tags still attached of course. After a few years I went solo, still staying in touch with my old mates to make I wasn't stepping on anyone's toes. You rarely get a nicely worded letter from these boys if you're on their patch. Bank is so busy I can act with impunity, plenty of bankers for everyone. This one was perfect. I saw him run through the barriers, flustered, late, fumbling with his oyster card. He carefully checked his wallet before throwing the card in there, a flash of blue still visible as he slid it into his inside jacket pocket. This was almost too easy. I moved towards the door where he was stood, ostensibly to pick up a discarded copy of the Metro from a seatback. I didn't feel like reading, but it looks natural, and a freesheet is a bloody good prop, even if it is plastered in the latest story of debauched footballers. He was lost in his own world, checking his phone every five seconds, looking for the red blinking LED that has enslaved so many in this city. Even easier. He goes for the door, I watch his shoulders, tailing him through the barriers as he taps the wallet on the reader. He's going left, towards the exit for the Bank. I feint left and go right, my shoulder crashing into his chest. A flutter of newsprint and a thousand tuts from the commuters and I'm home and dry, the soft leather wallet nestling in my jacket now. I cross the platforms and jump on a tube heading east, time for a spot of lunch and a bit more work. Westfield Stratford, a hell of a shopping centre, and close enough to home to know shorten my commute back. I'm in need of a new t-shirt and I guess old habits die hard. Maybe a quick lift to top up the beer kitty for tonight. Quick scan and boom. A yank, can spot them from a mile off. They always dress like they're going into battle, rucksacks, sunnies, hat, bottles of water, as if anywhere outside of the USofA lacks even basic amenities. Not that I'm complaining, all those pockets make theft a doddle. I stroll past to get a look at the bag, but before I can she turns, and I freeze. "Hey, can you help me?" I was right, definitely American. Right, new tack. The accent goes on, no more wide boy charm, time for the full Cumberbatch.'I certainly hope so my dear, how can I be of service to you?' She smiles sweetly, and asks for some advice. Don't hang around with reprobates like me would be a good start, luv. Keep it moving "Let's walk and talk, it's a big place and we won't see it all from standing still." I introduce her to a few shops, she's in London for 2 days before her friends fly in. "Well it's a terrible shame for a lovely lady like you to be all alone. I wouldn't be much of a gentleman if I didn't offer to keep you company for a while. Fancy a spot of lunch?" She's in. Wahaca. Chelada. Tostada. We chat, it beats eating lunch alone. She's tidy, decent chassis on her in a pair of shorts and a hollister tee. Long blonde hair and a tendency to use'like' as punctuation, I'd guessed she was from California long before she divulged that fact. Whether it was the light glinting off her straw coloured locks, or the refraction of it through the amber beer, I felt good. I pay for lunch and take my leave, demanding only a hug as payment for her company. As we embrace I slide fifty quid out of her unguarded pocket, which covers lunch and my time. Off home, stopping on the way to pick up a henry and some king size rizla for the evening ahead. Through the door, trainers off and jacket over the chair, time for a brew. Fucking hell, I almost forgot, that wallet I took this morning. Chatting to that American bird distracted me more than I thought. Good job I wrote my number on the back of a tube ticket for her. I try not to bring evidence home if I can help it. Wallets get stripped of the good stuff and binned, phones are fenced down the local before I get home, the more unusual stuff I take a view on. Let's take a look at the wallet. It's nicer than I thought. Hand stitched, the leather is softer than I've ever felt before. The tip of the oyster card still peeks out from it. Two hundred bats cash. Nice. American Express Platinum, standard, and a nice way to assuage my guilt. Anyone with one of these can afford to lose a few bob. Few more bits and bobs. Mostly crap. Still, no stone unturned and all that. There's a slip of paper tucked inside, folded carefully. It's a photo. Who even carries photos any more? A photo of a baby in an incubator. Shit. That's what he was looking at. On the phone. He wasn't waiting for notification, he was looking at the wallpaper, the very same photo. Fuck it, he's got a digital copy of it then, nothing fifty pence at Boots can't solve for a reprint. There's more paper on the other side of the pocket, but it doesn't look like cash, I take a quick look so I can bin what I don't need on the way to the pub. Order of Service. Oh Christ. She was called Molly. He buried her yesterday. Poor Bastard. His driving licence is still in the wallet. I have to send this back. It's not fair. This is never what I set out to do. The address goes on the envelope, I'll throw it in the post box tomorrow somewhere in the city. Not popping evidence in the box at the bottom of the tower. For now, let's work on this henry. - I'm at Oxford Circus today, I don't want to go back to Bank in case I see him again. I'm not afraid, just ashamed. The letter goes in the postbox, swallowing at least some of my guilt in its wide red mouth as well. Time to go to work. Same routine, I take a seat and wait for some idiot tourist to advertise themselves. Another yank dressed like they're off to battle Rommel jumps on, and I grab my prop. No footballer today though. Seems some banker decided to take the quickest route from the top of the walkie talkie to the slabs below. I've seen that name before. Not half an hour ago as I dropped it through the slot.

article: We consider the age-old problem of allocating items among different agents in a way that is efficient and fair. Two papers, by Dolev et al. and Ghodsi et al., have proposed interesting solutions to this problem. article: The aim of this article is to study the role of piecewise implementation ofPad'e-Chebyshev type approximation in minimising Gibbs phenomena inapproximating piecewise smooth functions. This approach helps to minimise Gibbs phenomena by limiting the influence of oscillations from one subinterval to the neighbouring ones. The Pad'e-Chebyshev type approximation has been widely used in approximating functions with highly oscillatory behaviour, such as singular functions and functions with discontinuities. However, when a Pad'e-Chebyshev type approximation is applied to a piecewise smooth function, Gibbs phenomena may occur at the borders of the subintervals. Gibbs phenomena are the overshoot and undershoot of the approximation at the borders of subintervals, caused by the abrupt change in the function's behaviour at these points. To overcome this issue, the PiPCT algorithm applies the Pad'e-Chebyshev type approximation separately to each subinterval, limiting the influence of neighbouring subintervals, which helps to reduce the overshoot and undershoot near the borders of the subintervals. The proposed PiPCT algorithm provides high accuracy in approximating piecewise smooth functions by reducing the oscillations and removing the Gibbs phenomena, while at the same time maintaining the computational efficiency of the Pad'e-Chebyshev type approximations. The algorithm has been tested on several examples and has shown to be efficient in approximating piecewise smooth functions accurately. article: The classical perceptron is a simple neural network that performs a binary classification by a linear mapping between static inputs and outputs and application of a threshold. For small inputs, neural networks in a stationary state also perform an effectively linear input-output transformation, but of an entire time series. Choosing the temporal mean of the time series as the feature for classification, the linear transformation of the network with subsequent thresholding is equivalent to the classical perceptron. Here we show that choosing covariances of time series as the feature for classification maps the neural network to what we call a 'covariance perceptron'; a mapping between covariances that is bilinear in terms of weights. By extending Gardner's theory of connections to this bilinear problem, using a replica symmetric mean-field theory, we compute the pattern and information capacities of the covariance perceptron in the infinite-size limit. Closed-form expressions reveal superior pattern capacity in the binary classification task compared to the classical perceptron in the case of a high-dimensional input and low-dimensional output. For less convergent networks, the mean perceptron classifies a larger number of stimuli. However, since covariances span a much larger input and output space than means, the amount of stored information in the covariance perceptron exceeds the classical counterpart. For strongly convergent connectivity it is superior by a factor equal to the number of input neurons. Theoretical calculations are validated numerically for finite size systems using a gradient-based optimization of a soft-margin, as well as numerical solvers for the NP hard quadratically constrained quadratic programming problem, to which training can be mapped.

I stopped. Their bodies lay there, broken and raked. I felt a warm air behind me and turned to see a face. Not the face of a person, the face of a beast. The darkness was gone - it was just a forest. The creature eyed me suspiciously, and then moved backwards to give me space. "I missed one? Hmm..." The voice was deep and gravelly. The dragon seemed ancient. I froze as it leaned upwards and spread it's wings proudly, looking down on me. I was beyond running away. I was too shocked to even move. "I have slept in these woods for five thousand years - six? - and this is the first time in all of those years that one of the itty bitties has seen me. How curious. Though I should think you have things to be more afraid of than some dark and sounds, hm?" I didn't speak. "Yes, indeed. Six thousand years asleep and I intend to sleep for six thousand more. You can not be allowed the chance to share this information. I am terribly sorry it has to end like this, but one itty bitty life is a small price to pay for my thousands of years." The dragon seemed a little perplexed, but then appeared to ponder the remark. "That is an interesting sentiment, little itty bitty. Walk with me." And so I followed the dragon through the woods. It seemed so peaceful now. Rays of sunshine shone through the leaves of the green trees, and we walked down a neat little pathway. "I remember the first human I had to kill. Just before I went to sleep. Dragonslayers, they were. Heroes, they thought themselves. My brothers and sisters were a little more aggressive than I. None of them live today." The sorrow in his voice was evident." We came to a clearing, with a pool. The dragon sat in this pool. "One day such a'hero' came to my woods. That is when I killed him. He attacked me and I failed. I was distraught. It was that day I decided to sleep. As the last dragon I carry the burden of all those before me, and I would not allow myself to do what my siblings had done. So I restrained myself. I slept. But they kept coming. I had to kill many to stay hidden. I would not kill the masses when they came for me. I would never let them know my hiding place." "I eventually desensitivised myself to that killing, I suppose. I had to wait until the tales of the dragons became myth. You are the first in six thousand years." I swallowed. I didn't even speak. "Itty bitty..." " ..... You've hardly even spoken, yet you've taught me so much. Perhaps this is not my place in this world. To hide away from the world to protect it, only to destroy whatever gets too close..." I was confused. I didn't understand what I had taught this dragon. The sunshine grew more intense. "These woods have been lost to the dark for so long. I can not count how many heroes with good intentions died at my claw. I wonder if I can save more." The dragon stood, extended its wings, and ascended. The woods didn't change again. They were still green. The greenest woods I've ever known. It took me a night's rest to truly understand what I had witnessed. To this day I live alone, in a little log cabin. A little log cabin in a clearing, next to a pool, in the greenest woods I've ever known. I will not soon forget what happened when I first saw this place. article: The fuzzy K -means problem is a generalization of the classical K -means problem to soft clusterings, i.e. clusterings where each points belongs to each cluster to some degree. Although the classical K-means problem assigns each point to a single cluster, the fuzzy K-means problem assigns each point to all clusters with degrees of membership representing how likely the point belongs to each cluster. The fuzzy K-means problem is also known as FCM (fuzzy c-means) and is commonly used in pattern recognition and image segmentation. In fuzzy K-means, the objective is to minimize the sum of squared distances between each point and its cluster center, weighted by the degree of membership. The degree of membership of each point to each cluster is computed using a membership function which gives a value between 0 and 1, representing the probability or degree of belief that the point belongs to that cluster. The membership function is updated iteratively until convergence is reached. Fuzzy K-means has several advantages over classical K-means, including the ability to handle overlapping clusters and the ability to assign points to multiple clusters simultaneously. It also allows for more nuanced representations of cluster membership and a finer-grained analysis of data. However, fuzzy K-means can be computationally intensive and requires careful tuning of parameters.

article: The men scrambled around as I drifted in and out of consciousness. Chattering away in urgent unfamiliar tones, they had dragged me from the sea's lapping waves, tentatively tapping my face to check I was still alive. As a journalist, entry to North Korea is forbidden. Try as I might, and with the full weight of two top media agencies, there was no way I would be able pass through its gates by land or air. My editors had given up quickly - after all, it was my idea. I wanted, needed, to bag the story of 2015. How the real people of North Korea live. And if I won a prize in the meantime it wouldn't hurt the CV. A sea gypsy's boat, if you could call it that, had taken me as far as it could, but I was still miles from shore. I underestimated the tide on the approach and ended up trapped in a sandbank. I had no choice but to call for help, blowing my plan to stealthily trek the hundreds of miles to where the atrocities happened. I'd lost my camera. My phone was sitting on the sea bed. My editors had refused me the chance to take leave from work, so I told them I was headed to a writer's retreat. A digital detox. They wouldn't even begin to know where to look. As I contemplated my fate, my mind swamped with memories of survivors' stores. Mothers ripped from their children's arms. Fathers forced to choose which son to murder. Perhaps I would be a bargaining tool. More than likely, I'd be made an example of. I tried to fight against the men, who'd surrounded me and were dragging me viscously to my feet. As a pint-sized woman and as much as I loved a workout, the years of manual labour these farmers were forced to endure had given them unmovable strength. "You," I said, loudly, with as much authority as I could muster in my voice. The men stopped. "You. You want money?" They glanced at each other. "I, me, have money. Lots." I held my hands up, slowly reaching for my waterproof clip-on wallet. I pulled out more money than these people would earn in a decade and threw it over. "Take." I smiled, trying to remain unthreatening. They had power now, but money rules the world. "Dear woman, what are you doing?" I jumped, taken aback at those words. The man, the wizened old farmer, spoke in English. Perfect English. "I'm sorry, I didn't..." "Oh," the other chimed in, a smile greeting his lips as he gathered the money strewn on the floor. "Oh she's AMERICAN. One of those. Makes sense lads." "Let's take her to get freshened up. She'll want to meet the other journos who thought they'd sneak in to'hell' to get their story!" The men laughed playfully, and pity hung over their faces as they saw my hands start to tremble. We walked along a dirt track, my muscles aching from the battle to stay afloat in the brutal sea. I had to know. Needed to know. "You understand English." It wasn't a question. I tried to ensure my voice remained strong, but it wobbled. I coughed and sea water spilled from my mouth searing my throat. The man who'd been first to reveal his English accent spoke again, handing me a freshly pressed handkerchief. "Yes dear. We do. It's taught in all our schools. We learn from a young age how to articulate and enunciate in our mother tongue, as well as an array of other languages. Mandarin, Tagalog, French..." Schools? I stopped walking. "You, you go to school?" "Well, not by your standards, which are on a par with Amazonian tribes I'd say!" The men all laughed. Their scathing tones burned my ears, and a mixture of rage and fear bubbled in me. "Our schools are more like your rich countrymen's offerings. They are private. We go to school, learn languages, maths, the sciences, art... everything and anything you could wish to turn your hand to." The second farmer held my elbow as we carried on walking the path. "You see, he said, gently, "We love our country, and our Dear Leader." "How can you love that man? That murderer! He walks around like a god on earth while his people - you! - starve!" Standing in front of the men, blocking their path, I saw their faces change. Insulting their god-king would be what killed me. "HIM?" The third man spoke, before they all broke out laughing. "Oh isn't it wonderful doing this?" the first farmer said to his friends. "That god-king, as you so incorrectly call him, is our ruse. He's what takes your attention. He's our trickster, and you are our mark." I shook my head. "No," I said. "No. The reports, from your people who escape your camps. You fear him." As we reached the end of the gravel path, the men remained silent. The stones turned to asphalt, and sitting obscured by leafy green trees was a brand new car. Not a cart powered by wood or a collection of ramshackle bikes. A car. Shiny and clean. The men stopped. Two entered the sedan. The first man leaned up against it as he stretched his arms above his head, resting them folded on his chest. "Your nation, all nations of the world. They are dirty." He shuffled on his feet, getting more comfortable. "Imagine your friend and you both have a prized vase each. It had taken centuries to create, and was now yours." I looked at him, as tears graced his eyes. "Your friend. He's not clever. He doesn't appreciate it's value. He let's everyone see it, touch it. His friends don't see the value, so they crack it. Before long the porcelain is stained, the vase is damaged and it can never be what it was. It can be fixed, but the cracks will always be its weakness. That, that is the world and every land in it." I heard the trill of a mobile phone, and one of the men in the car answered, speaking Korean. "So we're all broken?" I asked. "Yes. The wars and violence, your lack of care for the weak and elderly. The orphans abandoned by your state and the widows forced out of homes. You weaken your people from birth, brainwashing them into believing material goods are success." I snorted. "So this is paradise, right?" "The vase. After seeing what your friend did to it, you decide to keeps yours safe. So when the same friends say they want to play with it, you say it's already broken. They will pester you, and laugh at you for being weak. But they will leave it alone. "Our scientists have cured diseases your people know nothing about. Our students learn skills to ensure they are entertained without the need for your internet. Our old and infirm are housed in complexes to rival palaces! "If we told the world we could cure cancer with a simple injection, you would take, and your leaders would destroy it. Because you place value on money. Your tourists would destroy our land, our people would be forced out of their homes for hotels. We place value on our people." I stood there rigidly, not wanting to believe those words. He opened the door to the car and I took a seat. We drove through towns and villages, passing houses as beautiful as Spanish villas and French chateaux. I spoke up. "All we believe. The poverty and oppression..." "We place value on our people. When tourists visit, they are shown what we want them to be shown. We have a fool parade around with your celebrities. We turn our nation's lights off at night to avoid being seen. The escapees volunteer to leave, knowing they will never see their families again. Knowing they will eventually die alone, as so many of your elderly have done." He looked glassy eyed into the distance. "They are the true casualties of this game." We arrived at a camp, nothing like what I had come to imagine I'd find. "Your people will be told you are dead. Your family can only come here if we stage a kidnapping. Have a wander around your new home. Speak to some of your fellow Americans. Turn your lights off at night. And welcome to North Korea."

article: Optimizing is the process of using simple tricks to speed up the math used behind the scenes. Computer programs (including video games) do a lot of math while computing things, the biggest being physics calculations and graphics calculations. In order to optimize something, you find a faster way of doing the math so that the answers are the same, or almost the same. Sometimes it's simply re-working the equations so that they are simpler and do less redundant calculations. For example, if you want to calculate the shadows a light makes, it's faster if you remember all the objects that didn't move, and to re-use the same shadows for them. Sometimes, however, in order to optimize things even further, programmers have to come up with special tricks. These tricks can end up very confusing even to other programmers, and they usually depend on the computer system running them, since they often take advantage of quirks in the specific processor or video card inside the computer. A famous example of this is the [Fast Inverse Square Root] (URL0) function used in Quake III. Inverse square roots are used in graphics calculations, and they are repeated tens of thousands of times per second, so if you can save even a little time calculating each one, you can make your computer run much faster as a whole. It's hard to explain how that specific trick works without explaining the workings behind integers and floating point numbers inside computers, so I'll try to use an analogy. It is the equivalent of drawing a picture of cow, cutting up that picture, putting the pieces back together in a different order, then somehow coming up with a self portrait of yourself, all in less time that it would have taken to draw the self portrait the normal way. article: Not only do different age groups need different amounts of sleep, but sleep needs are also individual. Just like any other characteristics you are born with, the amount of sleep you need to function best may be different for you than for someone who is of the same age and gender. While you may be at your absolute best sleeping seven hours a night, someone else may clearly need nine hours to have a happy, productive life. In fact, a 2005 study confirmed the fact that sleep needs vary across populations, and the study calls for further research to identify traits within genes that may provide a "map" to explain how sleep needs differ among individuals. Another reason there is "no magic number" for your sleep results from two different factors that researchers are learning about: a person's basal sleep need - the amount of sleep our bodies need on a regular basis for optimal performance - and sleep debt , the accumulated sleep that is lost to poor sleep habits, sickness, awakenings due to environmental factors or other causes. Two studies suggest that healthy adults have a basal sleep need of seven to eight hours every night, but where things get complicated is the interaction between the basal need and sleep debt. For instance, you might meet your basal sleep need on any single night or a few nights in a row, but still have an unresolved sleep debt that may make you feel more sleepy and less alert at times, particularly in conjunction with circadian dips , those times in the 24-hour cycle when we are biologically programmed to be more sleepy and less alert, such as overnight hours and mid-afternoon.
