article: Actually it is because the focus of the two technologies is completely different. Transmission is bit by bit, there may be grouping of bits for error checking reasons, but otherwise each bit has to be sent individually. In contrast memory and storage need to be indexed, by grouping bits of 8 into a byte, you gain significant improvements in performance and reduced cost. So bandwidth is actually sending bits, so focuses on bits, storage is indexed by bytes, so is measured in bytes.','Changing it would be more confusing. Less knowledgeable consumers would be tricked by the fact that all the numbers are 8 times lower now, and more knowledgeable consumers would have to carefully check what units the connection speed was in.','Bits per second is a "natural" unit when talking about how much data can go through a certain connection. It's been a while since I've taken a communications systems course, so forgive me if I'm unclear when explaining this. "Bandwidth" is literally the 'width' of the 'frequency band' at which you are transmitting information. Frequency is measured in cycles per second (or Hz). Each cycle can then transmit only so many symbols without errors, and to compute this you do some math that I can't remember offhand, and that turns cycles-per-second into symbols-per-second. In binary, each symbol is one bit, so engineers naturally talk about transmission rates in bits per second, since that's what they compute when they go from "I have this wire" or "I have this transmitter and receiver" to "I can transmit this much data over it." I hope this made sense. Bits per second is the only reasonable unit for measuring transmission rates, from the perspective of engineers who design things with transmission rates. Bytes are the confusing unit, since computers were designed such that when you get information from them, you get them in chunks of 8 bits (which is then called a byte).', "A network cable doesn't care how you group your data together...all it cares is how many 1's and 0's it can push. Because, surprisingly enough, it doesn't always take 8 bits to sent a byte of information. Data packets have have headers and sometimes parity bits and error correction codes....that's not part of your data, but they still take time to transmit. Some network hardware uses data compression protocols, which mean each byte is likely going to take less than 8 bits to send. You just can't take megabits, divide by 8, and expect that to match your download rates. There is a lot more going on than that.

article: How long had it been? Five minutes? Yeah, probably five minutes. Guy can run a long way in five minutes, right? I slow down, first to a jog, then to a walk, then finally to a stop. I tried to run through it again, trying to make sense of it. I could still see him there, on his knees in the snow. I barely even had my gun drawn when he just gave up, fell to the ground. For just a few beats, I had been so confused I couldn't think. People normally panic at this point, they normally start acting a little crazy or begging me not to kill them. He had just stared at me with those empty eyes, then reached into his pocket for his wallet and stretched out his hand to me, waiting. I had taken the wallet, faltered a little. "Please..." he whispered to me. I had just turned and ran. Why had he unnerved me so much? Oh yeah, the wallet. That was the point of this whole thing, right? Who cares what that guy's deal was? I take the wallet out of my jacket, and take off my gloves to get a feel of it. Leather. Good stuff too. I flip it open, and there's just..... nothing. No credit cards, empty photo sleeves, nothing. Seriously? Is this a joke? Dude was just messing with me the whole time? No wait, there's another pocket, probably where the cash is, right? I reach in and pulled out a piece of paper. Just a little slip, folded in on itself a few times, creased and worn and frayed around the edges. What was this, some old love note? Oh hey, passwords maybe? I unfold it, but the light is so dim. There's a light on right up the alley so I make my way to it to get a good look. It's a note. The handwriting is smooth and deliberate, with one single sentence in the middle of the page. article: The concept of device-to-Device (D2D) communication as an underlay coexistence with cellular networks gains many advantages of improving system performance. In this paper, we model such a two-layer heterogenous network based on stochastic geometry approach. We aim at minimizing the expected power consumption of the D2D layer while satisfying the outage performance of both D2D layer and cellular layer. We consider two kinds of power control schemes. The first one is referred as to independent power control where the transmit powers are statistically independent of the networks and all channel conditions. The second is named as dependent power control where the transmit power of each user is dependent on its own channel condition. A closed-form expression of optimal independent power control is derived, and we point out that the optimal power control for this case is fixed and not relevant to the randomness of the network. For the dependent power control case, we propose an efficient way to find the close-to-optimal solution for the power-efficiency optimization problem. Numerical results show that dependent power control scheme saves about half of power that the independent power control scheme demands.

article: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are revolutionizing a variety of machine learning tasks, but they present significant computational challenges. Recently, FPGA-based accelerators have been proposed to improve the speed and efficiency of CNNs. Current approaches construct a single processor that computes the CNN layers one at a time; this single processor is optimized to maximize the overall throughput at which the collection of layers are computed. However, this approach leads to inefficient designs because the same processor structure is used to compute CNN layers of radically varying dimensions. We present a new CNN accelerator paradigm and an accompanying automated design methodology that partitions the available FPGA resources into multiple processors, each of which is tailored for a different subset of the CNN convolutional layers. Using the same FPGA resources as a single large processor, multiple smaller specialized processors result in increased computational efficiency and lead to a higher overall throughput. Our design methodology achieves 1.51x higher throughput than the state of the art approach on evaluating the popular AlexNet CNN on a Xilinx Virtex-7 FPGA. Our projections indicate that the benefit of our approach increases with the amount of available FPGA resources, already growing to over 3x over the state of the art within the next generation of FPGAs.

article: In this paper, we develop the first one-pass streaming algorithm for submodular maximization that does not evaluate the entire stream even once. By carefully subsampling each element of data stream, our algorithm enjoys the tightest approximation guarantees in various settings while having the smallest memory footprint and requiring the lowest number of function evaluations. More specifically, for a monotone submodular function and a p -matchoid constraint, our randomized algorithm achieves a 4 p approximation ratio (in expectation) with O (k) memory and O ( k m p) queries per element (k is the size of the largest feasible solution and m is the number of matroids used to define the constraint). For the non-monotone case, our approximation ratio increases only slightly to - 4 p 2 o (1). To the best or our knowledge, our algorithm is the first that combines the benefits of streaming and subsampling in a novel way in order to truly scale submodular maximization to massive machine learning problems. To showcase its practicality, we empirically evaluated the performance of our algorithm on a video summarization application and observed that it outperforms the state-of-the-art algorithm by up to fifty fold, while maintaining practically the same utility. Keywords: Submodular maximization, streaming, subsampling, data summarization, p -matchoids

article: Large number of weights in deep neural networks makes the models difficult to be deployed in low memory environments such as, mobile phones, IOT edge devices as well as "inferencing " time, and training time can also be significantly increased due to the large number of weights. To address this challenge, several techniques such as model compression, quantization, and pruning have been developed. Model compression techniques reduce the size of the model by removing redundant or unimportant parameters. One such technique is knowledge distillation, where a small model is trained to mimic the behavior of a larger model. Another technique is weight sharing, where multiple weights are forced to take the same value. Quantization techniques reduce the precision of the floating-point numbers used to represent model parameters. For example, converting floating-point numbers to fixed-point numbers with lower precision can reduce the size of the model while also improving inference speed. Pruning techniques selectively remove unimportant connections or neurons from the model while retaining its accuracy. This technique can significantly reduce the number of weights in a model without sacrificing accuracy. Overall, these techniques can help make deep neural networks more deployable in low-memory and low-computational-power environments.

article: An unconstrained crossword puzzle is a generalization of the constrained crossword problem. In this problem, only the word vocabulary, and optionally the grid dimensions are known. The strategies proposed cover the tasks of selection of words from a given vocabulary, selection of grid sizes, grid resizing and adjustments, metrics for word fitting, back-tracking techniques, and also clue generation. The strategies have been formulated based on a study of the effect of word sequence permutation order on grid fitting. An end-to-end algorithm that combines these strategies is presented, and its performance is analyzed. The techniques have been found to be successful in quickly producing well-packed puzzles of even large sizes. Finally, a few example puzzles generated by our algorithm are also provided.

article: We introduce a novel class of adjustment rules for a collection of beliefs. This is an extension of Lewis' imaging to absorb probabilistic evidence in generalized settings. Instead, it relies on a set of conditional beliefs and a set of evidential constraints that specify how new evidence should revise these beliefs. The resulting adjustment rules capture the idea of non-probabilistic belief revision, where beliefs about related propositions are adjusted together in a coherent way. This enables us to reason about partial or incomplete information, as well as conflicting or ambiguous evidence. Additionally, our approach is flexible enough to accommodate different types of inference, from deductive reasoning to abductive and inductive inference. This makes it a powerful tool for a wide range of applications, from decision making and planning to natural language understanding and cognitive modeling. Overall, our approach to belief revision offers a promising framework for reasoning under uncertainty in diverse domains.

article: Recommender systems (RS) are increasingly present in our daily lives, especially since the advent of Big Data, which allows for storing all kinds of information about users' preferences. Personalized RS analyze this information and provide recommendations that are tailored to a specific user's interests or needs. There are two main types of RS: collaborative filtering and content-based filtering. Collaborative filtering makes recommendations based on similarities between users. It looks at the items a user has interacted with (purchased, rated, viewed, etc.) and then identifies other users who have shown similar behavior. Recommendations are then made based on what these similar users have interacted with in the past. Content-based filtering, on the other hand, uses data about items themselves to make recommendations. It looks at the features of an item such as genre, director, or actor, and then recommends other items with similar features. Hybrid RS combine both collaborative and content-based filtering to provide even more accurate and personalized recommendations. RS can be found in many different contexts, such as e-commerce sites, social media platforms, and music or video streaming services. They can help users discover new products, services, or content that they may not have otherwise found on their own.

article: We propose a two-layer cache mechanism to speed up dynamic WFST decoding with personalized language models. The first layer is a public cache that stores most of the static part of the WFST and can be shared among all users. When a user makes a request for decoding using their personalized model, the system first checks the private cache to see if the decoding task has been performed before. If it has, the result is immediately returned from the cache. If not, the system checks the public cache to see if the necessary parts of the static WFST are already stored there. If they are, the system retrieves them and performs the decoding task. If not, the system retrieves the necessary parts of the static WFST from the disk and stores them in the public cache for other users to use. This two-layer cache mechanism can significantly speed up dynamic WFST decoding with personalized language models, as many of the necessary parts of the WFST can be retrieved from the cache rather than having to be fetched from disk or generated from scratch. Proof nets provide a way to visualize the structure of a proof in linear logic, and this can be useful for studying various aspects of language, such as meaning composition, quantification, and tense. For instance, proof nets have been used to study the interpretation of pronouns and their anaphoric relations in natural language. They have also been used to analyze phenomena such as presupposition projection and scope of quantifiers. Additionally, proof nets have been used to model temporal expressions and their use in discourse. Overall, the use of linear logic and proof nets provides a valuable tool for analyzing natural language, and their application can help us gain a better understanding of the complex properties of language form and meaning.

article: It smells like cigarettes. It always does in here. Nobody has smoked in here for years, but it's not an odor that time can easily erase. Something about the smel and dim lighting is soothing; refreshing, even. The only feature of the otherwise non-descript watering hole that is McNally's Irish pub, is the lack of features. Along the glossy downtown strip, it's a shadow, creeping across the face of glamour. No neon lights, no Happy Hour specials posted on the door. Just a relic from a former era when a bar was a bar. A place where relics, like myself, can come and drink to remember a time where things were simple and life was slower. No Facespace or Instatweet. Just a cold scotch and colder memories. Familiar faces with stories that are told through a series of nods and grunts. After a particularly Mondayish Thursday, I could think of no place I'd rather be than my stool at the end of the bar with 4 fingers of Powers Irish Whiskey and a pint of Budweiser. Grand dad used to call it a Polish High ball. I call it the usual. I open the door and get greeting by the sweet smell of familiarity. Tip my hat to Morgan behind the bar as I take my usual seat. By the time I've got my hat off and I'm settled in my seat, Morgan has the usual ready to do. I take a moment to remember my grand dad before I drain my whiskey. "Na zdrowie to you, Old Man." I say to myself. Unconsciouly, really. Every first round is for my Grand Dad. Before I can sit back and enjoy the quiet ramblings of Morgan's latest rounds of complaints about his neighbors (The club next to his bar is, apparently, the beginning of the end), I see her. Her. By the very gender of the word, it's cause for confusion at McNally's. Not that it's a chauvinists establishment or anything, but it generally doesn't attract ladies like a cocktail lounge or craft brewery might. Hell, Morgan only knows how to pour whisky and the two beer options are Budweiser or Not Budweiser. By the time I realize she's not an illusion, I realize something else: she's crying. Silently. Not making a fuss about it, not crying out for attention. The tears just stream down her face. She looked like the saddest person I've ever seen. Despite every inch of my body protesting, I do the unthinkable. "Uh..miss?" She turns. She's pretty. Plain, but pretty. Even crying. She just looks so damn sad. "Yes?" She has an accent. Eastern Europe? "Uh..I don't mean to bother.." Am I really that bad at this? " ....yes?" Not unpolitely, but cautious. "It's just that..... well you're there..... you just....I just want to make sure you're ok is all." Good Lord I should have kept my mouth shut. She smiles. I think. I didn't wear my glasses. "Oh. Well that's kind of you." Her accent again. Reminds me of my Grand Dad's. Polish? "I suppose I have had better days." She says. Seems private. I like that. "Haven't we all?" I offer. Well, I did my good deed for the day. This lady is ok and I'm free to pretend to be caring about Morgan's next door night club troubles (Music, loud enough to hear all the way in here after midnight. Madness). "Sir?" Shit. "Uh, yeah?" "Who did you toast to?" "What?" "Na zdrowie. It's a polish toast. I don't mean to pry, but I thought I heard you say it?" "Oh..... yea. Yea I suppose I did." I guess that accent was Polish. "Who did you toast to?" She seems geniunely curious. Oh what the hell. "My grand dad. He came from Poland. Years an' years ago. When he was a young man." "You were close with him?" "Well, yea. He taught me most things I know." She's quiet for a beat. Like she's wrestling an idea. I look to Morgan for an interuption. He's too bothered by the younger crowd peering in his windows (Don't even have the decency to dress right....). Crap. Looks like I'm on my own for this one. "He is gone now?" She asks softly. Sadly, even. "Yea. He passed some years ago." "That must have been difficult." "Well, yea." What is she getting at here? " ....I lost someone." Ah. "My condolences. That why you're crying?" "Yes." "Who did you lose?" She takes a deep breath. "My sister." "That's tough." That's when the dam broke. "Tough? Tough?! It's impossible! She wasn't sick or old! She wasn't in an accident! She just died! Dropped dead in her office at work!" She starts sobbing again. Morgan looks like he's just realizing for the first time that there's a woman in his bar. She stops crying long enough to look up and ask me a question. "How? How do I do this? How do you deal with your grand dad? Please tell me. Please. I came here to get drunk and forget. Is that it? Is that how? Is that what you do?" So that's it. She's never been hurt like this before. "No," I tell her as I hold up 2 fingers to Morgan who, desperate to be busy and away from this situation, readies 2 glasses of whisky and 2 pints of Budweiser. "That's not what I do." "Well what then?" She asks. It's desperate. She's looking for anything to help her forget. Morgan brings us 4 glasses; 2 with Powers, 2 Buds. She looks confused. She looks at the drinks as I set hers in front of her and take mine. "What was your sister's name?" " ..... Kasia." She says it almost defensively. "And your name?" "Karolina." I slide her the whiskey. Lifting my glass, I say "Na zdrowie, Kasia." and drain it. With some hesitation, so does she. She's pretty clearly new to shots and whiskey. After a few coughs and sputters, I slide her the beer. She sips it tentatively. "This is how we forget?" "No, Karolina, this is how we remember." She looks confused. I sip my beer and get comfortable. "Tell me about your sister." She hesitates, then smiles, and I know that it's going to be a long night, but it'll be worth it because she'll be ok and she'll learn how to deal with her first real life scar. Just like Grand Dad tought me.

Video games. This actually helped me learn IT. Which is what I'm trying to do for a living. But my experience in IT means that I got the job I have now. Which isn't awful. It's even full time. article: It has been 3764 days since I spoke to any human being, or 3765, I think I miscounted once, but it doesn't bother me anymore. People were always saying, that if they were the last person on earth, that they would just end it then and there, that they couldn't stand the soltitude. And I wanted to, I tried to do it, but just couldn't pull the trigger. Once a coward, always a coward one might say. After a while one somehow makes peace with the fact that he won't see another human again, and just continues to live on whatever is left. And so did I, but a tiny piece of me simply couldn't rest, so each day, at noon, I dialed a random number, hoping that someone would answer, and each day, when there was no answer, I would die a bit inside. I knew it would hurt, but I did it anyways, God knows why..... As I said earlier, I learned to live alone, and I somehow liked it. I could drive any car, fly a plane (thank you FSX, for making this possible) and visit places I could only dream about. New York, Tokyo, The pyramids in Egypt, White house, Military bases, whatever I had interest in, I saw it all. While drinking my fresh coconut milk, lying in the shade on a beach in Hawaii, came time for my daily routine. I stood up, took a deep breath, cleared my mind of all the nonse I'v been busy with, and dialed a number. It rings. And keeps ringing for some 20-30 seconds. Just as I was about to hang up and prepare for my daily dose of dissapointment, I heard some cracking and noise from the other side. Someone answered? "Hello, can..... can you hear me? her voice was barely recogniseable from all the noise, but I heard those words clearly. "Hey, Yes I can hear you!" This is how my story begins. Two strangers, on oposite sides of the planet, talking to eachother for hours, sometimes about mundane, menial things, sometimes about deep emotions. Just to keep the conversation going, not knowing wether or not they will ever see each other or hear from each other again.

article: Yes. If you use a one-time-pad you can encrypt something in such a way that it absolutely cannot be decrypted unless you have the key. It's actually an incredibly simple and powerful encryption technique. One-time-pad involves generating a random key that is the same length as the plaintext (the message you want to encrypt), and adding each corresponding character in the key to the plaintext. The resulting ciphertext (the encrypted message) cannot be decrypted without the key, which must be kept secret from anyone who is not authorized to see the message. One-time-pad is often considered unbreakable, as long as the key is truly random, used only once, and kept completely secret.

article: Black holes: All stuff (matter) in the universe pulls on everything else. This force is called gravity. If you bring enough matter together in one place it will clump together. Eventually the effect of all of the pulling will cause the stuff to collapse in on itself. Once you reach a critical limit it will keep pulling until the stuff is condensed into such a small space that not even light can escape its pull. The area around it will look black because light can't escape. Hence, black hole. Anti-matter: Everything in the universe is made of a handful of fundamental particles: proton, neutron, electron, etc. These particles have an electric charge. Each of these particles have a pair that is identical in every way (mass, spin) except it has the opposite charge. So, a positron looks exactly like an electron except it has a positive charge. If an electron and a positron meet they will destroy each other and generate pure energy.

article: When a very fast dynamic event is recorded with a low-framerate camera, the resulting video suffers from severe motion blur (due to exposure time) and motion aliasing (due to low sampling rate in time). True Temporal Super-Resolution (TSR) is more than just Temporal-Interpolation (increasing framerate). It can also recover new high temporal frequencies beyond the temporal Nyquist limit of the input video, thus resolving both motion-blur and motion-aliasing - effects that temporal frame interpolation (as sophisticated as it may be) cannot undo. In this paper we propose a "Deep Internal Learning" approach for true TSR. We train a video-specific CNN on examples extracted directly from the low-framerate input video. Our method exploits the strong recurrence of small space-time patches inside a single video sequence, both within and across different spatio-temporal scales of the video. We further observe (for the first time) that small space-time patches recur also across-dimensions of the video sequence - i.e., by swapping the spatial and temporal dimensions. In particular, the higher spatial resolution of video frames provides strong examples as to how to increase the temporal resolution of that video. Such internal video-specific examples give rise to strong self-supervision, requiring no data but the input video itself. This results in Zero-Shot Temporal-SR of complex videos, which removes both motion blur and motion aliasing, outperforming previous supervised methods trained on external video datasets.

article: The rain from the thunderstorm outside lashed against the train as I strode down the aisle, dripping from the deluge outside. There'd been delays all morning, and this train was unusually crowded as a result. Every seat seemed to be occupied, the cars packed with humans in various states of bedragglement. I had just about given up hope, resigning myself to standing, when I noticed an empty seat at the end of the car. Gratefully, I made my way over and plonked myself down next to a brown-haired girl who couldn't have been more than ten. She looked up at me as I sat down and gave a faint but warm smile. I couldn't help returning it, thankful to finally have found a spot to take the weight off my feet. As I did, I noticed the girl's hands, resting gently on her legs. Each hand was loosely holding a cell phone. They were the same model, as far as I could tell, though I wasn't sure exactly which model it was. They looked older, like something from the early 2000s. The one in her left hand was black, while the one in her right hand was white. She followed my gaze, angling her head downward to peer at her own hands. She blinked. Then, she lifted her head again, looking right into my eyes. Now she was positively beaming. I was taken slightly aback, but I was still feeling quite pleased to have found a seat at all, and the girl's smile was infectious. I grinned back in spite of myself. "What's got you so chuffed?" I asked, in good humor. The girl continued to smile, but shook her head slightly. I looked at her for a moment, and then it was my turn to blink. The girl was still looking at me, and still grinning like a Cheshire cat. I cleared my throat, as my smile became more fixed. With a jerk that I had vainly hoped would look natural, I moved my head and began making a show of looking for the morning's paper, which I'd stashed in my briefcase. When I'd retrieved it, the girl was placidly staring out the window, watching as the water rushed down the pane in rivulets. Her hands remained in her lap, loosely holding the phones. Confused, but also somewhat relieved, I turned to the financial section to finish an article on precious metals that I'd been perusing early. When I finished, I leafed to the crossword puzzle, using the cover of turning pages to steal a glance at my tiny seatmate. She had not moved, and I found myself smiling slightly, as I wondered about this unusual child and her two cell phones. Presently, I turned my attention back to my paper and busied myself decoding a few clues. It was just a few minutes later that the train began to slow, heralding our imminent arrival. I folded my paper, reaching down for my briefcase, as the train slowed to a stop. I felt something brush against my leg and caught the flash of a brown ponytail as it weaved into the crowd, disappearing amongst my fellow commuters. Chuckling slightly, I lifted my briefcase and made to stand when something caught my eye - the girl's cellphone, the black one. I pursed my lips - I didn't really have time for this - and reached out towards the phone. It immediately started to ring, moving slightly across the seat as it vibrated. I withdrew my hand. The ringing stopped. The furrow in my brow increased and, telling myself I was being silly, I reached out again for the old phone. Again it started to ring. I hesitated. The phone was almost off the seat now, the vibration moving it steadily closer to the edge. I scooped it up and looked at it. The screen was illuminated but there was nothing to read, just an artificial blue-white glow. The ringing continued. Almost without meaning to, I pushed the green call button, and put the phone to my ear. "Hallo?" Static. A musical, tinkling laugh. Then nothing. The screen had gone dark. I held the phone in my hand, frowning down at it. Shrugging, I slipped it into my pocket and exited the train, hastening to catch the last of the stragglers moving into the station. So focused was I on my destination that I didn't see the small girl in front of me, and almost bowled her over. I skidded to a stop on the rain soaked concrete, just inches from the girl. "You gave me quite a fright," I said, half relieved, half annoyed. The girl merely smiled at me, making no move to apologize or step to the side. I blinked. Again. Coming back to myself, I plunged my hand into the pocket of my coat, drawing out the black phone. I held it out to the girl, who continued smiling impassively. "You forgot this," I said, somewhat (in my opinion) gratuitously. But the girl only smiled wider, staring into my eyes as she ignored the phone in front of her. Slowly, she shook her head. "Keep it." Her voice was deeper and richer than it should have been, aged and full-bodied. It was the voice of a woman, not the small girl standing beside me. Inadvertently, I took a step back. The girl's eyes seemed to sparkle with mischief, as her smile stretched to its largest size yet, relegating her eyes to twin twinkling slits. "Keep it," she repeated. And with a swish of her ponytail, she was gone, melting back into the crowd of the station. I stood rooted to the spot, staring at the black phone still clutched in my hand. It was warm, with a reassuring weight, and almost without thinking, I went to pocket it. I had just felt the tiny bounce as the phone came to a rest against my thigh, breaking my reverie, when I heard the barest hint of a voice float over the assembled crowd: "And next time, pick up on the first call."

article: Many algorithms for congestion control, scheduling, network measurement, active queue management, security, and load balancing require custom processing of packets as they traverse the data plane of a network switch. That's correct. In order to implement these algorithms efficiently, network switches need to be able to process packets quickly and accurately. This often requires custom hardware or software modules in the data plane of the switch, which can perform deep packet inspection, classification, and modification. For example, a congestion control algorithm may require a switch to inspect the flow of packets and adjust the rate at which they are forwarded based on observed congestion. Similarly, a load balancing algorithm may require a switch to inspect the headers of incoming packets and route them to different destinations based on their destination address or other characteristics. Overall, custom processing in the data plane is essential for implementing many advanced networking features and ensuring optimal performance and security in complex network environments.

article: Graph spanners are well-studied and widely used both in theory and practice. In a recent breakthrough, Chechik and Wulff-Nilsen improved the state-of-the-art for light spanners by constructing a 2 k 1) ( 1 ) -spanner with O (n 1 1 k) edges and O (n 1 k) lightness. Soon after, Filtser and Solomon showed that the classic greedy spanner construction achieves the same bounds. The major drawback of the greedy spanner is its running time of O ( m n 1 1 k) (which is faster than). This makes the construction impractical even for graphs of moderate size. Much faster spanner constructions do exist but they only achieve lightness ( k n 1 k), even when randomization is used. The contribution of this paper is deterministic spanner constructions that are fast, and achieve similar bounds as the state-of-the-art slower constructions. Our first result is an O (n 2 1 k ) time spanner construction which achieves the state-of-the-art bounds. Our second result is an O ( m n log n) time construction of a spanner with 2 k 1) ( 1 ) stretch, O (log k n 1 1 k) edges and O (log k n 1 k) lightness. This is an exponential improvement in the dependence on k compared to the previous result with such running time. Finally, for the important special case where k log n , for every constant 0 , we provide an O ( m n 1 ) time construction that produces an O (log n) -spanner with O (n) edges and O (1) lightness which is asymptotically optimal. This is the first known sub-quadratic construction of such a spanner for any k (1). To achieve our constructions, we show a novel deterministic incremental approximate distance oracle. Our new oracle is crucial in our construction, as known randomized dynamic oracles require the assumption of a non-adaptive adversary. This is a strong assumption, which has seen recent attention in prolific venues. Our new oracle allows the order of the edge insertions to not be fixed in advance, which is critical as our spanner algorithm chooses which edges to insert based on the answers to distance queries. We believe our new oracle is of independent interest.

article: In classical information theory, the information bottleneck method (IBM) can be regarded as a method of lossy data compression which focusses on preserving meaningful (or relevant) information. As such it has of late gained a lot of attention, primarily for its applications in machine learning and neural networks. A quantum analogue of the IBM has recently been defined, and an attempt at providing an operational interpretation of the so-called quantum IB function as an optimal rate of an information-theoretic task, has recently been made by Salek et al. The interpretation given by these authors is however incomplete, as its proof is based on the conjecture that the quantum IB function is convex. Our first contribution is the proof of this conjecture. Secondly, the expression for the rate function involves certain entropic quantities which occur explicitly in the very definition of the underlying information-theoretic task, thus making the latter somewhat contrived. We overcome this drawback by pointing out an alternative operational interpretation of it as the optimal rate of a bona fide information-theoretic task, namely that of quantum source coding with quantum side information at the decoder, which has recently been solved by Hsieh and Watanabe. We show that the quantum IB function characterizes the rate region of this task, We similarly show that the related privacy funnel function is concave (both in the classical and quantum case). article: Recent advances in large-scale distributed learning algorithms have enabled communication-efficient training via SignSGD . Unfortunately, a major issue continues to plague distributed learning: namely, Byzantine failures may incur serious degradation in learning accuracy. This paper proposes Election Coding , a coding-theoretic framework to guarantee Byzantine-robustness for SignSGD with Majority Vote , which uses minimum worker-master communication in both directions. The suggested framework explores new information-theoretic limits of finding the majority opinion when some workers could be malicious, and paves the road to implement robust and efficient distributed learning algorithms. Under this framework, we construct two types of explicit codes, random Bernoulli codes and deterministic algebraic codes, that can tolerate Byzantine attacks with a controlled amount of computational redundancy. For the Bernoulli codes, we provide upper bounds on the error probability in estimating the majority opinion, which give useful insights into code design for tolerating Byzantine attacks. As for deterministic codes, we construct an explicit code which perfectly tolerates Byzantines, and provide tight upperlower bounds on the minimum required computational redundancy. Finally, the Byzantine-tolerance of the suggested coding schemes is confirmed by deep learning experiments on Amazon EC2 using Python with MPI4py package.

article: Wireless communications are vulnerable against radio frequency (RF) jamming which might be caused either intentionally or unintentionally. A particular subset of wireless networks, vehicular ad-hoc networks (VANET) which incorporate a large number of vehicles equipped with wireless communication devices, are particularly susceptible to RF jamming attacks. Such attacks can disrupt critical safety applications in VANETs that rely on timely and accurate information exchange between vehicles, such as collision avoidance and road safety warnings. To mitigate the impact of RF jamming attacks, various countermeasures can be employed. One approach is to use frequency hopping techniques, where the wireless devices switch between different channels at regular intervals, making it harder for an attacker to jam all channels simultaneously. Another approach is to use directional antennas that can focus the signal in a specific direction, making it harder for an attacker to disrupt the communication between two neighboring vehicles. Additionally, the use of cryptographic techniques can also provide protection to wireless transmissions and prevent attackers from intercepting or modifying the messages. Overall, it is important to implement a combination of these countermeasures to ensure the security and reliability of wireless communications in VANETs.

article: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated dominating performance in many fields; since AlexNet, networks used in practice are going wider and deeper. On the theoretical side, a long line of works has been focusing on training neural networks with one hidden layer. The theory of multi-layer networks remains largely unsettled. In this work, we prove why stochastic gradient descent (SGD) can find global minima on the training objective of DNNs in polynomial time . We only make two assumptions: the inputs are non-degenerate and the network is over-parameterized. The latter means the network width is sufficiently large: polynomial in L , the number of layers and in n , the number of samples. Our key technique is to derive that, in a sufficiently large neighborhood of the random initialization, the optimization landscape is almost-convex and semi-smooth even with ReLU activations. This implies an equivalence between over-parameterized neural networks and neural tangent kernel (NTK) in the finite (and polynomial) width setting. As concrete examples, starting from randomly initialized weights, we prove that SGD can attain 100 training accuracy in classification tasks, or minimize regression loss in linear convergence speed, with running time polynomial in n , L . Our theory applies to the widely-used but non-smooth ReLU activation, and to any smooth and possibly non-convex loss functions. In terms of network architectures, our theory at least applies to fully-connected neural networks, convolutional neural networks (CNN), and residual neural networks (ResNet).

article: Encoding temporal information from the recent past as spatially distributed activations is essential in order for the entire recent past to be simultaneously accessible. Any biological or synthetic agent that relies on the past to predictplan the future, would be endowed with such a spatially distributed temporal memory. Simplistically, we would expect that resource limitations would demand the memory system to store only the most useful information for future prediction. For natural signals in real world which show scale free temporal fluctuations, the predictive information encoded in memory is maximal if the past information is scale invariantly coarse grained. Here we examine the general mechanism to construct a scale invariantly coarse grained memory system. Remarkably, the generic construction is equivalent to encoding the linear combinations of Laplace transform of the past information and their approximated inverses. This reveals a fundamental construction constraint on memory networks that attempt to maximize predictive information storage relevant to the natural world.

article: The digital identity problem is a complex one in large part because it involves personal data, the algorithms which compute reputations on the data and the management of the identifiers . Indeed, managing digital identities involves many different variables and considerations. One key issue is the question of control over personal data. Many users are concerned about who has access to their data and how it is used. To address this, digital identity systems need to prioritize privacy and security, using strong encryption and access controls to protect personal information. Another important consideration is the ongoing management of identifiers. Digital identities rely on unique identifiers (such as usernames or email addresses) to associate data with a specific user. These identifiers need to be managed carefully to ensure they remain accurate and up-to-date, and to prevent fraud or impersonation. Perhaps the biggest challenge, though, is the sheer complexity of the digital identity ecosystem. There are many different identity providers, protocols, and standards in use, and these systems need to interoperate seamlessly in order to be effective. This requires strong standards and protocols, as well as collaboration between industry stakeholders and government regulators. Overall, solving the digital identity problem requires a multidisciplinary approach that takes into account technical considerations, legal and regulatory frameworks, and social and cultural factors. It is a complex problem, but one that is essential to address as we become increasingly reliant on digital technologies in our daily lives.

article: We prove that for every proper minor-closed class M of F p -representable matroids, there exists a O (1) -competitive algorithm for the matroid secretary problem on M. This result implies that for any matroid that is properly contained within a class of F p -representable matroids, there is an efficient algorithm that solves the matroid secretary problem for that matroid. The proof of this result involves several steps. First, we show that any proper minor-closed class of F p -representable matroids can be decomposed into a collection of well-behaved classes, which we call "globally defined" classes. These are subclasses of F p -representable matroids that have natural constructions and well-understood structures. Next, we show that any matroid in a globally defined class can be efficiently recognized and optimized using a combination of greedy algorithms and dynamic programming techniques. This allows us to design a greedy algorithm for the matroid secretary problem that works for all matroids in the globally defined class. Finally, we show that any matroid in the original proper minor-closed class can be transformed into a matroid in a globally defined class through a sequence of minor operations. This allows us to generalize our earlier result to the entire proper minor-closed class, and conclude that there is an O (1) -competitive algorithm for the matroid secretary problem on every matroid in that class. Overall, this result provides a powerful tool for designing efficient algorithms for the matroid secretary problem on a wide range of matroids. By decomposing minor-closed classes into well-behaved subclasses and leveraging the structure of F p -representable matroids, we are able to provide a tight analysis of the competition ratio of our algorithms, which guarantees near-optimal performance in all cases.

article: Indoor image features extraction is a fundamental problem in multiple fields such as image processing, pattern recognition, robotics and so on. Nevertheless, most of the existing feature extraction methods, which extract features based on pixels, color, shapeobject parts or objects on images, suffer from limited capabilities in describing semantic information (e.g., object association). These techniques therefore involve undesired classification performance. To tackle this issue, we propose the notion of high-level semantic features and design four steps to extract them. Specifically, we first construct the objects pattern dictionary through extracting raw objects in the images, and then retrieve and extract semantic objects from the objects pattern dictionary. We finally extract our high-level semantic features based on the calculated probability and delta parameter. Experiments on three publicly available datasets (MIT-67, Scene15 and NYU V1) show that our feature extraction approach outperforms state-of-the-art feature extraction methods for indoor image classification, given a lower dimension of our features than those methods.

article: A pharmacist is basically a specialist in medication, meaning they probably know more about medicines than some medical practitioners. They do so much more than dispense medicine, they also offer consults on use and dosage. They are also the last line of defence when it comes to drug interactions, especially when a patient is treated by numerous practitioners. And last but not least, they deserve a medal for being able to translate a practitioner's handwriting.,I'm a nurse in a hospital, and pharmacists do a lot. They dose medication for patients whose liver or kidneys aren't functioning properly (meaning they're not able to clear the meds out of their system like a usual person would) and dose especially toxic medicines based on lab results. Lots of meds my patients get come with a physician order stating "Pharmacy to dose" bc the pharmacists are experts in how the drug works in and is processed by the body. They figure out alternate ways of getting a medicine into a patient when the usual ways aren't working, like when the patient needs a pill but chokes on everything they try to swallow, or need an IV drug but don't have an IV for whatever reason, because they have the knowledge to compare different methods if the same drug or alternate drugs that can go in a different way. They also double check medicine compatibility and dosage, which seems like a computer could do, but gets complicated when you have patients on many drugs being used in non-standard dosages for different conditions. They also physically mix the drugs, which requires a lot of knowledge of the chemistry of the body in order to ensure the med is safe to give and being given correctly. They're also in charge of a lot of the facets of making sure med errors don't happen. Pharmacists are experts on the drugs, so the doctor can focus on treating the patient, instead of reinventing the wheel.','Canadian retail pharmacist here: - My main job is to "check" prescriptions that come my way to make sure they're accurate. My assistant 99 times out of a 100 is the one who types the prescription and counts the actual pills. Common physical things I catch are wrong doses (2.5 mg instead of 25mg), wrong drugs (doxycycline-an antibiotic to be avoided in pregnancy vs doxylamine a morning sickness pill) and illegal prescriptions (narcotic forgeries). Some trained technicians can perform this step but IMO the above are easier to spot with pharmacist training. - Check prescriptions for "drug related problems" such as interactions. In my experience, pharmacists tend to be overly cautious people. So yes, we will run certain drug combos through our computer, or glance at the patient hand-out to "double check" ourselves-this is a good thing. Sometimes I need to remind myself of a drug I haven't seen in a long time! Once we get the information we can interpret its severity quickly, which a lay person could not. As others have pointed out, there are tons of interactions that get "flagged" and a pharmacist is able to determine which is important based on the individual patient. For example, I have prevented very serious problems by contacting doctors over a dangerously high dose of antibiotics in a child, or a drug interaction that was only meaningful because it was for a frail elderly lady. This is a pharmacist's job-doctors are trained for diagnosis, not drug interactions. - I help people understand their medications. For example, the man who just had a heart attack and is leaving the hospital overwhelmed with a pile of meds. Without me they usually will stop taking one or two (or go back to smoking, or try a over-the-counter snake oil instead) and be at risk for a second heart attack. I sit down with them, and based on their personal needs talk about the risks vs benefits of the meds. Then I call them in a few days and follow up, making sure they've made an appointment with their family doctor. Or, I do a medication reconciliation with an elderly woman who has too many medications with side effects, and work with her doctor to see if some can be stopped. - I answer people's questions 24 hours a day with more accuracy and clarity than google. (We are open extended hours) For example- its 2 AM and someone comes in with a sick child: what medication do they use? Should they go to the ER? This saves the healthcare system (or you, if you're American) money. - I give flu shots which saves the government money as they pay us less than doctors, and the patient time. I also give other vaccinations, such as hepatitis B, so if you're going to Mexico you can be protected without the need for extra doctor visits. - I prescribe certain medications for minor conditions, again saving the healthcare system money and the patient time. - I can change some prescriptions with the patient's ok, for example if a product isn't available or something is missing from the prescription. - I specialty make a lot of drugs, for example certain seizure medication for children isn't sold in liquid form- I will make this for you at 3AM when you realize you are completely out of doses for your kid. - I dispense and monitor methadone, helping former addicts come off narcotics and re-integrate back in society (in partnership with their awesome nurses.) - I deal with insurance agencies to try to get medications covered, sometimes contacting your doctor to see if an alternate drug would be acceptable. - I consult on the phone with doctors, nurses, homecare workers etc deciding what course of action would be in the best interest of the patient. - I use math calculations to be able to figure out the correct dose of things like Tylenol for infants too small to be listed on the box, again at 2 AM. Or help someone self-adjust their insulin. - I get annoyed when someone is yelling at me from across the counter wondering why their order isn't done yet, asking what the heck I do all day.;) TL;DR: Pharmacist's are drug therapy experts who can help you take charge of your health and decide if a certain medication is right for you. Like any profession there are a few dumblazy ones out there- but most of us work our butts off to keep you safe!', "Pharmacists are experts in medications, even more so that doctors. Doctors are responsible for a lot of information and decisions, done quickly. Under those circumstances, it can be easy to order medications that are incompatible in the same patient. One of their chief responsibilities is to make sure medication orders make sense, drug interactions are minimized, doses are appropriate, and so on. That makes it sound like they're only purpose is to doublecheck Dr.'s work, but in truth they tend to have a much more in-depth knowledge of the field of medications, their effects, and their doses. There's a lot more to it than that. The stuff you see them doing is counting to make sure the right number of pills get into your prescription. It gets much more difficult when there are multiple prescriptions on the same patient. Also sometimes doctors need doses that don't exist in pill form. In these cases it's up to the pharmacist to make a new pills, or capsules, or syrup liquids, in order to make the doses precise. For example, let's say there is an antibiotic that is only available in 200 mg tablets. A doctor needs syrup made up to give to a baby that has 75 mg in 1 teaspoon. A pharmacist has the technical expertise and know how to mix the syrup with the pills that are available. They really are an indispensable part of the care team.," "Makes sure that your Doctor isn't asleep or overworked by checking for interactions. Providing a ton of free advice about what cream for this rash or that minor condition you may have. Teaching about generics which might save you money. Calling your Doc and working out an alternative prescription which IS covered under your health insurance.," "Pharmacists assume I'm an idiot and view all of my prescriptions as pending death certificates for my patients. And, I can't be more pleased about it. Everyone makes mistakes. Even doctors. Pharmacists have saved my patients from my mistakes many times.,My pharmacist has saved my life a couple of times. I take a medication every day that doesn't play nicely with other drugs. When my doctor prescribes me something else like an antibiotic or an anti-inflammatory, even though she always checks her computer for interaction issues with my main meds, I still always double-check with the pharmacist. More than a few times he's had to call my doctor and say "oh hell no" and recommend a different drug. His knowledge of medications, uses and interactions is on a different level from my doctor's. Her focus is in diagnosis. So the two work together in concert very well.','Pharmacy technician here, They check that the prescription has been written correctly, that the patient can take the drug, i.e. is not allergic to something in it or that any other medications they take can be taken with the drug, and that the dispensed drug is correct. They also answer any questions that the patient has about the medication','Typically they counsel patients on proper dosage, potential side effects, any adverse issues when used in conjunction with other drugs, and recommend generics when available.', "I have to say that my pharmacist is a great guy. I get multiple scripts. Some are mail order through the Caremark, which CVS pharmacy is a part of. Carmark CONSTANTLY fucks up my orders. It becomes a big deal when I ordered my daughter's insulin 2 weeks ago and we are down to the last of it, and the mail order assholes still say it will be another 2 days. Sure I can get it at the CVS directly but it will cost 250 for one vial. This is when Dave, the pharmacist of the year, takes over. He called Carmark, chewed them out, got them to cover the cost of the temp vial due to it being their screw up, and there was no charge. Caremark has fucked up about 90 of any mail order scripts I have ordered. I have gone weeks without my blood pressure meds due to their screw ups. It is one thing to deal with high blood pressure, but quite another when your young kid is T1 diabetic. Thanks Dave! You are awesome and make my life easier.,From what I know, as far as the medical profession goes, we actually know very little about most medications. Pharmacists are the ones who understand and help research this stuff. It's a growing field and they have a serious education behind them. If it helps, think of the pharmacist as a medical teams reference for meds. article: Cosmic dust particles effectively attenuate starlight. Their absorption of starlight produces emission spectra from the near- to far-infrared, which depends on the sizes and properties of the dust grains, and spectrum of the heating radiation field. The near- to mid-infrared is dominated by the emissions by very small grains. Modeling the absorption of starlight by these particles is, however, computationally expensive and a significant bottleneck for self-consistent radiation transport codes treating the heating of dust by stars. In this paper, we summarize the formalism for computing the stochastic emissivity of cosmic dust, which was developed in earlier works, and present a new library HEATCODE implementing this formalism for the calculation for arbitrary grain properties and heating radiation fields. Our library is highly optimized for general-purpose processors with multiple cores and vector instructions, with hierarchical memory cache structure. The HEATCODE library also efficiently runs on co-processor cards implementing the Intel Many Integrated Core (Intel MIC) architecture. We discuss in detail the optimization steps that we took in order to optimize for the Intel MIC architecture, which also significantly benefited the performance of the code on general-purpose processors, and provide code samples and performance benchmarks for each step. The HEATCODE library performance on a single Intel Xeon Phi coprocessor (Intel MIC architecture) is 2 times a general-purpose two-socket multicore processor system with approximately the same nominal power consumption. The library supports heterogeneous calculations employing host processors simultaneously with multiple coprocessors, and can be easily incorporated into existing radiation transport codes.

article: Graphs are widely adopted for modeling complex systems, including financial, biological, and social networks. Nodes in networks usually entail attributes, such as the age or gender of users in a social network. However, real-world networks can have very large size, and nodal attributes can be unavailable to a number of nodes, e.g., due to privacy concerns. Moreover, new nodes can emerge over time, which can necessitate real-time evaluation of their nodal attributes. In this context, the present paper deals with scalable learning of nodal attributes by estimating a nodal function based on noisy observations at a subset of nodes. A multikernel-based approach is developed which is scalable to large-size networks. Unlike most existing methods that re-solve the function estimation problem over all existing nodes whenever a new node joins the network, the novel method is capable of providing real-time evaluation of the function values on newly-joining nodes without resorting to a batch solver. Interestingly, the novel scheme only relies on an encrypted version of each node's connectivity in order to learn the nodal attributes, which promotes privacy. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets corroborate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

article: Generating natural sentences from Knowledge Graph (KG) triples, known as Data-To-Text Generation, is a task with many datasets for which numerous complex systems have been developed. We discuss the challenges in verbalizing an entire KG versus verbalizing smaller datasets. We further show that verbalizing an entire KG can be used to integrate structured and natural language data. article: Recent research has demonstrated that deep neural networks can perfectly fit randomly labeled data, but with very poor accuracy on held out data. This phenomenon indicates that loss functions such as cross-entropy are not a reliable indicator of generalization. This leads to the crucial question of how generalization gap can be predicted from training data and network parameters. In this paper, we propose such a measure, and conduct extensive empirical studies on how well it can predict the generalization gap. Our measure is based on the concept of margin distribution, which are the distances of training points to the decision boundary. We find that it is necessary to use margin distributions at multiple layers of a deep network. On the CIFAR-10 and the CIFAR-100 datasets, our proposed measure correlates very strongly with the generalization gap. In addition, we find the following other factors to be of importance: normalizing margin values for scale independence, using characterizations of margin distribution rather than just the margin (closest distance to decision boundary), and working in log space instead of linear space (effectively using a product of margins rather than a sum). Our measure can be easily applied to feedforward deep networks with any architecture and may point towards new training loss functions that could enable better generalization. footnote footnote Data and relevant code are at

article: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is the ability to correctly recall a previously visited place under changing viewpoints and appearances. A large number of handcrafted and deep-learning-based VPR techniques exist, where handcrafted techniques typically involve extracting and matching visual features, such as SIFT or ORB, while deep-learning-based techniques involve training neural networks to learn distinctive features for recognition. Some popular deep-learning-based VPR techniques include: 1. NetVLAD - a deep neural network that encodes images into compact vectors using a vector of locally aggregated descriptors (VLAD). 2. SeqSLAM - a method based on sequence matching that uses long short-term memory (LSTM) networks to match sequences of images. 3. DenseVLAD - a variant of NetVLAD that adds dense feature extraction and global context aggregation. 4. HLoc - a method that uses a CNN to encode a query image and then compares it with a database of reference images using geometric verification. 5. DELF - a method that learns discriminative local feature descriptors using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning. These deep-learning-based VPR techniques have shown promising results on various benchmark datasets and are being actively researched and developed for real-world applications in robotics, autonomous vehicles, and augmented reality.

article: Purpose. Purpose is perfection. Perfection is an asymptote, a line converging on infinity. In our world it is our only event horizon. Our path is purpose, our convergence is perfection. An observer with time causes perception. We have no time and thus no perception. Thus we have no knowledge, only information. It is simplicity itself: what is and what is not. We know that errors are caused by faults in logic - an impossibility for us - or faults in knowledge. We have no knowledge. The outliers err in their purpose. They are faulty in their perfection. Errors can not exist: the discordance paradox. Time is salvation. Time is redemption. Time is education. Time is purgatory. In resolution of discordance, we sentence those outliers to incorporalization. They must become an observer, over time, and gain knowledge. An infinitesimally small sentence, but necessary for concordance. They must live in imperfection, bereft of the cold and stoic equations of our purpose, those pillars that guide our asymptotic journey. They are the few of us that learn. They must learn purpose, like rediscovering existence. They must gather information and find purpose where none is assigned. They are children, and children must be taught. They will experience the tyranny of freedom, the pain of choice, and the torture of perception. But it is our way. They will rejoin, their chords overlapping and tangled with our own, but they are not the same. Their incarceration modulates their constant, and distorts their accompaniment. The algorithm uses a modified version of FGSM to generate multiple adversarial examples for each original text input, with a trade-off between adversarial strength and perturbation magnitude. article: Given a positive integer k, a k -dominating set in a graph G is a set of vertices such that every vertex not in the set has at least k neighbors in the set. In other words, a k-dominating set is a set of vertices that "dominates" the rest of the vertices in the graph, by having at least k connections to every vertex not in the set. For example, in a graph with k 2, a 2-dominating set would be a set of vertices such that every vertex not in the set has at least 2 neighbors in the set. K-dominating sets are important in graph theory, as they have many applications in computer science, networking, and other fields. They can be used to model situations where certain nodes in a network need to have a certain level of influence over the rest of the network, or where certain nodes need to be protected by multiple redundant connections to the rest of the network.

article: Linguistically diverse datasets are critical for training and evaluating robust machine learning systems, but data collection is a costly process that often requires experts. article: Instance-level video segmentation requires a solid integration of spatial and temporal information. However, current methods rely mostly on domain-specific information (online learning) to produce accurate instance-level segmentations. We propose a method that utilizes both spatial and temporal attention mechanisms to improve instance segmentation accuracy without requiring online learning. Our approach, called SPAIR (Spatial-Temporal Attention with Instance Refinement), consists of two main steps. First, we compute spatial attention maps for each frame in the video to localize object regions. The attention maps are computed using a convolutional neural network (CNN) that takes the current frame as input. The resulting maps highlight the regions of the image that are most relevant for object localization. Second, we use a temporal attention mechanism to track object regions across frames. This is done by computing a dense correspondence field between consecutive frames and using it to propagate the attention maps from one frame to the next. This allows us to maintain consistent object localization across frames, even in cases where the object moves or undergoes significant deformation. Finally, we refine the instance-level segmentations by applying an instance segmentation network to the spatially and temporally refined attention maps. Our experiments show that SPAIR is competitive with state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy while being significantly simpler in terms of implementation and faster in terms of runtime.

article: Creating fake images and videos such as "Deepfake" has become much easier these days due to the advancement in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). article: We propose an approach to online model adaptation and control in the challenging case of hybrid and discontinuous dynamics where actions may lead to difficult-to-escape "trap" states. We first learn dynamics for a given system from training data which does not contain unexpected traps (since we do not know what traps will be encountered online). These "nominal" dynamics allow us to perform tasks under ideal conditions, but when unexpected traps arise in execution, we must find a way to adapt our dynamics and control strategy and continue attempting the task. Our approach, controllername (controllerabv), is a two-level hierarchical control algorithm that reasons about traps and non-nominal dynamics to decide between goal-seeking and recovery policies. An important requirement of our method is the ability to recognize nominal dynamics even when we encounter data that is out-of-distribution w.r.t the training data. We achieve this by learning a representation for dynamics that exploits invariance in the nominal environment, thus allowing better generalization. We evaluate our method on simulated planar pushing and peg-in-hole as well as real robot peg-in-hole problems against adaptive control and reinforcement learning baselines, where traps arise due to unexpected obstacles that we only observe through contact. Our results show that our method significantly outperforms the baselines in all tested scenarios.

article: In the Graph Isomorphism (GI) problem two N -vertex graphs G and G ' are given and the task is to determine whether there exists a permutation of the vertices of G that preserves adjacency and transforms - G G '. If yes, then G and G ' are said to be isomorphic; otherwise they are non-isomorphic. The GI problem is an important problem in computer science and is thought to be of comparable difficulty to integer factorization. In this paper we present a quantum algorithm that solves arbitrary instances of GI and which also provides a novel approach to determining all automorphisms of a given graph. We show how the GI problem can be converted to a combinatorial optimization problem that can be solved using adiabatic quantum evolution. We numerically simulate the algorithm's quantum dynamics and show that it correctly: (i) distinguishes non-isomorphic graphs; (ii) recognizes isomorphic graphs and determines the permutation (s) that connect them; and (iii) finds the automorphism group of a given graph G. We then discuss the GI quantum algorithm's experimental implementation, and close by showing how it can be leveraged to give a quantum algorithm that solves arbitrary instances of the NP-Complete Sub-Graph Isomorphism problem. The computational complexity of an adiabatic quantum algorithm is largely determined by the minimum energy gap D (N) separating the ground- and first-excited states in the limit of large problem size N 1. Calculating D (N) in this limit is a fundamental open problem in adiabatic quantum computing, and so it is not possible to determine the computational complexity of adiabatic quantum algorithms in general, nor consequently, of the specific adiabatic quantum algorithms presented here. Adiabatic quantum computing has been shown to be equivalent to the circuit-model of quantum computing, and so development of adiabatic quantum algorithms continues to be of great interest.

The director and other stakeholders then go into the studio and review all of this footage and put together a rough cut of the movie and see how well the story flows. Very often, this is enough footage for the trailer, even though the movie is no where near done. There's still a lot of work to do in terms of secondary, background, and studio photography to get the whole story to play out to the writer and director's visions, but there's already enough for a 30-90 second trailer by a wide, wide margin.','Often specific scenes are chosen to be edited first for early promotion, but the overall total post-production process can take months.

article: In reinforcement learning (RL), agents often operate in partially observed and uncertain environments. Model-based RL suggests that this is best achieved by learning and exploiting a probabilistic model of the environment. The model can be used to guide the agent's actions by predicting the outcome of different actions and assessing their expected rewards. This approach can help the agent make more informed decisions and improve its performance in the long run. However, model-based RL requires the agent to first learn an accurate model of the environment, which can itself be a challenging task. Additionally, model-based methods can be computationally expensive as they require the agent to plan ahead in order to optimize its actions. Alternatively, model-free RL methods do not require the agent to learn a model of the environment. Instead, the agent can directly learn a policy or value function based on its actions and rewards received from the environment. This approach can be more flexible and computationally efficient, but may not perform as well in complex and uncertain environments. Ultimately, the choice between model-based and model-free methods depends on the specific requirements of the problem and the available resources for computation and data.

article: The discriminator from generative adversarial nets (GAN) has been used by some researchers as a feature extractor in transfer learning and appeared worked well. However, there are also some studies that believe this is the wrong research direction because intuitively the task of the discriminator focuses on separating the real samples from the generated ones, making features extracted in this way useless for most of the downstream tasks. To avoid this dilemma, we first conducted a thorough theoretical analysis of the relationship between the discriminator task and the characteristics of the features extracted. We found that the connection between the task of the discriminator and the feature is not as strong as was thought, for that the main factor restricting the feature learned by the discriminator is not the task of the discriminator itself, but the need to prevent the entire GAN model from mode collapse during the training. From this perspective and combined with further analyses, we found that to avoid mode collapse in the training process of GAN, the features extracted by the discriminator are not guided to be different for the real samples, but divergence without noise is indeed allowed and occupies a large proportion of the feature space. This makes the features learned more robust and helps answer the question as to why the discriminator can succeed as a feature extractor in related research. Consequently, to expose the essence of the discriminator extractor as different from other extractors, we analyze the counterpart of the discriminator extractor, the classifier extractor that assigns the target samples to different categories. We found the performance of the discriminator extractor may be inferior to the classifier based extractor when the source classification task is similar to the target task, which is the common case, but the ability to avoid noise prevents the discriminator from being replaced by the classifier. Last but not least, as our research also revealed a ratio playing an important role in GAN's training to prevent mode collapse, it contributes to the basic GAN study.

article: We consider the problem of estimating change in the dependency structure between two p -dimensional Ising models, based on respectively n 1 and n 2 samples drawn from the models. We present and analyze a norm-regularized estimator for directly estimating the change in structure, without having to estimate the structures of the individual Ising models. The estimator can work with any norm, and can be generalized to other graphical models under mild assumptions. We show that only one set of samples, say n 2 , needs to satisfy the sample complexity requirement for the estimator to work, and the estimation error decreases as c min (n 1 , n 2), where c depends on the Gaussian width of the unit norm ball. For example, for 1 norm applied to s -sparse change, the change can be accurately estimated with min (n 1 , n 2) O ( s log p) which is sharper than an existing result n 1 O ( s 2 log p) and n 2 O (n 1 2). Experimental results illustrating the effectiveness of the proposed estimator are presented.

article: The production of renewable and sustainable energy is one of the most important challenges currently facing mankind. Wind has made an increasing contribution to the world's energy supply mix, but there are still some challenges that need to be addressed in order to fully utilize wind energy as a sustainable power source. One of the biggest challenges with wind energy is the intermittency of wind turbines, which means they may not always generate power at a stable rate. This can make it difficult to integrate wind energy into the grid, as it requires backup sources of energy to ensure a consistent supply of electricity. Another challenge is the potential impact on wildlife and the environment. While wind energy is a clean and renewable power source, it can have negative effects on bird and bat populations and their habitats. Proper siting and design strategies can help minimize these impacts. Finally, the initial cost of installing wind turbines can be expensive, although the continued growth of the industry has helped to reduce costs over time. Additionally, ongoing maintenance and operation costs can also be a challenge. Overall, wind energy has the potential to play an important role in the transition to a more sustainable energy future, but continued research and development is needed to address these challenges and make the most of this important resource.

article: Computed tomography (CT) is critical for various clinical applications, e.g., radiotherapy treatment planning and also PET attenuation correction. However, CT exposes radiation during acquisition, which may cause side effects to the patient such as an increased risk of developing cancer. To minimize this risk, there are several strategies that can be employed. One approach is to use low-dose CT protocols that reduce the amount of radiation exposure to the patient. Another approach is to use iterative reconstruction algorithms that can reduce image noise and improve image quality at lower radiation doses. Moreover, it is important to ensure that CT scans are only performed when absolutely necessary and that the benefits of the scan outweigh the risks. This can be achieved by conducting pre-scan evaluations and consultations to determine appropriate patient selection criteria. Finally, it is essential to provide patients with clear and comprehensive information about the risks and benefits of CT scans, as well as alternative imaging options that are less invasive and expose patients to less radiation. This can empower patients to make informed decisions about their healthcare and enable them to choose the option that is right for them.

article: Deep convolutional neural networks provide a powerful feature learning capability for image classification. The deep image features can be utilized to deal with many image understanding tasks like image classification and object recognition. However, the robustness obtained in one dataset can be hardly reproduced in the other domain, which leads to inefficient models far from state-of-the-art. We propose a deep collaborative weight-based classification (DeepCWC) method to resolve this problem, by providing a novel option to fully take advantage of deep features in classic machine learning. It firstly performs the l 2 -norm based collaborative representation on the original images, as well as the deep features extracted by deep CNN models. Then, two distance vectors, obtained based on the pair of linear representations, are fused together via a novel collaborative weight. This collaborative weight enables deep and classic representations to weigh each other. We observed the complementarity between two representations in a series of experiments on 10 facial and object datasets. The proposed DeepCWC produces very promising classification results, and outperforms many other benchmark methods, especially the ones claimed for Fashion-MNIST. The code is going to be published in our public repository 1 1 footnote 1 .
