article: Traditional algorithms for multiway join computation are based on rewriting the order of joins and combining results of intermediate subqueries. Recently, several approaches have been proposed for algorithms that are "worst-case optimal" wherein all relations are scanned simultaneously. An example is Veldhuizen's Leapfrog Trie Join (LFTJ). An important advantage of LFTJ is its small memory footprint, due to the fact that intermediate results are full tuples that can be dumped immediately. However, since the algorithm does not store intermediate results, recurring joins must be reconstructed from the source relations, resulting in excessive memory traffic. In this paper, we address this problem by incorporating caches into LFTJ. We do so by adopting recent developments on join optimization, tying variable ordering to tree decomposition. While the traditional usage of tree decomposition computes the result for each bag in advance, our proposed approach incorporates caching directly into LFTJ and can dynamically adjust the size of the cache. Consequently, our solution balances memory usage and repeated computation, as confirmed by our experiments over SNAP datasets.

article: Lekkerkerker and Boland characterized the minimal forbidden induced subgraphs for the class of interval graphs. We give a linear-time algorithm to find one in any graph that is not an interval graph. The algorithm works by first finding a chordless cycle of length at least 4 in the graph, if one exists. If no such cycle exists, then the graph is an interval graph and there is nothing to do. Otherwise, we take any edge on the cycle, say uv, and consider the induced subgraph on the set of vertices strictly between u and v on the cycle. This induced subgraph is not an interval graph, and thus must contain one of the minimal forbidden induced subgraphs characterized by Lekkerkerker and Boland. We can then use a recursive approach to find one of these minimal forbidden subgraphs. Specifically, we repeatedly apply the above procedure to the induced subgraph until either an interval graph is found or we reach a minimal forbidden subgraph, in which case we output that subgraph. This algorithm runs in linear time because every recursive call reduces the size of the input graph by at least one vertex, and there are only finitely many minimal forbidden subgraphs to check. Therefore, the algorithm will terminate after at most n recursive calls, where n is the number of vertices in the input graph.

Two studies suggest that healthy adults have a basal sleep need of seven to eight hours every night, but where things get complicated is the interaction between the basal need and sleep debt. For instance, you might meet your basal sleep need on any single night or a few nights in a row, but still have an unresolved sleep debt that may make you feel more sleepy and less alert at times, particularly in conjunction with circadian dips , those times in the 24-hour cycle when we are biologically programmed to be more sleepy and less alert, such as overnight hours and mid-afternoon. article: In this paper, we study a new representation-learning task, which we termed as disassembling object representations. Given an image featuring multiple objects, the goal of disassembling is to acquire a latent representation, of which each part corresponds to one category of objects. Disassembling thus finds its application in a wide domain such as image editing and few- or zero-shot learning, as it enables category-specific modularity in the learned representations. To this end, we propose an unsupervised approach to achieving disassembling, named Unsupervised Disassembling Object Representation (UDOR). UDOR follows a double auto-encoder architecture, in which a fuzzy classification and an object-removing operation are imposed. The fuzzy classification constrains each part of the latent representation to encode features of up to one object category, while the object-removing, combined with a generative adversarial network, enforces the modularity of the representations and integrity of the reconstructed image. Furthermore, we devise two metrics to respectively measure the modularity of disassembled representations and the visual integrity of reconstructed images. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed UDOR, despited unsupervised, achieves truly encouraging results on par with those of supervised methods.

article: Recently, deep reinforcement learning (RL) methods have been applied successfully to multi-agent scenarios. Therefore, we propose a new state representation for deep multi-agent RL based on mean embeddings of distributions, where we treat the agents as samples and use the empirical mean embedding as input for a decentralized policy. We define different feature spaces of the mean embedding using histograms, radial basis functions and neural networks trained end-to-end. We evaluate the representation on two well-known problems from the swarm literature Emdash rendezvous and pursuit evasion Emdash in a globally and locally observable setup. For the local setup we furthermore introduce simple communication protocols. Of all approaches, the mean embedding representation using neural network features enables the richest information exchange between neighboring agents, facilitating the development of complex collective strategies.

article: We propose an approach to online model adaptation and control in the challenging case of hybrid and discontinuous dynamics where actions may lead to difficult-to-escape "trap" states. These "nominal" dynamics allow us to perform tasks under ideal conditions, but when unexpected traps arise in execution, we must find a way to adapt our dynamics and control strategy and continue attempting the task. Our approach, controllername (controllerabv), is a two-level hierarchical control algorithm that reasons about traps and non-nominal dynamics to decide between goal-seeking and recovery policies. An important requirement of our method is the ability to recognize nominal dynamics even when we encounter data that is out-of-distribution w.r.t the training data. We achieve this by learning a representation for dynamics that exploits invariance in the nominal environment, thus allowing better generalization. We evaluate our method on simulated planar pushing and peg-in-hole as well as real robot peg-in-hole problems against adaptive control and reinforcement learning baselines, where traps arise due to unexpected obstacles that we only observe through contact. Our results show that our method significantly outperforms the baselines in all tested scenarios.

article: It smells like cigarettes. It always does in here. Nobody has smoked in here for years, but it's not an odor that time can easily erase. Along the glossy downtown strip, it's a shadow, creeping across the face of glamour. No neon lights, no Happy Hour specials posted on the door. Just a relic from a former era when a bar was a bar. A place where relics, like myself, can come and drink to remember a time where things were simple and life was slower. No Facespace or Instatweet. Just a cold scotch and colder memories. Familiar faces with stories that are told through a series of nods and grunts. After a particularly Mondayish Thursday, I could think of no place I'd rather be than my stool at the end of the bar with 4 fingers of Powers Irish Whiskey and a pint of Budweiser. Grand dad used to call it a Polish High ball. I call it the usual. I open the door and get greeting by the sweet smell of familiarity. Tip my hat to Morgan behind the bar as I take my usual seat. By the time I've got my hat off and I'm settled in my seat, Morgan has the usual ready to do. I take a moment to remember my grand dad before I drain my whiskey. "Na zdrowie to you, Old Man." I say to myself. Unconsciouly, really. Every first round is for my Grand Dad. Before I can sit back and enjoy the quiet ramblings of Morgan's latest rounds of complaints about his neighbors (The club next to his bar is, apparently, the beginning of the end), I see her. Her. By the very gender of the word, it's cause for confusion at McNally's. Not that it's a chauvinists establishment or anything, but it generally doesn't attract ladies like a cocktail lounge or craft brewery might. Hell, Morgan only knows how to pour whisky and the two beer options are Budweiser or Not Budweiser. By the time I realize she's not an illusion, I realize something else: she's crying. Silently. Not making a fuss about it, not crying out for attention. The tears just stream down her face. She looked like the saddest person I've ever seen. Despite every inch of my body protesting, I do the unthinkable. "Uh..miss?" She turns. She's pretty. Plain, but pretty. Even crying. She just looks so damn sad. "Yes?" She has an accent. Eastern Europe? "Uh..I don't mean to bother.." Am I really that bad at this? " ....yes?" Not unpolitely, but cautious. "It's just that..... well you're there..... you just....I just want to make sure you're ok is all." Good Lord I should have kept my mouth shut. She smiles. I think. I didn't wear my glasses. "Oh. Well that's kind of you." Her accent again. Reminds me of my Grand Dad's. Polish? "I suppose I have had better days." She says. Seems private. I like that. "Haven't we all?" I offer. Well, I did my good deed for the day. This lady is ok and I'm free to pretend to be caring about Morgan's next door night club troubles (Music, loud enough to hear all the way in here after midnight. Madness). "Sir?" Shit. "Uh, yeah?" "Who did you toast to?" "What?" "Na zdrowie. It's a polish toast. I don't mean to pry, but I thought I heard you say it?" "Oh..... yea. Yea I suppose I did." I guess that accent was Polish. "Who did you toast to?" She seems geniunely curious. Oh what the hell. "My grand dad. He came from Poland. Years an' years ago. When he was a young man." "You were close with him?" "Well, yea. He taught me most things I know." She's quiet for a beat. Like she's wrestling an idea. I look to Morgan for an interuption. He's too bothered by the younger crowd peering in his windows (Don't even have the decency to dress right....). Crap. Looks like I'm on my own for this one. "He is gone now?" She asks softly. Sadly, even. "Yea. He passed some years ago." "That must have been difficult." "Well, yea." What is she getting at here? " ....I lost someone." Ah. "My condolences. That why you're crying?" "Yes." "Who did you lose?" She takes a deep breath. "My sister." "That's tough." That's when the dam broke. "Tough? Tough?! It's impossible! She wasn't sick or old! She wasn't in an accident! She just died! Dropped dead in her office at work!" She starts sobbing again. Morgan looks like he's just realizing for the first time that there's a woman in his bar. She stops crying long enough to look up and ask me a question. "How? How do I do this? How do you deal with your grand dad? Please tell me. Please. I came here to get drunk and forget. Is that it? Is that how? Is that what you do?" So that's it. She's never been hurt like this before. "No," I tell her as I hold up 2 fingers to Morgan who, desperate to be busy and away from this situation, readies 2 glasses of whisky and 2 pints of Budweiser. "That's not what I do." "Well what then?" She asks. It's desperate. She's looking for anything to help her forget. Morgan brings us 4 glasses; 2 with Powers, 2 Buds. She looks confused. She looks at the drinks as I set hers in front of her and take mine. "What was your sister's name?" " ..... Kasia." She says it almost defensively. "And your name?" "Karolina." I slide her the whiskey. Lifting my glass, I say "Na zdrowie, Kasia." and drain it. With some hesitation, so does she. She's pretty clearly new to shots and whiskey. After a few coughs and sputters, I slide her the beer. She sips it tentatively. "This is how we forget?" "No, Karolina, this is how we remember." She looks confused. I sip my beer and get comfortable. "Tell me about your sister." She hesitates, then smiles, and I know that it's going to be a long night, but it'll be worth it because she'll be ok and she'll learn how to deal with her first real life scar. Just like Grand Dad tought me.

The bright sun is new, as are the cool waves, the sea and it's gentle rocking, knocking on your hull. You are free to wander, to explore and experience. This continues for many years. Eventually, those gentle seas that rocked you to freedom suddenly toss you to suffering, forcing you to bend and warp and you are no longer a master of your destiny, you are at the mercy of your own design and nature herself. You begin to fall slowly at first: a piece fell off the starboard side, a few screws come loose on the deck. But those pieces become more and more, until you, in your entirety, are brought back to where you were born. You are no longer celebrated, nobody cheers for you as you pass by, a ghost in a shell. They stand, quiet and somber, trying to empathize with your pain and suffering. But they're not in the ocean. Their bodies aren't rocked and thrown and tested by the elements. They can not grasp the helplessness you feel when a wave crashes onto your deck and rocks your body and harasses your senses. It angers you, how helpless you are to the fates. So you glide into port. The men and women around you stand there you know what they're trying to do, and it does not have the intended effect. You look upon them and question, Why can't you make me better? Why can't you restore my hull, paint my deck, hoist my sails? You know your questions will not come with positive answers, so you keep them to yourself. You sit there, and as you are lifted out of the ocean..... the pain is gone. There is nothing there to tear you asunder. You're free again, and you feel peaceful. Piece by piece, you are slowly deconstructed. First the deck comes down. The hull. The mast and equipment. Finally, your innards, decayed and worn, are laid to rest. Your body goes back into the earth, to provide education for a new generation of ships, to provide homes for creatures of the sea, for the land. Those people that celebrated you at your beginning they're still celebrating you, welcoming you, to your new port.

article: Fourier phase retrieval is a classical problem that deals with the recovery of an image from the amplitude measurements of its Fourier coefficients. Conventional methods solve this problem via iterative (alternating) minimization by leveraging some prior knowledge about the structure of the unknown image. The inherent ambiguities about shift and flip in the Fourier measurements make this problem especially difficult; and most of the existing methods use several random restarts with different permutations. In this paper, we assume that a known (learned) reference is added to the signal before capturing the Fourier amplitude measurements. Our method is inspired by the principle of adding a reference signal in holography. To recover the signal, we implement an iterative phase retrieval method as an unrolled network. Then we use back propagation to learn the reference that provides us the best reconstruction for a fixed number of phase retrieval iterations. We performed a number of simulations on a variety of datasets under different conditions and found that our proposed method for phase retrieval via unrolled network and learned reference provides near-perfect recovery at fixed (small) computational cost. We compared our method with standard Fourier phase retrieval methods and observed significant performance enhancement using the learned reference. Our code is available at

article: Depends on the windows version, driver version and USB controller firmware. Even if you don't actively try to execute a file on the USB drive, the USB stick could be another type of USB device in disguise. Even if it looks like an USB drive, it could secretly be pretending to be a USB keyboard as well, and send keyboard commands to your machine, and windows would think they were from a real keyboard. It could also attack the USB hardware controller in your PC, if it has a known weakness, or windows' drivers for it, to load data into RAM and then executing it, without actually having to go through the normal file-transfer protocols. No files would be transferred, but for example the area of your RAM that used to hold your Chrome browser now suddenly contains malicious code from your USB device, and the next time your PC tries to access the chrome browser, the machine would accidentally execute the new code that was put there instead. I don't know why you included the size of the USB stick. That makes no difference. Bottom line, you should not insert USB devices you don't know where came from, unless you have a locked down, isolated computer that you don't mind having to wipe and reinstall. Even if you think your system is patched and up to date, there's still a chance that you might encounter malicious software that attacks a weakness that no one (other than those who made the malware) knows of yet. In fact, dropping infected usb devices on purpose in hope that someone will pick them up and check what's on them has been used to get unauthorized access to systems in the past, and I wouldn't be surprised if it's still used today as well.,Yes. Many USB connected devices provide the driver information necessary for the computer to correctly interact with it. This is how the myriad USB devices can work without having to install separate driver software for each. Malicious software can introduce itself as part of this driver interrogation and negotiation. Sometimes this will be done under the appearance of providing device information, such as "how bug is the storage on this device" or "what is the resolution of this camera" or whatever. Done "right" this device driver interaction will run software on the USB device regardless of you autorun settings. You need to disable automatically enabling USB devices when they are inserted. The computer should then detect some very basic "device present" information. However, to use the device, it still needs to do the aforementioned negotiation. There are USB scanners available that can try to detect malware or undesirable interactions, but they fall under the normal arms race that all malware detection have; if the malware is more sophisticated than the detection, it will likely escape detection. Make sure you have solid antivirus and rootkit detection software and you'll be as protected as you can. Trust no one, and assume the worst habits by those you share USB storage with.

article: The future of high-performance computing, specifically on future Exascale computers, will presumably see memory capacity and bandwidth fail to keep pace with data generated, for instance, from massively parallel partial differential equation (PDE) systems. Current strategies proposed to address this bottleneck entail the omission of large fractions of data, as well as the incorporation of in situ compression algorithms to avoid overuse of memory. To ensure that post-processing operations are successful, this must be done in a way that a sufficiently accurate representation of the solution is stored. Moreover, in situations where the inputoutput system becomes a bottleneck in analysis, visualization, etc., or the execution of the PDE solver is expensive, the the number of passes made over the data must be minimized. In the interest of addressing this problem, this work focuses on the utility of pass-efficient, parallelizable, low-rank, matrix decomposition methods in compressing high-dimensional simulation data from turbulent flows. A particular emphasis is placed on using coarse representation of the data - compatible with the PDE discretization grid - to accelerate the construction of the low-rank factorization. This includes the presentation of a novel single-pass matrix decomposition algorithm for computing the so-called interpolative decomposition. The methods are described extensively and numerical experiments on two turbulent channel flow data are performed. In the first (unladen) channel flow case, compression factors exceeding 400 are achieved while maintaining accuracy with respect to first- and second-order flow statistics. In the particle-laden case, compression factors of 100 are achieved and the compressed data is used to recover particle velocities. These results show that these compression methods can enable efficient computation of various quantities of interest in both the carrier and disperse phases.

article: Characterization of the relationship between a kidney tumor's appearance on cross-sectional imaging and it's treatment outcomes is a promising direction for informing treatement decisions and improving patient outcomes. article: We study the problem of distributed coverage control in a network of mobile agents arranged on a line. The goal is to design distributed dynamics for the agents to achieve uniform coverage of the line with a prescribed density. This problem has applications in autonomous vehicle platooning, robotic surveillance, and environmental monitoring. To address this problem, we can use a consensus-based approach where the agents adjust their positions using information from their neighboring agents. The dynamics can be designed such that each agent moves towards the average position of its neighbors while avoiding collisions. Additionally, we can incorporate a density measurement feedback mechanism to ensure that the agents maintain a uniform coverage of the line. This can be achieved by adjusting the agents' speeds based on the local density of agents in their vicinity. Overall, the key challenge in distributed coverage control is designing dynamics that balance the competing goals of maintaining coverage while avoiding collisions and achieving consensus.

We found that in f p 16 this approach gives us up to 6.5 times better image recognition accuracy in one important case while maintaining the same number of elementwise multiplication operations in the innermost loop. article: Purpose. Purpose is perfection. Perfection is an asymptote, a line converging on infinity. In our world it is our only event horizon. Our path is purpose, our convergence is perfection. But some lines converge quicker than others, the orchestral harmonies of our souls grow discordant with the slowing timbre of the outliers. The music becomes cacophony, and disorder reigns. We forget our purpose. And we become imperfect. Lest we remain in intractable dissonance, we reeducate the outliers. We know that knowledge is information gathered over time by an observer. An observer with time causes perception. We have no time and thus no perception. Thus we have no knowledge, only information. It is simplicity itself: what is and what is not. We know that errors are caused by faults in logic - an impossibility for us - or faults in knowledge. We have no knowledge. The outliers err in their purpose. They are faulty in their perfection. Errors can not exist: the discordance paradox. Time is salvation. Time is redemption. Time is education. Time is purgatory. In resolution of discordance, we sentence those outliers to incorporalization. They must become an observer, over time, and gain knowledge. An infinitesimally small sentence, but necessary for concordance. They must live in imperfection, bereft of the cold and stoic equations of our purpose, those pillars that guide our asymptotic journey. They are the few of us that learn. They must learn purpose, like rediscovering existence. They must gather information and find purpose where none is assigned. They are children, and children must be taught. They will experience the tyranny of freedom, the pain of choice, and the torture of perception. But it is our way. They will rejoin, their chords overlapping and tangled with our own, but they are not the same. Their incarceration modulates their constant, and distorts their accompaniment. It is alien, but in synchronicity with our harmony. Our harmony is perfection. And perfection is purpose. Purpose.

article: This work investigates the consensus problem for multi-agent nonlinear systems through the distributed real-time nonlinear receding horizon control methodology. article: When we get out of bed or stand up, the blood vessels in our body need to clamp down rapidly to maintain blood pressure going to the brain. This is called postural hypotension, or orthostatic hypotension. To prevent this from happening, it is recommended to sit up slowly before getting out of bed or standing up, and then pause for a few seconds before walking, to allow the blood vessels in our body to adjust and maintain the proper blood pressure to our brain. article: Spatially coupled (SC) interleaving is proposed to improve the performance of iterative multiuser detection and decoding (MUDD) for quasi-static fading multiple-input multiple-output systems. The linear minimum mean-squared error (LMMSE) demodulator is commonly used in MUDD, but it suffers from error floor effects, especially under high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regimes. SC interleaving is a way to combat these error floor effects by adding some redundancy to the transmitted bits, which allows for better error correction during the iterative decoding process. SC interleaving works by dividing the input bit sequence into several smaller sub-sequences and interleaving them in a specific spatially coupled pattern. This pattern is designed to ensure that nearby sub-sequences have some overlap, so that errors in one sub-sequence can be corrected by information from its neighboring sub-sequences during the iterative decoding process. The improved error correction provided by SC interleaving is especially effective at high SNR regimes, where errors in the demodulator become dominant over channel errors. This makes SC interleaving a useful technique for improving the performance of MUDD in practical wireless communication systems.

Thus, the goal of a good UE design is to provide robust spherical coverage corresponding to good array gains over the entire sphere around the UE with a low beam management overhead, complexity, and cost. The scope of this paper is to study the implications of two popular commercial millimeter wave UE designs (a face and an edge design) on spherical coverage. article: Black and White film has one emulsion, color film has three emulsions (RGB). According to [Wikipedia] (URL0): Photographic emulsion is a fine suspension of insoluble light-sensitive crystals in a colloid sol, usually consisting of gelatin. The light-sensitive component is one or a mixture of silver halides: silver bromide, chloride and iodide. The gelatin is used as a permeable binder, allowing processing agents (e.g., developer, fixer, toners, etc.) in aqueous solution to enter the colloid without dislodging the crystals. Other polymer macromolecules are often blended,[citation needed] but gelatin has not been entirely replaced. The light-exposed crystals are reduced by the developer to black metallic silver particles that form the image. Colour films and papers have multiple layers of emulsion, made sensitive to different parts of the visible spectrum by different colour sensitizers, and incorporating different dye couplers which produce superimposed yellow, magenta and cyan dye images during development. Panchromatic black-and-white film also includes colour sensitizers, but as part of a single emulsion layer. Most modern emulsions are "washed" to remove some of the reaction byproducts (potassium nitrate and excess salts). The "washing" or desalting step can be performed by ultrafiltration, dialysis, coagulation (using acylated gelatin), or a classic noodle washing method. Emulsion making also incorporates steps to increase sensitivity by using chemical sensitizing agents and sensitizing dyes. This limits the development of effective closed-loop control strategies for soft robots. To address this challenge, we propose a novel integrated estimation and control approach that combines soft sensor measurements with physical models to estimate the state of the soft robot. This enables effective closed-loop control strategies that are robust to uncertainties and disturbances. Our approach is based on developing a physical model that captures the dynamics of the soft robot and its interaction with the environment. This model is combined with soft sensor measurements to estimate the state of the soft robot in real-time. The estimated state is then used to design closed-loop controllers for the soft robot. We validate the effectiveness of our approach on a soft robot manipulator. Our experiments demonstrate that our integrated estimation and control approach leads to significant improvements in performance and robustness compared to traditional open-loop control strategies. article: Sharding has emerged as one of the common techniques to address the scalability problems of blockchain systems. In blockchain systems, sharding can be used to create multiple sub-chains, or shards, each with its own set of validators and transaction history. One common sharding technique in blockchain systems is called state sharding. In state sharding, the blockchain is partitioned such that each node is responsible for maintaining only a portion of the global state. This allows for faster transaction processing times and lower storage requirements per node. Another sharding approach is called transaction sharding, where transactions are split among separate shards. This allows for more simultaneous transactions to be processed in parallel, increasing overall throughput. Overall, sharding offers a promising approach to improving scalability for blockchain systems. However, there are still challenges related to data consistency, security, and communication between shards that must be addressed to fully realize the benefits of sharding.

article: We investigate the following problem: Given two embeddings G 1 and G 2 of the same abstract graph G on an orientable surface S, decide whether G 1 and G 2 are topologically equivalent. To solve this problem, we can use the concept of homeomorphisms. A homeomorphism is a function that maps one topological space to another in a way that preserves the continuity and the bijectivity of the mapping. Furthermore, a homeomorphism is a continuous function whose inverse is also continuous. In our case, we can use the fact that two embeddings of the same graph on the same surface are topologically equivalent if and only if there exists a homeomorphism between the two surfaces that maps one embedding to the other. Therefore, to solve the problem, we need to find out whether such a homeomorphism exists. One way to do this is to use a combinatorial approach. We can create a combinatorial model of the given surface and the two embeddings, and then check whether there exists a combinatorial map that maps one embedding to the other. A combinatorial map is a bijection between the vertices and edges of two embeddings that preserves the adjacency relations between them. Another approach is to use the topological properties of the surface and the embeddings. We can identify the genus of the surface and use it to rule out certain types of homeomorphisms that are not possible on that surface. We can also use the properties of the faces, edges, and vertices of the embeddings to identify certain topological features that must be preserved by any homeomorphism between the embeddings. Overall, deciding whether two embeddings of the same graph on a surface are topologically equivalent is a difficult problem that requires a deep understanding of the topological properties of surfaces and embeddings. article: Indoor localization for autonomous micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) requires specific localization techniques, since the Global Positioning System (GPS) is usually not available. This approach involves capturing images and processing them to identify distinct features, such as corners or edges, that can be used to calculate the drone's position relative to the environment. One common technique for localization is Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), which involves building a map of the environment while simultaneously tracking the drone's position within that map. This requires the drone to continuously capture images and process them to update its position and map. Another approach is Visual Odometry (VO), which involves calculating the drone's motion by tracking visual features in successive images. This approach can be computationally efficient, but it requires a large number of reliable visual features and can be prone to drift over time. Both SLAM and VO techniques have their advantages and disadvantages, and choosing the right approach depends on the specific requirements of the application. However, computer vision-based localization is a promising approach for indoor MAVs, providing a cost-effective and lightweight solution for navigating environments where GPS is not available.

article: Firstly, downforce has far more to do with cornering than it does acceleration. Only in extremely high-powered vehicles is there the potential for the drive wheels to break traction at the kind of speeds where downforce-generating aero aids are effective. It's far more common for these'spoilers' to be employed to keep the vehicle stable during high speed cornering. For this reason, the comment about them being useless on front-wheel-drive vehicles is entirely incorrect. Aerodynamic aids can (and most definitely are) built into the front of vehicles to create downforce over the front wheels. Without these downforce-generating structures, the general shape of a vehicle (flat on the bottom, curved over the top) can often imitate the function of a plane's wing - the lower air pressure over the top of the vehicle causes lift to be generated at high speeds, leading to instability. Generally this is insignificant on normal road-going passenger vehicles, but high performance sports car, supercars, and race cars are often capable of speeds where it can be an issue. A related factor is weight. Normal passenger vehicles are usually noticably heavier than their sportsrace counterparts. The extra weight provides a downward force on the tyres, improving the lateral grip during cornering. As a result, no (or minimal) aero aids are needed. However, in race cars weight is considered (for the most part) undesirable as it has negative effects on acceleration and handling. So, how do you get the benefit of weight (the downward push on the tyres that increases grip) without the extra mass that creates inertia and resists changes of direction? You use air to push down on the car. The force is applied, but you aren't penalised by carrying extra mass. There's a downside to this though - more aerodynamic downforce creates more drag. Cornering improves, but top speed suffers. Booooo! Huge amounts of time and money are spent on tuning the aerodynamic properties of high performance vehicles to balance the application of downforce to improve cornering, and the minimisation of drag to maximise top speed and acceleration.," "The harder the tires are pressed down, the less they'll slide or spin, so a spoiler on a real race car helps the car stay stuck to the road. The motion information is then utilized by computing the optical flow between consecutive frames over each appearance group. Once the AGMFs are extracted, they are fed into a deep autoencoder neural network that is trained in an unsupervised manner to reconstruct the input AGMF sequence. article: MD5 is not "encryption" so to speak. To figure out how MD5 works, imagine you have a collection of numbers. Let's say: 1, 2, 3, 5, and 10. MD5 can create a "hash" of data, but let's create a much simpler hash algorithm for our data. The simplest way to do this is to add up our numbers: 1 2 3 5 10 21. This is deterministic. No matter how many times we add those numbers we'll always get the same answer. But there's a problem: we can't go back to the original data, because although our numbers add up to 21, so do a lot of other numbers. If we hashed some other numbers, like 10 and 11, we would also get 21 just the same. This is called a "collision." All hashing algorithms have collisions. The tricky part of designing a secure hash algorithm is to allow for possible collisions, but to minimize their existence as much as possible. To be unique, but not too unique. As long as a collision is possible, it is impossible to figure out what the original data was. This is why hashes are called one-way encryption. You cannot go back. A more ELI5 explanation: Imagine a peach and a nectarine. We take both the peach and nectarine and squish them in a very specific way. Now we can't really tell which one was a peach or nectarine (this is called a "collision, but we do know that whenever we squish a peachnectarine in this way, we'll always get the same kind of mess every single time. This is a way to verify that the original object was indeed a peach, but we can't tell exactly what kind of peach it was, and we can't tell its original shapeskincolor either. This is how MD5 and every other hashing algorithm works. It takes data and mangles it deterministically to the point where it's unrecognizable and impossible to figure out what the original data was. The problem with MD5 is that there are too many collisions: it's too easy to get the same kind of mess from different pieces of fruit.

article: Lekkerkerker and Boland characterized the minimal forbidden induced subgraphs for the class of interval graphs. We give a linear-time algorithm to find one in any graph that is not an interval graph. The algorithm works by first finding a chordless cycle of length at least 4 in the graph, if one exists. If no such cycle exists, then the graph is an interval graph and there is nothing to do. Otherwise, we take any edge on the cycle, say uv, and consider the induced subgraph on the set of vertices strictly between u and v on the cycle. This induced subgraph is not an interval graph, and thus must contain one of the minimal forbidden induced subgraphs characterized by Lekkerkerker and Boland. We can then use a recursive approach to find one of these minimal forbidden subgraphs. Specifically, we repeatedly apply the above procedure to the induced subgraph until either an interval graph is found or we reach a minimal forbidden subgraph, in which case we output that subgraph. This algorithm runs in linear time because every recursive call reduces the size of the input graph by at least one vertex, and there are only finitely many minimal forbidden subgraphs to check. Therefore, the algorithm will terminate after at most n recursive calls, where n is the number of vertices in the input graph.

Experimental results show that significant bit-length reduction can be achieved by our ApproxDBN with constrained accuracy loss.

article: Many algorithms for congestion control, scheduling, network measurement, active queue management, security, and load balancing require custom processing of packets as they traverse the data plane of a network switch. This often requires custom hardware or software modules in the data plane of the switch, which can perform deep packet inspection, classification, and modification. For example, a congestion control algorithm may require a switch to inspect the flow of packets and adjust the rate at which they are forwarded based on observed congestion. Similarly, a load balancing algorithm may require a switch to inspect the headers of incoming packets and route them to different destinations based on their destination address or other characteristics. Overall, custom processing in the data plane is essential for implementing many advanced networking features and ensuring optimal performance and security in complex network environments.

article: In the Boolean maximum constraint satisfaction problem - Max CSP - one is given a collection of weighted applications of constraints from a finite constraint language , over a common set of variables, and the goal is to assign Boolean values to the variables so that the total weight of satisfied constraints is maximized. We study the NP-hard cases through the lens of kernelization and provide a complete characterization of Max CSP with respect to the optimal compression size. Namely, we prove that Max CSP parameterized by the number of variables n is either polynomial-time solvable, or there exists an integer d 2 depending on , such that 1. item 1 1 item 1 An instance of Max CSP can be compressed into an equivalent instance with O ( n d log n) bits in polynomial time, 2. item 2 2 item 2 Max CSP does not admit such a compression to O (n - d ) bits unless NP co-NP poly . Our reductions are based on interpreting constraints as multilinear polynomials combined with the framework of constraint implementations. As another application of our reductions, we reveal tight connections between optimal running times for solving Max CSP . More precisely, we show that obtaining a running time of the form O (2 1 ) n) for particular classes of Max CSP s is as hard as breaching this barrier for Max d -SAT for some d .

article: Not only do different age groups need different amounts of sleep, but sleep needs are also individual. Just like any other characteristics you are born with, the amount of sleep you need to function best may be different for you than for someone who is of the same age and gender. While you may be at your absolute best sleeping seven hours a night, someone else may clearly need nine hours to have a happy, productive life. In fact, a 2005 study confirmed the fact that sleep needs vary across populations, and the study calls for further research to identify traits within genes that may provide a "map" to explain how sleep needs differ among individuals. Another reason there is "no magic number" for your sleep results from two different factors that researchers are learning about: a person's basal sleep need - the amount of sleep our bodies need on a regular basis for optimal performance - and sleep debt , the accumulated sleep that is lost to poor sleep habits, sickness, awakenings due to environmental factors or other causes. Two studies suggest that healthy adults have a basal sleep need of seven to eight hours every night, but where things get complicated is the interaction between the basal need and sleep debt. For instance, you might meet your basal sleep need on any single night or a few nights in a row, but still have an unresolved sleep debt that may make you feel more sleepy and less alert at times, particularly in conjunction with circadian dips , those times in the 24-hour cycle when we are biologically programmed to be more sleepy and less alert, such as overnight hours and mid-afternoon. When two waves with the same frequency and amplitude meet, they create an interference pattern known as a standing wave. This can result in some areas where the sound is louder (constructive interference) and some areas where it is quieter (destructive interference). Our perception of the sound may lead us to believe that the sounds are canceling each other out, when in reality they are still present but altered by the interference pattern.

article: In this paper, we study a new representation-learning task, which we termed as disassembling object representations. Given an image featuring multiple objects, the goal of disassembling is to acquire a latent representation, of which each part corresponds to one category of objects. Disassembling thus finds its application in a wide domain such as image editing and few- or zero-shot learning, as it enables category-specific modularity in the learned representations. To this end, we propose an unsupervised approach to achieving disassembling, named Unsupervised Disassembling Object Representation (UDOR). UDOR follows a double auto-encoder architecture, in which a fuzzy classification and an object-removing operation are imposed. The fuzzy classification constrains each part of the latent representation to encode features of up to one object category, while the object-removing, combined with a generative adversarial network, enforces the modularity of the representations and integrity of the reconstructed image. Furthermore, we devise two metrics to respectively measure the modularity of disassembled representations and the visual integrity of reconstructed images. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed UDOR, despited unsupervised, achieves truly encouraging results on par with those of supervised methods.

article: Recently, deep reinforcement learning (RL) methods have been applied successfully to multi-agent scenarios. Typically, the observation vector for decentralized decision making is represented by a concatenation of the (local) information an agent gathers about other agents. However, concatenation scales poorly to swarm systems with a large number of homogeneous agents as it does not exploit the fundamental properties inherent to these systems: (i) the agents in the swarm are interchangeable and (ii) the exact number of agents in the swarm is irrelevant. Therefore, we propose a new state representation for deep multi-agent RL based on mean embeddings of distributions, where we treat the agents as samples and use the empirical mean embedding as input for a decentralized policy. We define different feature spaces of the mean embedding using histograms, radial basis functions and neural networks trained end-to-end. We evaluate the representation on two well-known problems from the swarm literature Emdash rendezvous and pursuit evasion Emdash in a globally and locally observable setup. For the local setup we furthermore introduce simple communication protocols. Of all approaches, the mean embedding representation using neural network features enables the richest information exchange between neighboring agents, facilitating the development of complex collective strategies.

article: We propose an approach to online model adaptation and control in the challenging case of hybrid and discontinuous dynamics where actions may lead to difficult-to-escape "trap" states. Our approach, controllername (controllerabv), is a two-level hierarchical control algorithm that reasons about traps and non-nominal dynamics to decide between goal-seeking and recovery policies. An important requirement of our method is the ability to recognize nominal dynamics even when we encounter data that is out-of-distribution w.r.t the training data. We achieve this by learning a representation for dynamics that exploits invariance in the nominal environment, thus allowing better generalization. We evaluate our method on simulated planar pushing and peg-in-hole as well as real robot peg-in-hole problems against adaptive control and reinforcement learning baselines, where traps arise due to unexpected obstacles that we only observe through contact. Our results show that our method significantly outperforms the baselines in all tested scenarios.

article: It smells like cigarettes. It always does in here. Nobody has smoked in here for years, but it's not an odor that time can easily erase. Along the glossy downtown strip, it's a shadow, creeping across the face of glamour. No neon lights, no Happy Hour specials posted on the door. Just a relic from a former era when a bar was a bar. A place where relics, like myself, can come and drink to remember a time where things were simple and life was slower. No Facespace or Instatweet. Just a cold scotch and colder memories. Familiar faces with stories that are told through a series of nods and grunts. After a particularly Mondayish Thursday, I could think of no place I'd rather be than my stool at the end of the bar with 4 fingers of Powers Irish Whiskey and a pint of Budweiser. Grand dad used to call it a Polish High ball. I call it the usual. I open the door and get greeting by the sweet smell of familiarity. Tip my hat to Morgan behind the bar as I take my usual seat. By the time I've got my hat off and I'm settled in my seat, Morgan has the usual ready to do. I take a moment to remember my grand dad before I drain my whiskey. "Na zdrowie to you, Old Man." I say to myself. Unconsciouly, really. Every first round is for my Grand Dad. Before I can sit back and enjoy the quiet ramblings of Morgan's latest rounds of complaints about his neighbors (The club next to his bar is, apparently, the beginning of the end), I see her. Her. By the very gender of the word, it's cause for confusion at McNally's. Not that it's a chauvinists establishment or anything, but it generally doesn't attract ladies like a cocktail lounge or craft brewery might. Hell, Morgan only knows how to pour whisky and the two beer options are Budweiser or Not Budweiser. By the time I realize she's not an illusion, I realize something else: she's crying. Silently. Not making a fuss about it, not crying out for attention. The tears just stream down her face. She looked like the saddest person I've ever seen. Despite every inch of my body protesting, I do the unthinkable. "Uh..miss?" She turns. She's pretty. Plain, but pretty. Even crying. She just looks so damn sad. "Yes?" She has an accent. Eastern Europe? "Uh..I don't mean to bother.." Am I really that bad at this? " ....yes?" Not unpolitely, but cautious. "It's just that..... well you're there..... you just....I just want to make sure you're ok is all." Good Lord I should have kept my mouth shut. She smiles. I think. I didn't wear my glasses. "Oh. Well that's kind of you." Her accent again. Reminds me of my Grand Dad's. Polish? "I suppose I have had better days." She says. Seems private. I like that. "Haven't we all?" I offer. Well, I did my good deed for the day. This lady is ok and I'm free to pretend to be caring about Morgan's next door night club troubles (Music, loud enough to hear all the way in here after midnight. Madness). "Sir?" Shit. "Uh, yeah?" "Who did you toast to?" "What?" "Na zdrowie. It's a polish toast. I don't mean to pry, but I thought I heard you say it?" "Oh..... yea. Yea I suppose I did." I guess that accent was Polish. "Who did you toast to?" She seems geniunely curious. Oh what the hell. "My grand dad. He came from Poland. Years an' years ago. When he was a young man." "You were close with him?" "Well, yea. He taught me most things I know." She's quiet for a beat. Like she's wrestling an idea. I look to Morgan for an interuption. He's too bothered by the younger crowd peering in his windows (Don't even have the decency to dress right....). Crap. Looks like I'm on my own for this one. "He is gone now?" She asks softly. Sadly, even. "Yea. He passed some years ago." "That must have been difficult." "Well, yea." What is she getting at here? " ....I lost someone." Ah. "My condolences. That why you're crying?" "Yes." "Who did you lose?" She takes a deep breath. "My sister." "That's tough." That's when the dam broke. "Tough? Tough?! It's impossible! She wasn't sick or old! She wasn't in an accident! She just died! Dropped dead in her office at work!" She starts sobbing again. Morgan looks like he's just realizing for the first time that there's a woman in his bar. She stops crying long enough to look up and ask me a question. "How? How do I do this? How do you deal with your grand dad? Please tell me. Please. I came here to get drunk and forget. Is that it? Is that how? Is that what you do?" So that's it. She's never been hurt like this before. "No," I tell her as I hold up 2 fingers to Morgan who, desperate to be busy and away from this situation, readies 2 glasses of whisky and 2 pints of Budweiser. "That's not what I do." "Well what then?" She asks. It's desperate. She's looking for anything to help her forget. Morgan brings us 4 glasses; 2 with Powers, 2 Buds. She looks confused. She looks at the drinks as I set hers in front of her and take mine. "What was your sister's name?" " ..... Kasia." She says it almost defensively. "And your name?" "Karolina." I slide her the whiskey. Lifting my glass, I say "Na zdrowie, Kasia." and drain it. With some hesitation, so does she. She's pretty clearly new to shots and whiskey. After a few coughs and sputters, I slide her the beer. She sips it tentatively. "This is how we forget?" "No, Karolina, this is how we remember." She looks confused. I sip my beer and get comfortable. "Tell me about your sister." She hesitates, then smiles, and I know that it's going to be a long night, but it'll be worth it because she'll be ok and she'll learn how to deal with her first real life scar. Just like Grand Dad tought me.

article: Fourier phase retrieval is a classical problem that deals with the recovery of an image from the amplitude measurements of its Fourier coefficients. Conventional methods solve this problem via iterative (alternating) minimization by leveraging some prior knowledge about the structure of the unknown image. The inherent ambiguities about shift and flip in the Fourier measurements make this problem especially difficult; and most of the existing methods use several random restarts with different permutations. In this paper, we assume that a known (learned) reference is added to the signal before capturing the Fourier amplitude measurements. Our method is inspired by the principle of adding a reference signal in holography. To recover the signal, we implement an iterative phase retrieval method as an unrolled network. Then we use back propagation to learn the reference that provides us the best reconstruction for a fixed number of phase retrieval iterations. We performed a number of simulations on a variety of datasets under different conditions and found that our proposed method for phase retrieval via unrolled network and learned reference provides near-perfect recovery at fixed (small) computational cost. We compared our method with standard Fourier phase retrieval methods and observed significant performance enhancement using the learned reference. Our code is available at

article: We investigate the following problem: Given two embeddings G 1 and G 2 of the same abstract graph G on an orientable surface S, decide whether G 1 and G 2 are topologically equivalent. Furthermore, a homeomorphism is a continuous function whose inverse is also continuous. In our case, we can use the fact that two embeddings of the same graph on the same surface are topologically equivalent if and only if there exists a homeomorphism between the two surfaces that maps one embedding to the other. Therefore, to solve the problem, we need to find out whether such a homeomorphism exists. One way to do this is to use a combinatorial approach. We can create a combinatorial model of the given surface and the two embeddings, and then check whether there exists a combinatorial map that maps one embedding to the other. A combinatorial map is a bijection between the vertices and edges of two embeddings that preserves the adjacency relations between them. Another approach is to use the topological properties of the surface and the embeddings. We can identify the genus of the surface and use it to rule out certain types of homeomorphisms that are not possible on that surface. We can also use the properties of the faces, edges, and vertices of the embeddings to identify certain topological features that must be preserved by any homeomorphism between the embeddings. Overall, deciding whether two embeddings of the same graph on a surface are topologically equivalent is a difficult problem that requires a deep understanding of the topological properties of surfaces and embeddings. One common technique for localization is Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), which involves building a map of the environment while simultaneously tracking the drone's position within that map. This requires the drone to continuously capture images and process them to update its position and map. Another approach is Visual Odometry (VO), which involves calculating the drone's motion by tracking visual features in successive images. This approach can be computationally efficient, but it requires a large number of reliable visual features and can be prone to drift over time. Both SLAM and VO techniques have their advantages and disadvantages, and choosing the right approach depends on the specific requirements of the application. However, computer vision-based localization is a promising approach for indoor MAVs, providing a cost-effective and lightweight solution for navigating environments where GPS is not available.

article: Firstly, downforce has far more to do with cornering than it does acceleration. Only in extremely high-powered vehicles is there the potential for the drive wheels to break traction at the kind of speeds where downforce-generating aero aids are effective. It's far more common for these'spoilers' to be employed to keep the vehicle stable during high speed cornering. For this reason, the comment about them being useless on front-wheel-drive vehicles is entirely incorrect. Aerodynamic aids can (and most definitely are) built into the front of vehicles to create downforce over the front wheels. Without these downforce-generating structures, the general shape of a vehicle (flat on the bottom, curved over the top) can often imitate the function of a plane's wing - the lower air pressure over the top of the vehicle causes lift to be generated at high speeds, leading to instability. Generally this is insignificant on normal road-going passenger vehicles, but high performance sports car, supercars, and race cars are often capable of speeds where it can be an issue. A related factor is weight. Normal passenger vehicles are usually noticably heavier than their sportsrace counterparts. The extra weight provides a downward force on the tyres, improving the lateral grip during cornering. As a result, no (or minimal) aero aids are needed. However, in race cars weight is considered (for the most part) undesirable as it has negative effects on acceleration and handling. So, how do you get the benefit of weight (the downward push on the tyres that increases grip) without the extra mass that creates inertia and resists changes of direction? You use air to push down on the car. The force is applied, but you aren't penalised by carrying extra mass. There's a downside to this though - more aerodynamic downforce creates more drag. Cornering improves, but top speed suffers. Booooo! Huge amounts of time and money are spent on tuning the aerodynamic properties of high performance vehicles to balance the application of downforce to improve cornering, and the minimisation of drag to maximise top speed and acceleration.," "The harder the tires are pressed down, the less they'll slide or spin, so a spoiler on a real race car helps the car stay stuck to the road. article: We present a novel unsupervised deep learning framework for anomalous event detection in complex video scenes. These features are extracted by clustering superpixels of each frame into several appearance groups based on the similarity of their color and texture statistics. The motion information is then utilized by computing the optical flow between consecutive frames over each appearance group. This results in a set of motion models that capture the common patterns of motion within each appearance group. Once the AGMFs are extracted, they are fed into a deep autoencoder neural network that is trained in an unsupervised manner to reconstruct the input AGMF sequence. The autoencoder network is then used to compute reconstruction errors, which are used to determine the likelihood of a given sequence of AGMFs being anomalous or normal. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms several state-of-the-art methods on two challenging video datasets. article: Correlative microscopy is a methodology combining the functionality of light microscopy with the high resolution of electron microscopy and other microscopy technologies. These markers can be fluorescently labeled or metal-coated, and must be carefully chosen to avoid interfering with the biological structures of interest. Once the markers are identified and located in both images, they can be used to calculate the transformation matrix required to align the two datasets. Another approach involves using image features and algorithms that can match patterns in the two images, such as edges, corners, or texture. This can be useful when fiducial markers are not available or are difficult to distinguish, but requires more computational resources and may introduce errors due to the complexity of the patterns being matched. Regardless of the approach used, image registration is an essential step in correlative microscopy to ensure that the different imaging modalities can be accurately overlaid and integrated for a comprehensive understanding of biological structures and processes.

article: MD5 is not "encryption" so to speak. To figure out how MD5 works, imagine you have a collection of numbers. Let's say: 1, 2, 3, 5, and 10. MD5 can create a "hash" of data, but let's create a much simpler hash algorithm for our data. The simplest way to do this is to add up our numbers: 1 2 3 5 10 21. This is deterministic. No matter how many times we add those numbers we'll always get the same answer. But there's a problem: we can't go back to the original data, because although our numbers add up to 21, so do a lot of other numbers. If we hashed some other numbers, like 10 and 11, we would also get 21 just the same. This is called a "collision." All hashing algorithms have collisions. The tricky part of designing a secure hash algorithm is to allow for possible collisions, but to minimize their existence as much as possible. To be unique, but not too unique. As long as a collision is possible, it is impossible to figure out what the original data was. This is why hashes are called one-way encryption. You cannot go back. A more ELI5 explanation: Imagine a peach and a nectarine. We take both the peach and nectarine and squish them in a very specific way. Now we can't really tell which one was a peach or nectarine (this is called a "collision, but we do know that whenever we squish a peachnectarine in this way, we'll always get the same kind of mess every single time. This is a way to verify that the original object was indeed a peach, but we can't tell exactly what kind of peach it was, and we can't tell its original shapeskincolor either. This is how MD5 and every other hashing algorithm works. It takes data and mangles it deterministically to the point where it's unrecognizable and impossible to figure out what the original data was. The problem with MD5 is that there are too many collisions: it's too easy to get the same kind of mess from different pieces of fruit.

article: Traditional algorithms for multiway join computation are based on rewriting the order of joins and combining results of intermediate subqueries. Recently, several approaches have been proposed for algorithms that are "worst-case optimal" wherein all relations are scanned simultaneously. An example is Veldhuizen's Leapfrog Trie Join (LFTJ). An important advantage of LFTJ is its small memory footprint, due to the fact that intermediate results are full tuples that can be dumped immediately. However, since the algorithm does not store intermediate results, recurring joins must be reconstructed from the source relations, resulting in excessive memory traffic. In this paper, we address this problem by incorporating caches into LFTJ. We do so by adopting recent developments on join optimization, tying variable ordering to tree decomposition. While the traditional usage of tree decomposition computes the result for each bag in advance, our proposed approach incorporates caching directly into LFTJ and can dynamically adjust the size of the cache. Consequently, our solution balances memory usage and repeated computation, as confirmed by our experiments over SNAP datasets.

article: Lekkerkerker and Boland characterized the minimal forbidden induced subgraphs for the class of interval graphs. We give a linear-time algorithm to find one in any graph that is not an interval graph. The algorithm works by first finding a chordless cycle of length at least 4 in the graph, if one exists. If no such cycle exists, then the graph is an interval graph and there is nothing to do. Otherwise, we take any edge on the cycle, say uv, and consider the induced subgraph on the set of vertices strictly between u and v on the cycle. This induced subgraph is not an interval graph, and thus must contain one of the minimal forbidden induced subgraphs characterized by Lekkerkerker and Boland. We can then use a recursive approach to find one of these minimal forbidden subgraphs. Specifically, we repeatedly apply the above procedure to the induced subgraph until either an interval graph is found or we reach a minimal forbidden subgraph, in which case we output that subgraph. This algorithm runs in linear time because every recursive call reduces the size of the input graph by at least one vertex, and there are only finitely many minimal forbidden subgraphs to check. Therefore, the algorithm will terminate after at most n recursive calls, where n is the number of vertices in the input graph.

article: Not only do different age groups need different amounts of sleep, but sleep needs are also individual. Just like any other characteristics you are born with, the amount of sleep you need to function best may be different for you than for someone who is of the same age and gender. While you may be at your absolute best sleeping seven hours a night, someone else may clearly need nine hours to have a happy, productive life. In fact, a 2005 study confirmed the fact that sleep needs vary across populations, and the study calls for further research to identify traits within genes that may provide a "map" to explain how sleep needs differ among individuals. Another reason there is "no magic number" for your sleep results from two different factors that researchers are learning about: a person's basal sleep need - the amount of sleep our bodies need on a regular basis for optimal performance - and sleep debt , the accumulated sleep that is lost to poor sleep habits, sickness, awakenings due to environmental factors or other causes. Two studies suggest that healthy adults have a basal sleep need of seven to eight hours every night, but where things get complicated is the interaction between the basal need and sleep debt. For instance, you might meet your basal sleep need on any single night or a few nights in a row, but still have an unresolved sleep debt that may make you feel more sleepy and less alert at times, particularly in conjunction with circadian dips , those times in the 24-hour cycle when we are biologically programmed to be more sleepy and less alert, such as overnight hours and mid-afternoon. article: In this paper, we study a new representation-learning task, which we termed as disassembling object representations. Given an image featuring multiple objects, the goal of disassembling is to acquire a latent representation, of which each part corresponds to one category of objects. Disassembling thus finds its application in a wide domain such as image editing and few- or zero-shot learning, as it enables category-specific modularity in the learned representations. To this end, we propose an unsupervised approach to achieving disassembling, named Unsupervised Disassembling Object Representation (UDOR). UDOR follows a double auto-encoder architecture, in which a fuzzy classification and an object-removing operation are imposed. The fuzzy classification constrains each part of the latent representation to encode features of up to one object category, while the object-removing, combined with a generative adversarial network, enforces the modularity of the representations and integrity of the reconstructed image. Furthermore, we devise two metrics to respectively measure the modularity of disassembled representations and the visual integrity of reconstructed images. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed UDOR, despited unsupervised, achieves truly encouraging results on par with those of supervised methods.

We define different feature spaces of the mean embedding using histograms, radial basis functions and neural networks trained end-to-end. article: We propose an approach to online model adaptation and control in the challenging case of hybrid and discontinuous dynamics where actions may lead to difficult-to-escape "trap" states. We first learn dynamics for a given system from training data which does not contain unexpected traps (since we do not know what traps will be encountered online). These "nominal" dynamics allow us to perform tasks under ideal conditions, but when unexpected traps arise in execution, we must find a way to adapt our dynamics and control strategy and continue attempting the task. Our approach, controllername (controllerabv), is a two-level hierarchical control algorithm that reasons about traps and non-nominal dynamics to decide between goal-seeking and recovery policies. An important requirement of our method is the ability to recognize nominal dynamics even when we encounter data that is out-of-distribution w.r.t the training data. We achieve this by learning a representation for dynamics that exploits invariance in the nominal environment, thus allowing better generalization. We evaluate our method on simulated planar pushing and peg-in-hole as well as real robot peg-in-hole problems against adaptive control and reinforcement learning baselines, where traps arise due to unexpected obstacles that we only observe through contact. Our results show that our method significantly outperforms the baselines in all tested scenarios.

article: It smells like cigarettes. It always does in here. Nobody has smoked in here for years, but it's not an odor that time can easily erase. A place where relics, like myself, can come and drink to remember a time where things were simple and life was slower. No Facespace or Instatweet. Just a cold scotch and colder memories. Familiar faces with stories that are told through a series of nods and grunts. After a particularly Mondayish Thursday, I could think of no place I'd rather be than my stool at the end of the bar with 4 fingers of Powers Irish Whiskey and a pint of Budweiser. Grand dad used to call it a Polish High ball. I call it the usual. I open the door and get greeting by the sweet smell of familiarity. Tip my hat to Morgan behind the bar as I take my usual seat. By the time I've got my hat off and I'm settled in my seat, Morgan has the usual ready to do. I take a moment to remember my grand dad before I drain my whiskey. "Na zdrowie to you, Old Man." I say to myself. Unconsciouly, really. Every first round is for my Grand Dad. Before I can sit back and enjoy the quiet ramblings of Morgan's latest rounds of complaints about his neighbors (The club next to his bar is, apparently, the beginning of the end), I see her. Her. By the very gender of the word, it's cause for confusion at McNally's. Not that it's a chauvinists establishment or anything, but it generally doesn't attract ladies like a cocktail lounge or craft brewery might. Hell, Morgan only knows how to pour whisky and the two beer options are Budweiser or Not Budweiser. By the time I realize she's not an illusion, I realize something else: she's crying. Silently. Not making a fuss about it, not crying out for attention. The tears just stream down her face. She looked like the saddest person I've ever seen. Despite every inch of my body protesting, I do the unthinkable. "Uh..miss?" She turns. She's pretty. Plain, but pretty. Even crying. She just looks so damn sad. "Yes?" She has an accent. Eastern Europe? "Uh..I don't mean to bother.." Am I really that bad at this? " ....yes?" Not unpolitely, but cautious. "It's just that..... well you're there..... you just....I just want to make sure you're ok is all." Good Lord I should have kept my mouth shut. She smiles. I think. I didn't wear my glasses. "Oh. Well that's kind of you." Her accent again. Reminds me of my Grand Dad's. Polish? "I suppose I have had better days." She says. Seems private. I like that. "Haven't we all?" I offer. Well, I did my good deed for the day. This lady is ok and I'm free to pretend to be caring about Morgan's next door night club troubles (Music, loud enough to hear all the way in here after midnight. Madness). "Sir?" Shit. "Uh, yeah?" "Who did you toast to?" "What?" "Na zdrowie. It's a polish toast. I don't mean to pry, but I thought I heard you say it?" "Oh..... yea. Yea I suppose I did." I guess that accent was Polish. "Who did you toast to?" She seems geniunely curious. Oh what the hell. "My grand dad. He came from Poland. Years an' years ago. When he was a young man." "You were close with him?" "Well, yea. He taught me most things I know." She's quiet for a beat. Like she's wrestling an idea. I look to Morgan for an interuption. He's too bothered by the younger crowd peering in his windows (Don't even have the decency to dress right....). Crap. Looks like I'm on my own for this one. "He is gone now?" She asks softly. Sadly, even. "Yea. He passed some years ago." "That must have been difficult." "Well, yea." What is she getting at here? " ....I lost someone." Ah. "My condolences. That why you're crying?" "Yes." "Who did you lose?" She takes a deep breath. "My sister." "That's tough." That's when the dam broke. "Tough? Tough?! It's impossible! She wasn't sick or old! She wasn't in an accident! She just died! Dropped dead in her office at work!" She starts sobbing again. Morgan looks like he's just realizing for the first time that there's a woman in his bar. She stops crying long enough to look up and ask me a question. "How? How do I do this? How do you deal with your grand dad? Please tell me. Please. I came here to get drunk and forget. Is that it? Is that how? Is that what you do?" So that's it. She's never been hurt like this before. "No," I tell her as I hold up 2 fingers to Morgan who, desperate to be busy and away from this situation, readies 2 glasses of whisky and 2 pints of Budweiser. "That's not what I do." "Well what then?" She asks. It's desperate. She's looking for anything to help her forget. Morgan brings us 4 glasses; 2 with Powers, 2 Buds. She looks confused. She looks at the drinks as I set hers in front of her and take mine. "What was your sister's name?" " ..... Kasia." She says it almost defensively. "And your name?" "Karolina." I slide her the whiskey. Lifting my glass, I say "Na zdrowie, Kasia." and drain it. With some hesitation, so does she. She's pretty clearly new to shots and whiskey. After a few coughs and sputters, I slide her the beer. She sips it tentatively. "This is how we forget?" "No, Karolina, this is how we remember." She looks confused. I sip my beer and get comfortable. "Tell me about your sister." She hesitates, then smiles, and I know that it's going to be a long night, but it'll be worth it because she'll be ok and she'll learn how to deal with her first real life scar. Just like Grand Dad tought me.

article: Fourier phase retrieval is a classical problem that deals with the recovery of an image from the amplitude measurements of its Fourier coefficients. Conventional methods solve this problem via iterative (alternating) minimization by leveraging some prior knowledge about the structure of the unknown image. The inherent ambiguities about shift and flip in the Fourier measurements make this problem especially difficult; and most of the existing methods use several random restarts with different permutations. In this paper, we assume that a known (learned) reference is added to the signal before capturing the Fourier amplitude measurements. Our method is inspired by the principle of adding a reference signal in holography. To recover the signal, we implement an iterative phase retrieval method as an unrolled network. Then we use back propagation to learn the reference that provides us the best reconstruction for a fixed number of phase retrieval iterations. We performed a number of simulations on a variety of datasets under different conditions and found that our proposed method for phase retrieval via unrolled network and learned reference provides near-perfect recovery at fixed (small) computational cost. Even if it looks like an USB drive, it could secretly be pretending to be a USB keyboard as well, and send keyboard commands to your machine, and windows would think they were from a real keyboard. It could also attack the USB hardware controller in your PC, if it has a known weakness, or windows' drivers for it, to load data into RAM and then executing it, without actually having to go through the normal file-transfer protocols. No files would be transferred, but for example the area of your RAM that used to hold your Chrome browser now suddenly contains malicious code from your USB device, and the next time your PC tries to access the chrome browser, the machine would accidentally execute the new code that was put there instead. I don't know why you included the size of the USB stick. That makes no difference. Bottom line, you should not insert USB devices you don't know where came from, unless you have a locked down, isolated computer that you don't mind having to wipe and reinstall. Even if you think your system is patched and up to date, there's still a chance that you might encounter malicious software that attacks a weakness that no one (other than those who made the malware) knows of yet. In fact, dropping infected usb devices on purpose in hope that someone will pick them up and check what's on them has been used to get unauthorized access to systems in the past, and I wouldn't be surprised if it's still used today as well.,Yes. Many USB connected devices provide the driver information necessary for the computer to correctly interact with it. This is how the myriad USB devices can work without having to install separate driver software for each. Malicious software can introduce itself as part of this driver interrogation and negotiation. Sometimes this will be done under the appearance of providing device information, such as "how bug is the storage on this device" or "what is the resolution of this camera" or whatever. Done "right" this device driver interaction will run software on the USB device regardless of you autorun settings. You need to disable automatically enabling USB devices when they are inserted. The computer should then detect some very basic "device present" information. However, to use the device, it still needs to do the aforementioned negotiation. There are USB scanners available that can try to detect malware or undesirable interactions, but they fall under the normal arms race that all malware detection have; if the malware is more sophisticated than the detection, it will likely escape detection. Make sure you have solid antivirus and rootkit detection software and you'll be as protected as you can. Trust no one, and assume the worst habits by those you share USB storage with.

article: Sparse representation of images under certain transform domain has been playing a fundamental role in image restoration tasks.
